title: Recitation 3
text: using LinearAlgebra, Plots, Distributions, Random

title: Recitation 3
text:
Setup and definitions
Let there be a unit measure of agents in the economy, indexed by \(i\in[0,1]\). As before, assume that agents rank probabilistic sequences of consumption according to:
\[ V^{r}_{i} = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\beta^{t}u(c^{r}_{i,t})\right]\]
where \(\{c^{r}_{i,t}\}_{t=0}^{T-1}\) is the sequence of consumption that agent \(i\) enjoys under regime \(r\in\{A,B\}\). Utilitarian welfare is \(W^{r} = \int V^{r}_{i}di\).
Let \(\mathcal{V}(c)\) be the value of receiving consumption \(c\) for sure in every period: \[\mathcal{V}(c) = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\beta^{t}u(c) = \frac{1-\beta^{T}}{1-\beta}u(c).\] The certainty equivalent \(\bar{c}^{r}_{i}\) solves \(\mathcal{V}(\bar{c}^{r}_{i}) = V^{r}_{i}\) for \(r\in\{A,B\}\), and the average certainty equivalent is \[ \bar{C}^{r} = \int \bar{c}^{r}_{i}di.\] Finally, let \(C^{*}=\int y_{i,t}di = \int c_{i,t}di\) be average consumption in the economy. We assume that the resource constraint always holds and there is no aggregate uncertainty, so \(C^*\) is the same in both regimes, and \(\mathcal{V}(C^*)\) is the welfare that perfect insurance would deliver.

title: Recitation 3
text:
The decomposition
Following the lecture, we split welfare in regime \(r\) into the perfect-insurance benchmark minus two costs: \[ W^{r} = \mathcal{V}(C^{*}) - \underbrace{\Big[\mathcal{V}(C^{*}) - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{r})\Big]}_{\text{cost of imperfect insurance}} - \underbrace{\Big[\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{r}) - W^{r}\Big]}_{\text{cost of unequal certainty equivalents}}\]
The first cost is the loss from risk: even if everyone received the average certainty equivalent, this is lower than average consumption because people face uninsured risk. The second cost is the loss from inequality: certainty equivalents differ across people, and with concave utility this unequal allocation is worth less than giving everyone \(\bar{C}^{r}\).
Since \(C^*\) is unchanged by the policies we consider, the welfare change when moving from regime \(A\) to regime \(B\) is: \[ W^{B} - W^{A} = \underbrace{\Big[\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B}) - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})\Big]}_{\text{insurance}} + \underbrace{\Big[\big(W^{B} - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})\big) - \big(W^{A} - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})\big)\Big]}_{\text{redistribution}}\]

title: Recitation 3
Recitation 1
text:
In this recitation we’re going to work with extracts of the CPS-ASEC from the survey years (1970,1980,1990,2000,2010,2019), which record income for the calendar years (1969,1979,1989,1999,2009,2018). This is a slightly smaller dataset than the version I’m using in class, but will nonetheless capture the same trends.
Our focus in this class will be earned income at the individual and household level, as well as government transfers at the individual and household level. The code below loads the data and creates some variables:

EARN which will be the sum of wages and business income
GOV which will be the sum of welfare, social security income, supplemental security income, the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) and the Child Tax Credit (CTC).

Some other things to note:

These are limited measures of income and if you peruse the variables in IPUMS you will find many more categories.
Wage and business income is subject to top coding and we are not doing anything to solve that issue here, but you should be aware of it. See Heathcote et al. (2023) for one approach to this problem.
Many of the variables we are analyzing are assigned dummy values (e.g. 9999999) if they are missing or not asked for an individual in the survey (“Not in Universe”). One should normally check to make sure these dummy values don’t appear in the final data.
Our measure of transfers does not include in-kind transfers such as Medicaid and Food Stamps (which comprise a very large share of overall transfers).
Income questions in the ASEC refer to the previous calendar year. For example, the 2019 survey records income earned in 2018. We create a variable INCYEAR = YEAR - 1 and deflate using the price index of the income year. All plots below are labelled by income year.
The CPS is not a simple random sample, so we use survey weights. Since our analysis is at the household level, we use the household weight ASECWTH.

With that being said, below is code to load the data and create these variables:

using DataFrames, CSV, StatsPlots, DataFramesMeta, StatsBase
pce = @select(CSV.read("../data/PCE_index.csv",DataFrame), :INCYEAR = :YEAR, :PCE)

data = @chain CSV.read("../data/asec_1970_2019.csv",DataFrame) begin
  @transform :INCYEAR = :YEAR .- 1 #<- income questions refer to the previous calendar year
  innerjoin(pce,on=:INCYEAR) #<- deflate with the price index of the income year
  @transform begin 
    # fill in some missing values and deflat
    :EITC = 100 * coalesce.(:EITCRED,0.) ./ :PCE
    :CTC = 100 * coalesce.(:ACTCCRD,0.) ./ :PCE
    :SSI = 100 * coalesce.(:INCSSI,0.) ./ :PCE
    :WELF = 100 * :INCWELFR ./ :PCE
    :SS = 100 * :INCSS ./ :PCE
    # create the income measures
    :EARN = 100 * (:INCWAGE .+ :INCBUS) ./ :PCE #<- deflate earnings (2017 base)
    end
    @transform :GOV = :EITC .+ :CTC .+ :SSI .+ :WELF .+ :SS
end

Each row of thse data corresponds to an individual in a particular year. For some questions, we may instead be interested in per-person (or equivalized) measures of these income variables. The code below constructs those measures by summing over all individuals within a household, where CPSID is a unique identifier for each household in the survey.

# - gov transfers
# - Create a household-level dataset by summing CPSID (the household ID variable)
house = @chain data begin
    @subset .!ismissing.(:CPSID) #<- drop all obs where this variable is missing (all of 1970)
    @select :CPSID :CPSIDP :INCYEAR :ASECWTH :EARN :GOV :SS :SSI :WELF :CTC :EITC
    stack(Not([:CPSID,:CPSIDP,:INCYEAR]))
    groupby([:INCYEAR,:CPSID,:variable])
    @combine :value = mean(:value)
    unstack([:INCYEAR,:CPSID],:variable,:value)
    disallowmissing #<- unstack allows missing values; we have none
end

Some notes:

Try commenting out the code that follows the stack() command to see how the stack and unstack functions work here.
ASECWTH is the same for everyone in a household, so taking its mean just returns the household weight.
Notice that we are calculating the mean only over individuals 25-64 in the sample (since we dropped everyone else before even pulling the data from IPUMS). Ideally one would want to include other household members as well for this equivalized measure.




How prominently do government transfers feature in the household budget constraint? And how has this evolved over time? Although our measures of income and transfers are not exhaustive, we can use them to get a partial answer to this question.
The code below calculates average transfers relative to average net income for the poorest 20% of households (as measured by per-person household earnings, our variable EARN) and produces a plot. Quantiles and means are weighted by the household weight.

@chain house begin
    groupby(:INCYEAR)
    @transform :q20 = quantile(:EARN,weights(:ASECWTH),0.2) #<- keep bottom 20% in each year
    @subset :EARN .< :q20
    groupby(:INCYEAR)
    @combine begin 
        :gov_share = mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))  / (mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH)) + mean(:EARN,weights(:ASECWTH)))
    end
    @df _ begin 
        plot(:INCYEAR,:gov_share,linewidth=3,xlabel="Income year")
        scatter!(:INCYEAR,:gov_share,legend=false)
    end
end




  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  






























Note that these fluctuations can be caused by fluctuations in the numerator or the denominator. An exercise for you to complete is to verify that these fluctuations are driven by fluctuations in earned income. What event around income year 2009 could explain the large drop in earned income?


Over this time, what sources of government transfers are most prevalent? The code below plots the five sources of transfers that we included in our measure as a fraction of the total in each year.

@chain house begin
    groupby(:INCYEAR)
    @combine  begin 
        :eitc = mean(:EITC,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
        :ssi = mean(:SSI,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
        :welf = mean(:WELF,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
        :ctc = mean(:CTC,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
        :ss = mean(:SS,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
    end
    stack(Not(:INCYEAR))
    @df _ plot(:INCYEAR,:value,group = :variable,linewidth = 3.,xlabel="Income year")
end

title: Recitation 1
text:
Each row of thse data corresponds to an individual in a particular year. For some questions, we may instead be interested in per-person (or equivalized) measures of these income variables. The code below constructs those measures by summing over all individuals within a household, where CPSID is a unique identifier for each household in the survey.

# - gov transfers
# - Create a household-level dataset by summing CPSID (the household ID variable)
house = @chain data begin
    @subset .!ismissing.(:CPSID) #<- drop all obs where this variable is missing (all of 1970)
    @select :CPSID :CPSIDP :INCYEAR :ASECWTH :EARN :GOV :SS :SSI :WELF :CTC :EITC
    stack(Not([:CPSID,:CPSIDP,:INCYEAR]))
    groupby([:INCYEAR,:CPSID,:variable])
    @combine :value = mean(:value)
    unstack([:INCYEAR,:CPSID],:variable,:value)
    disallowmissing #<- unstack allows missing values; we have none
end

title: Recitation 1
text:
How prominently do government transfers feature in the household budget constraint? And how has this evolved over time? Although our measures of income and transfers are not exhaustive, we can use them to get a partial answer to this question.
The code below calculates average transfers relative to average net income for the poorest 20% of households (as measured by per-person household earnings, our variable EARN) and produces a plot. Quantiles and means are weighted by the household weight.

@chain house begin
    groupby(:INCYEAR)
    @transform :q20 = quantile(:EARN,weights(:ASECWTH),0.2) #<- keep bottom 20% in each year
    @subset :EARN .< :q20
    groupby(:INCYEAR)
    @combine begin 
        :gov_share = mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))  / (mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH)) + mean(:EARN,weights(:ASECWTH)))
    end
    @df _ begin 
        plot(:INCYEAR,:gov_share,linewidth=3,xlabel="Income year")
        scatter!(:INCYEAR,:gov_share,legend=false)
    end
end




  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  






























Note that these fluctuations can be caused by fluctuations in the numerator or the denominator. An exercise for you to complete is to verify that these fluctuations are driven by fluctuations in earned income. What event around income year 2009 could explain the large drop in earned income?


Over this time, what sources of government transfers are most prevalent? The code below plots the five sources of transfers that we included in our measure as a fraction of the total in each year.

@chain house begin
    groupby(:INCYEAR)
    @combine  begin 
        :eitc = mean(:EITC,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
        :ssi = mean(:SSI,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
        :welf = mean(:WELF,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
        :ctc = mean(:CTC,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
        :ss = mean(:SS,weights(:ASECWTH))  / mean(:GOV,weights(:ASECWTH))
    end
    stack(Not(:INCYEAR))
    @df _ plot(:INCYEAR,:value,group = :variable,linewidth = 3.,xlabel="Income year")
end

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Overview


So far: theory of human capital formation and mobility
Today: empirical evidence on policy and skill formation
Focus: social safety net programs
Key questions:

Do income transfers affect child development?
What are the long-run effects on education and earnings?
How do these findings connect to our models?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
A Brief Recap


For unconstrained households, investments are not affected by resources

Effects of resources signal constraints \(\Rightarrow\) welfare and efficiency gains

But would it be a good idea to simply run OLS?



\[ \log(H_{t+1}) = \beta_{0} + \beta_{1}\log(\Omega_{t}) + \epsilon_{t} \]


No!! e.g. \(z_{t-1}\rightarrow \Omega\) and \(z_{t}\rightarrow H_{t+1}\)
Need experimental and quasi-experimental evidence

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
What is the EITC?


Refundable tax credit for low-income working families
Phases in with earnings, plateaus, then phases out
Max credit about $8,000 (3+ children, 2025)
Key features:

Conditional on working (labor supply incentive)
Varies with number of children
Expanded significantly in 1993

A few ways to use this variation

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
EITC Schedule


Three regions:

Phase-in: credit increases with earnings
Plateau: credit remains constant
Phase-out: credit decreases with earnings

Creates variation in income while holding work incentives roughly constant

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Research Question


Does family income causally affect child achievement?
Previous research showed correlations, but hard to separate:

Direct income effect
Selection (parents with higher income have other advantages)

Innovation: use EITC expansions as exogenous income shocks
Focus on test scores as outcomes

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Identification Strategy


Compare children in families eligible for large vs small EITC increases
Key variation: 1993 EITC expansion differentially affected families by initial earnings level
Use predicted income growth conditional on earnings as an instrument for actual income growth
To use this variation, must also control for initial earnings

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Main Results
From (Dahl and Lochner 2012):


Outcome: combined math and reading test scores (PIAT, NLSY79 children)
Effect size: the published paper reports that a $1,000 increase in income raises scores by about 6% of a standard deviation
Correction (Dahl and Lochner 2017): a coding error in family income made the first stage too small; corrected IV estimates are about 30% smaller, roughly 4% of a standard deviation per $1,000

Reduced-form estimates and statistical significance are unchanged

Larger effects for:

Younger children
More disadvantaged families

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Long-Run Effects of EITC
(Bastian and Michelmore 2018) ask: what are the lifetime impacts of EITC exposure?


Follow children exposed to EITC expansions into adulthood
Outcomes:

Educational attainment
Employment
Earnings

Key insight: childhood income may have persistent effects

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Identification Strategy


Exploit state-level EITC programs (additional to federal)
Timing: states adopted at different times
Compare children in same state, different birth cohorts
State, year, family size \(\rightarrow\) different max credit

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Variation in EITC Exposure

Source: (Bastian and Michelmore 2018, fig. 2)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Specification
\[ \begin{aligned} Y_{i} = {}& \beta_{1}EITC_{i,0-5} + \beta_{2}EITC_{i,6-12} + \beta_{3}EITC_{i,13-18} \\ &+ \eta X_{i} + \psi V_{s,t} + \lambda Z_{s} + \pi W_{t} + \epsilon_{i} \end{aligned} \]

\(EITC_{i,-}\): maximum available EITC credit given state, year, family size
\(X_{i}\): family characteristics
\(Z_{s}\): state fixed effects
\(W_{t}\): year fixed effects
\(V_{s,t}\): state-year policy variables

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Main Findings


$1,000 increase in EITC exposure (age 13-18) leads to:

1.3% increase in the likelihood of completing high school
4.2% increase in the likelihood of completing college
2.2% increase in earnings as a young adult

The EITC is a work incentive and had an effect on maternal labor supply

Changes in money and time with children

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
section: Tax Benefits and the Birthday Lottery
text:
Tax Benefits and the Birthday Lottery
(Barr, Eggleston, and Smith 2022) exploit a natural experiment: the January 1 birthdate cutoff


U.S. child tax benefits determined by December 31 cutoff
Born December 31 → family gets full tax year benefits
Born January 1 → family waits a year for benefits
Natural randomization: due date doesn’t predict birth date precisely
Sample: low-income families having their first child
Average difference: ~$1,300 (~10% of annual income)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
The Cash Transfer Discontinuity

Source: (Barr, Eggleston, and Smith 2022, fig. I)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Research Question
Do cash transfers in the first year of life affect long-run child outcomes?


Focus: transfer received (or not) right after birth
Compare children born just before vs just after January 1
Innovation: use universe of administrative tax data
Follow children into adulthood (measure earnings in 20s)
Also examine intermediate outcomes (test scores, graduation)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Identification Strategy


Key assumption: children born Dec 31 vs Jan 1 are similar except for transfer timing
Potential threats:

C-sections scheduled to manipulate birth date?
Response: show no bunching around January 1
Different demographics around cutoff?
Response: show balance on observables

Window: focus on births within days of cutoff

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Main Results
Effects of the transfer in the first year of life:


Long-run earnings: 1-2% higher in their twenties, per $1,000 received

2-3% per $1,000 at ages 29-34
Larger effects for males (2-3% per $1,000)
Sample is low-income first births, so these are effects for poor families

Intermediate outcomes:

Higher math and reading test scores
Increased high school graduation rates

Effects emerge early and persist



Pays for itself? The authors estimate that the discounted increase in federal income tax revenue from the child’s higher adult earnings alone exceeds the ~$1,300 cost: a negative net cost to government

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Effect on Adult Earnings

Source: (Barr, Eggleston, and Smith 2022, fig. III)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Mechanisms and Timing
Why do transfers in infancy matter?


Critical period: first year of life is developmentally important

Brain development
Nutrition and health
Parent-child bonding

Families may be especially credit-constrained after birth
Small amounts can have large effects if spent on high-return investments

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Effects Grow with Age

Source: (Barr, Eggleston, and Smith 2022, fig. V)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Effect on Test Scores (North Carolina)

Source: (Barr, Eggleston, and Smith 2022, fig. VII)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
The Food Stamp Program


In-kind transfer program (now called SNAP)
Provides food benefits to low-income households
Rolled out county-by-county between 1961-1975
Research opportunity: quasi-experimental variation in timing of access

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Food Stamp Program Rollout

Source: (Bailey et al. 2024, fig. 1)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Bailey et al. (2024) Study Design
(Bailey et al. 2024) leverage rollout timing:


Compare cohorts born just before vs just after Food Stamps arrived
Within-county variation in exposure by birth year
Link 2000 Census and 2001-13 ACS (17.5 million people) to county of birth via SSA records
Long-run outcomes (pre-specified indices): human capital, economic self-sufficiency, neighborhood quality, physical ability; plus longevity and incarceration

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Specification
\[ Y_{cbt} = \theta_{c} + \delta_{s(c)b} + \psi_{t} + X_{cb}\beta + \sum_{a=-5,\,a\neq 10}^{17}\pi_{a}\mathbf{1}\{FS_{c}-b = a\} + \epsilon_{cbt} \]

\(c\): county of birth; \(s(c)\): its state
\(b\): birth year
\(t\): year of observation
\(FS_{c}\): year in which county \(c\) gets FS program, so \(a\) is age when Food Stamps arrived
\(X_{cb}\): county-by-birth year covariates
\(\pi_{a}\): effect of access starting at age \(a\), relative to \(a = 10\) (omitted)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Logic of Study Design

Source: (Bailey et al. 2024, fig. 2)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Main Findings
Effect on the treated (TOT, ~16% participation) of full access from conception to age 5:


Human capital index: +6% of a SD (e.g. more college)
Economic self-sufficiency index: +3% of a SD (more income, less poverty and assistance)
Neighborhood quality in adulthood: +8% of a SD
Longevity: +1.2 years of life expectancy
Incarceration: 0.5 percentage points less likely
Timing: effects come from exposure in utero to age 5; little effect of exposure at older ages (exception: incarceration among nonwhite men)
Earlier PSID evidence (Hoynes, Schanzenbach, and Almond 2016): reduced metabolic syndrome in adulthood



Interpretation: resources (and nutrition) in early childhood have lifelong consequences

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Event Study: Example

Source: (Bailey et al. 2024, fig. 3)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Return on Investment: the MVPF
Marginal value of public funds (Hendren and Sprung-Keyser 2020): \[ MVPF = \frac{\text{recipients' willingness to pay for the policy}}{\text{net cost to the government}} \]


Net cost subtracts fiscal externalities: extra taxes paid, lower transfers and incarceration costs
Per $1 of Food Stamps spending (Bailey et al. 2024):

WTP: $0.80 (parents’ value of benefits) + $0.45 (children’s after-tax earnings) + $61 (longer life, valued with the value of a statistical life)
Net cost: about $0 (labor supply distortion offset by revenue gains and lower incarceration)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
The MVPF of Food Stamps


MVPF \(\approx\) 62 (62.25), larger than for Perry Preschool or Abecedarian
Note: almost all of it comes from the longevity gain, so it depends on how we value life-years
Interpretation: Food Stamps are an investment not just consumption
Compare: in Barr, Eggleston, and Smith (2022), the net cost is negative, so the MVPF is infinite

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
The Child Development Grant Programme (CDGP)
(Carneiro et al. 2021) study a multifaceted intervention in Northern Nigeria:


Information provision to mothers and fathers on pregnancy and infant feeding practices
Cash transfers to mothers: $22/month (85% of women’s earnings)
Transfers begin during pregnancy, continue until child is 24 months
Implemented at village level, targeted to pregnant women
Randomized controlled trial with 3,688 pregnant women at baseline

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Why This Context Matters


Northern Nigeria: extreme poverty (70% below $1.90/day)
High stunting rates (67% of children under 5)
Infant mortality: 90 per 1,000 births
Low knowledge of child nutrition practices
Women retain control over resources they bring into household
Agricultural lean season creates food insecurity

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Main Results


Child anthropometrics (2 years post-intervention):

Height-for-age Z-score increases by 0.22σ
Stunting reduced by 8%, extreme stunting by 15%
At age 4 (~2 years post-transfers): HAZ 0.14σ, stunting effects almost unchanged

Child health:

18% reduction in diarrhea episodes
Increased vaccination and deworming rates

Mother’s labor supply:

21% increase in earnings at 2 years, sustained at 4 years
Increased livestock ownership (key for protein-rich diets)

Development: muted effects on (untargeted) cognitive/noncognitive skills at age 4

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Effect on Food Consumption

Source: (Carneiro et al. 2021, fig. 3)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Effect on Resources

Source: (Carneiro et al. 2021, fig. 4)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Long-Run Impacts and Mechanisms


Key mechanisms:

Increased parental knowledge and improved practices (breastfeeding, antenatal care)
Women invest transfers in livestock assets → protein-rich foods for children
Labor supply increases (no reduction despite transfers)
Food security improves, especially during lean season

Sustained effects: impacts persist 2 years after transfers end
Return on investment (counting only earnings gains from greater height): internal rate of return of 6.1% for boys and 3.6% for girls

A lower bound; closer to 20% if some short-run gains to children are counted

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
What Have We Learned?
If we believe the findings:


Income matters: Causal evidence from EITC, tax refunds at birth, Food Stamps, cash transfers in Nigeria
Timing matters: Largest effects for early childhood exposure (mostly)
Long-run effects: Childhood resources affect adult outcomes



Policy implication: Safety net programs are investments in human capital, not just transfers

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
A Contrast: Baby’s First Years
An RCT designed to test exactly this question:


About 1,000 low-income mothers recruited at birth in 4 U.S. cities (New Orleans, New York City, Omaha, Twin Cities)
Randomized to $333/month (high-cash) or $20/month (low-cash) unconditional cash, starting at birth
Age 1 (Troller-Renfree et al. 2022): high-cash infants show more power in mid- and high-frequency EEG brain activity (n = 435)

Patterns correlated with later cognitive skills in other studies
But significance depends on the specification and on multiple-testing adjustments

Age 4 (Noble et al. 2025): no significant effects on preregistered primary outcomes (language, executive function, social-emotional problems, brain activity) or on secondary outcomes

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Reconciling the Evidence


What do you think? Why might Baby’s First Years find little, when the quasi-experiments find lasting effects?
Some candidate explanations:

Size and timing: about $4,000 per year for several years vs. a one-time ~$1,300 (Barr, Eggleston, and Smith 2022); is the difference in timing, liquidity, or permanence?
Outcomes measured: test scores at age 4 vs. earnings, longevity, incarceration decades later; effects might emerge later (recall Barr, Eggleston, and Smith (2022): effects grow with age)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Reconciling the Evidence (cont.)


More candidate explanations:

Power: ~900 children vs. millions of tax records; can the RCT rule out effects the size of Dahl and Lochner (2017)?
Context: both groups also had access to other benefits (EITC, SNAP) and to pandemic-era transfers (stimulus payments, the 2021 expanded Child Tax Credit)
Mechanisms: how did families spend the money? Did parental investment change?

Which of these could we test with the data?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
Remaining Questions


Mechanisms: how does income translate to better outcomes?

Direct purchases (food, books, healthcare); parental time allocation
Stress reduction; neighborhood quality

Optimal design: conditional or not? Cash or in-kind?
General equilibrium: what if everyone receives transfers?
Cost-effectiveness: which interventions have highest returns?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: The Safety Net
text:
References


Bailey, Martha J, Hilary Hoynes, Maya Rossin-Slater, and Reed Walker. 2024. “Is the Social Safety Net a Long-Term Investment? Large-Scale Evidence from the Food Stamps Program.” Review of Economic Studies 91 (3): 1291–1330.


Barr, Andrew, Jonathan Eggleston, and Alexander A. Smith. 2022. “Investing in Infants: The Lasting Effects of Cash Transfers to New Families.” The Quarterly Journal of Economics, no. 4: 2539–83. https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjac023.

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Overview


Last time: Becker-Tomes showed how ability transmits across generations
Today: What are the skills that drive inequality?
Three main points:

Cognitive and noncognitive skills explain life-cycle differences
The technology of skill formation can be estimated; skills are malleable early
Latent factor models deal with measurement error

Key papers: Heckman, Stixrud, and Urzua (2006), Cunha and Heckman (2007), Cunha and Heckman (2008b), Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach (2010)

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
The Importance of Skills


Standard human capital theory: education → wages
But which skills drive labor market outcomes?
Two broad categories emerge:

Cognitive skills: IQ, achievement tests, reasoning
Noncognitive skills: personality, motivation, self-control

Question: Do both types matter for economic outcomes?

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
section: What Do We Mean by Noncognitive Skills?
text:
What Do We Mean by Noncognitive Skills?
Examples from psychology literature:


Locus of control: belief about control over life outcomes
Self-esteem: confidence in one’s abilities
Time preference: ability to delay gratification
Conscientiousness: persistence, organization
Emotional stability: managing stress and emotions



These are often harder to measure than cognitive ability, but may be equally important.

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
section: Evidence from Heckman, Stixrud, and Urzua (2006)
text:
Evidence from Heckman, Stixrud, and Urzua (2006)
Key empirical findings using NLSY79 data:


Both skill types significantly affect:

Wages and schooling attainment
Risky behaviors: smoking, crime, teen pregnancy (large!)

For many outcomes, noncognitive skills matter more
The effects persist over the entire life cycle

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Measuring Skills: The Challenge
How do we measure cognitive and noncognitive ability?


Cognitive: ASVAB (Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery)

Arithmetic reasoning, word knowledge, paragraph comprehension, etc.

Noncognitive: psychological scales

Rotter Locus of Control; Rosenberg Self-Esteem

Problem: Measurement error!

Tests are noisy proxies for true ability
Cannot use test scores as if they were true ability

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Wages and Skills
After correcting for measurement error:

Wages grow with both cognitive and non-cognitive skill
Slopes are comparable in magnitude
Some pictures to follow…

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Complementarity with Schooling
From Heckman, Stixrud, and Urzua (2006):


Higher cognitive ability → higher wages at all schooling levels
But the gradient is steeper for college graduates
This suggests complementarity between skills and education
Cognitive skills have bigger payoffs with more schooling
Conversely, the gradient in non-cognitive skill gets flatter

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Noncognitive Skills are Important


Noncognitive skills also predict wages
The pattern is similar: higher noncognitive ability → higher wages
Effects are large and persistent
For some outcomes (e.g., crime), noncognitive effects dominate cognitive

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Educational Attainment and Skills


Both cognitive and noncognitive skills predict years of schooling
Noncognitive skills are particularly important for college completion

Requires persistence, motivation, delayed gratification
Not just ability to do the work
Also willingness to persist, study habits, etc.

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Skills Are Produced
From the Becker-Tomes model, we had: \[ H_{t+1} = f(X_t, z_t) \]


But what is the technology \(f(\cdot)\)?
How do cognitive and noncognitive skills interact?
Are there critical periods for investment?
Can we compensate for early disadvantage with late investment?

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
The Technology of Skill Formation
Following Cunha and Heckman (2007), skills evolve according to a vector technology:
\[
\theta_{t+1} = f_t(\theta_{C,t}, \theta_{N,t}, I_t), \qquad \theta_{t} = (\theta_{C,t},\theta_{N,t})
\]


\(\theta_{C,t}\), \(\theta_{N,t}\): cognitive and noncognitive skill at stage \(t\) of childhood
\(I_t\): parental investment at stage \(t\)
Both skills can enter the production of each skill next period

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
A CES Specification
A simplified version of the CES technology in Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach (2010) (which also includes parental skills), for skill \(k \in \{C, N\}\):
\[
\theta_{k,t+1} = \left[\gamma_{1,k}\theta_{C,t}^{\phi_k} + \gamma_{2,k}\theta_{N,t}^{\phi_k} + \gamma_{3,k}I_{t}^{\phi_k}\right]^{1/\phi_k}, \quad \sum_{j}\gamma_{j,k} = 1
\]


Within a period, \(\phi_k\) governs substitution between current investment and the current skill stock

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Key Parameters: Elasticity of Substitution
The elasticity of substitution is: \[ \sigma_k = \frac{1}{1-\phi_k} \]


\(\phi_k = 1\) (\(\sigma_k = \infty\)): perfect substitutes
\(\phi_k \to 0\) (\(\sigma_k = 1\)): Cobb-Douglas
\(\phi_k < 0\) (\(\sigma_k < 1\)): inputs are (gross) complements
\(\phi_k \to -\infty\) (\(\sigma_k \to 0\)): Leontief, \(\min\{\cdot\}\) (perfect complements)
Low \(\sigma_k\): hard to make up for a low skill stock with more investment
Empirical question: What are \(\sigma_{\text{cog}}\) and \(\sigma_{\text{noncog}}\), and do they change with age?

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
section: From One Period to Early vs. Late Investment
text:
From One Period to Early vs. Late Investment
Take one skill, two stages of childhood, and a common \(\phi\) (Cunha and Heckman 2007):
\[
\theta_{2} = \left[\gamma_1\theta_1^{\phi} + (1-\gamma_1)I_1^{\phi}\right]^{1/\phi}, \qquad
\theta_{3} = \left[\gamma_2\theta_2^{\phi} + (1-\gamma_2)I_2^{\phi}\right]^{1/\phi}
\]

Substitute \(\theta_2\) into the second stage:
\[
\theta_{3} = \left[\gamma_2\gamma_1\theta_1^{\phi} + \gamma_2(1-\gamma_1)I_1^{\phi} + (1-\gamma_2)I_2^{\phi}\right]^{1/\phi}
\]


Only through this nesting does \(\phi\) also govern substitution between early (\(I_1\)) and late (\(I_2\)) investment
\(\gamma_2(1-\gamma_1)\): productivity of early investment, which works through the skill stock \(\theta_2\) (what Cunha and Heckman (2007) call the “skill multiplier”)
\((1-\gamma_2)\): productivity of late investment
Cunha and Heckman (2007) write the reduced form as \(\theta_3 = [\gamma I_1^{\phi} + (1-\gamma)I_2^{\phi}]^{1/\phi}\)

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Exercise
Two-period model (ignore \(\theta_1\)): \[ \theta = f(I_1, I_2) = \left[\gamma I_{1}^{\phi} + (1-\gamma)I_{2}^{\phi}\right]^{1/\phi} \]


Solve the problem: \[ \min p_{1}I_{1} + p_{2}I_{2}\ s.t.\ f(I_{1},I_{2}) \geq 1 \] where \(I_{t}\) is investment in period \(t\) and \(p_t\) its price
Show that \(\frac{I_1}{I_2} = \left(\frac{\gamma}{1-\gamma}\frac{p_2}{p_1}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\phi}}\)
What happens when investment is more costly in period 1? How does the answer depend on \(\phi\)?

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Self-Productivity and Dynamic Complementarity
Two key properties:


Self-productivity: \(\frac{\partial \theta_{k,t+1}}{\partial \theta_{k,t}} > 0\)

Skills beget skills
Early advantage compounds over time

Dynamic complementarity: \(\frac{\partial^2 \theta_{k,t+1}}{\partial I_{t} \partial \theta_{k,t}} > 0\)

Higher skills today make investment today more productive
Early investment raises \(\theta_t\) and so raises the return to later investment




These properties have profound implications for policy timing.

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Exercise: Dynamic Complementarity
Take the one-skill CES technology: \[ \theta' = \left[\gamma\theta^{\phi} + (1-\gamma)I^{\phi}\right]^{1/\phi}, \quad \gamma\in(0,1) \]


Show self-productivity: \(\partial\theta'/\partial\theta > 0\)
Show that \[ \frac{\partial^2\theta'}{\partial I\,\partial\theta} = (1-\phi)\gamma(1-\gamma)\,\theta^{\phi-1}I^{\phi-1}\left[\gamma\theta^{\phi} + (1-\gamma)I^{\phi}\right]^{\frac{1}{\phi}-2} \]
Conclude: dynamic complementarity holds whenever \(\phi < 1\), and disappears with perfect substitutes (\(\phi = 1\))
Does dynamic complementarity require \(\phi < 0\) (gross complements)?

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Connecting to the Becker-Tomes Model
Map our notation to Lecture 5: \(\theta \leftrightarrow H\) and \(I \leftrightarrow X\)
\[ H_{t+1} = \exp(\mu + z_t)X_t^{\delta} \]


The child’s human capital depends on investment \(X_t\) and ability \(z_t\)
But not on a previous stock of skills: \(\partial H_{t+1}/\partial H_t = 0\)

No self-productivity, so no dynamic complementarity between stocks and investment
Childhood is a single period: no distinction between early and late investment

Ability \(z_t\) plays a role similar to the initial endowment \(\theta_1\)
What do you think? How would optimal investment and the IGE change if \(H_{t+1}\) depended on \(H_t\)?

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Critical and Sensitive Periods
Cunha and Heckman (2007) define these in terms of the productivity of investment at each stage:


Critical period: investment is productive in stage \(t^*\) only

\(\partial\theta_3/\partial I_{t^*} > 0\) but \(\partial\theta_3/\partial I_{s} = 0\) for \(s\neq t^*\)

Sensitive period: at the same level of inputs, investment is more productive in \(t^*\) than in other stages
In the nested CES with \(I_1 = I_2\): \(\frac{\partial\theta_3/\partial I_1}{\partial\theta_3/\partial I_2} = \frac{\gamma_2(1-\gamma_1)}{1-\gamma_2}\)

Stage 1 is sensitive if \(\gamma_2(1-\gamma_1) > 1-\gamma_2\); critical if \(1-\gamma_2 = 0\)

These are statements about the share parameters (\(\gamma\)), not about \(\phi\)

\(\phi\) tells us how costly it is to compensate for a missed stage
Limiting case: Leontief (\(\phi\to-\infty\)) makes both periods critical

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Evidence on Sensitive Periods
From Cunha and Heckman (2008b) (linear technology, CNLSY data):


Sensitive periods exist for parental investment in both skill types
Cognitive sensitive periods come earlier than noncognitive ones
Parental investment is more effective for noncognitive skills
Noncognitive skills remain more malleable into later childhood and adolescence

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
The Importance of Early Investment
Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach (2010) estimate a nonlinear (CES) technology with stage-specific \(\phi\):


Cognitive skills: the elasticity of substitution between investment and the skill stock is higher in early childhood and falls in later childhood

Early remediation of a low cognitive endowment is relatively easy
Late remediation is costly: more investment is needed to make up the same deficit

Noncognitive skills: the elasticity is roughly constant across stages

Leaves more room for remediation of noncognitive skills in adolescence




Policy implication: Early childhood interventions may have the highest returns, and adolescent interventions may do better by targeting noncognitive skills.

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Cross-Productivity of Skills
With the vector technology \(\theta_{t+1} = f_t(\theta_{C,t},\theta_{N,t}, I_t)\), cross-productivity means:
\[
\frac{\partial \theta_{C,t+1}}{\partial \theta_{N,t}} > 0 \quad \text{and/or} \quad \frac{\partial \theta_{N,t+1}}{\partial \theta_{C,t}} > 0
\]


Cunha and Heckman (2008b) find that noncognitive skills foster cognitive skills
But, in most specifications, cognitive skills do not foster noncognitive skills
A child who is attentive and persistent learns more
Investments in noncognitive skills have a second payoff through cognition

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
The Measurement Problem


We want the effect of true skills \(\theta\) on outcomes \(Y\)
But we only observe noisy measures \(M\) of skills
If we use \(M\) instead of \(\theta\):

Attenuation bias: underestimate true effects
Omitted variable bias: measures are imperfect proxies

Classical error \(M = \theta + \varepsilon\) biases estimates toward zero:



\[ \text{plim}\,\hat{\beta} = \beta \frac{\text{Var}(\theta)}{\text{Var}(\theta) + \text{Var}(\varepsilon)} \]

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
section: Simulation: Attenuation Bias and a Second Measure
text:
Simulation: Attenuation Bias and a Second Measure
True model: \(Y = 1 + 0.5\theta + u\). We observe test scores \(M_j = \lambda_j\theta + \varepsilon_j\) with \(\lambda_1 = 1\) and independent errors.


Code
using Random, Statistics, DataFrames
Random.seed!(4538)
N = 5_000
β = 0.5                         # true effect of skill on outcome
θ = randn(N)                    # true (latent) skill, Var(θ) = 1
Y = 1.0 .+ β .* θ .+ 0.5 .* randn(N)
M1 = θ .+ randn(N)              # test 1 (loading normalized to 1), reliability 0.5
M2 = 0.8 .* θ .+ randn(N)       # test 2: different scale, independent error
M3 = 1.2 .* θ .+ randn(N)       # test 3

β_true = cov(Y, θ) / var(θ)                         # infeasible: uses true skill
β_ols  = cov(Y, M1) / var(M1)                       # attenuated toward zero
β_iv   = cov(Y, M2) / cov(M1, M2)                   # IV: instrument M1 with M2
var_θ  = cov(M1, M2) * cov(M1, M3) / cov(M2, M3)    # factor model: recover Var(θ)
β_fac  = cov(Y, M1) / var_θ                         # replace Var(M1) with Var(θ)

results = DataFrame(estimator = ["OLS on true θ (infeasible)", "OLS on M1", "IV: M1 instrumented by M2", "Factor model (3 measures)"],
                    estimate = round.([β_true, β_ols, β_iv, β_fac], digits = 3))
HTML(sprint(io -> show(io, MIME("text/html"), results; summary = false, eltypes = false)))






Row
estimator
estimate




1
OLS on true θ (infeasible)
0.493


2
OLS on M1
0.245


3
IV: M1 instrumented by M2
0.498


4
Factor model (3 measures)
0.501

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
What the Simulation Shows


OLS on one noisy test recovers about half of \(\beta\): the reliability of \(M_1\) is \(1/(1+1) = 0.5\)
A second measure with independent error is a valid instrument: \(\text{Cov}(Y,M_2)/\text{Cov}(M_1,M_2) = \beta\lambda_2/\lambda_2\)
With three measures, covariances identify \(\text{Var}(\theta)\) directly: the factor approach
Exercise: show that \(\text{Cov}(M_1,M_2)\text{Cov}(M_1,M_3)/\text{Cov}(M_2,M_3) = \text{Var}(\theta)\)

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
The Latent Factor Approach
Example from Heckman, Stixrud, and Urzua (2006):


Assume there are \(K\) latent factors \(\theta = (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_K)\)
We observe \(J\) measurements \(M = (M_1, \ldots, M_J)\)
Each measurement loads on the factors: \(M_j = \mu_j + \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_{jk}\theta_k + \varepsilon_j\)
Use multiple measures to identify the factors
Correct for measurement error in effects on outcomes

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Factor Model Structure
The system has three components:
Measurement equations: \[ M_j = \mu_j + \alpha_{j1}\theta_1 + \alpha_{j2}\theta_2 + \varepsilon_j, \quad j = 1, \ldots, J \]
Outcome equations: \[ Y = X\beta + \gamma_1\theta_1 + \gamma_2\theta_2 + u \]
Choice equations: \[ S = \mathbb{1}[Z\delta + \lambda_1\theta_1 + \lambda_2\theta_2 + v > 0] \]
where \(\theta_1, \theta_2\) are latent factors (e.g., cognitive and noncognitive ability).

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Identification Strategy
How do we identify this model?


Normalizations: set the scale of factors, e.g., \(\alpha_{11} = 1\), \(\alpha_{22} = 1\)
Exclusion restrictions: some measures don’t load on all factors

Cognitive tests only load on \(\theta_1\)
Personality scales only load on \(\theta_2\)

Multiple measurements: Need \(J \geq 2K + 1\) typically
Covariance structure: implies testable restrictions

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
section: What the Factor Model Buys Us
text:
What the Factor Model Buys Us


Correct inference about effects of skills on outcomes

No attenuation bias from measurement error

Decomposition of outcomes into skill components

How much is due to cognitive vs. noncognitive?

Predicted factors for each individual

Can use in subsequent analysis

Tests of model assumptions

Overidentification restrictions

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Example: NLSY79 Data
Heckman, Stixrud, and Urzua (2006) use:

Cognitive: ASVAB arithmetic reasoning, word knowledge, paragraph comprehension, math knowledge, coding speed
Noncognitive: Rotter Locus of Control and Rosenberg Self-Esteem scales


With two factors and multiple measures, the model is overidentified and can be tested.

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Separating Heterogeneity from Uncertainty
Another interesting use of factor models (Cunha and Heckman 2008a, building on Cunha, Heckman, and Navarro (2005)):


Observed wage variance has two sources:

Heterogeneity: differences in \(\theta\) known to agent at age 17
Uncertainty: shocks \(\varepsilon\) unknown at age 17

Factor model + choice data lets us separate these
How? If \(\theta \in I\) (agent’s info set), it affects choices
If \(\varepsilon \notin I\), it doesn’t affect choices
By using choice data, we learn what agents knew when

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Findings on Predictability
From Cunha and Heckman (2008a) (NLSY79 white males, high school vs. college):


About 80% of the variance in the returns to college is forecastable at age 17, when schooling decisions are made
The levels of lifetime earnings are even more predictable in their baseline model
Robustness: with earnings split into more periods, predictability falls to around 60% (55% for returns)
Either way, most dispersion is due to heterogeneity in skills, not “luck”
This heterogeneity is measurable using factor methods



Implication: Early interventions can have large effects because most variance is in place early.

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Bringing It Together
What have we learned?


Both cognitive and noncognitive skills matter enormously
Noncognitive skills are often more important than we thought
Skills have a production technology with:

Self-productivity
Dynamic complementarity
Cross-productivity (noncognitive \(\rightarrow\) cognitive)
For cognitive skills, substitutability between investment and skills falls with age

Measurement error is severe; factor models are essential
Most earnings inequality is heterogeneity (not luck)

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Policy Implications


Invest early: Sensitive periods (especially for cognitive skills) suggest high returns to early childhood
Holistic interventions: Target both cognitive and noncognitive skills
Compensatory programs: Late remediation of cognitive deficits is costly because substitutability falls with age; noncognitive skills remain more malleable

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Policy Implications (cont.)


Measurement matters:

Policy evaluations need to account for measurement error
Standard approaches may severely understate program effects

Targeting: Focus on children from disadvantaged backgrounds

They face both low \(\theta\) and low \(I\)
Dynamic complementarity means early intervention is most effective for them
No equity-efficiency trade-off for early investment (but there is one for late investment) (Cunha and Heckman 2007)




Coming up: we will test these predictions against evidence from early childhood programs such as Perry Preschool.

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Key Takeaways


Skills are multidimensional: cognitive and noncognitive both matter
Skills are produced by a technology with key properties
Early childhood is a sensitive period (esp. for cognitive skills); late remediation is costly
Measurement error is first-order; factor models solve it
Most inequality is heterogeneity, not luck
Policy: Invest early, invest holistically, target disadvantaged

title: Skills, Inequality, and the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
References


Cunha, Flavio, and James Heckman. 2007. “The Technology of Skill Formation.” The American Economic Review, no. 2: 31–47. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.97.2.31.


———. 2008a. “A New Framework for the Analysis of Inequality.” Macroeconomic Dynamics, no. S2: 315–54. https://doi.org/10.1017/S136510050807034X.


Cunha, Flavio, and James J. Heckman. 2008b. “Formulating, Identifying and Estimating the Technology of Cognitive and Noncognitive Skill Formation.” The Journal of Human Resources, no. 4: 738–82. https://doi.org/10.1353/jhr.2008.0019.

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Overview


Previous lectures: inequality, welfare, and income processes within individuals over time
Today: how does economic status persist across generations?
Key questions:

How strong is the link between parent and child earnings?
Why is it so hard to measure? (Our income process tools will help.)
Does the U.S. have more or less mobility than other countries?
What drives geographic variation in mobility? Is it causal?

Building up to a theory of intergenerational inequality

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
The Intergenerational Elasticity (IGE)
Most common measure: regression of child log income on parent log income
\[y_{\text{child}, i} = \alpha + \beta \cdot y_{\text{parent}, i} + \varepsilon_i\]


\(\beta\) = intergenerational elasticity (IGE)
\(\beta = 0\): no relationship (perfect mobility)
\(\beta = 1\): perfect persistence (no mobility)
Typical U.S. estimates: \(\beta \approx 0.4\) to 0.6
Notation: \(\beta\) is the standard symbol for the IGE. In other lectures (and next lecture), \(\beta\) is also a discount factor or altruism weight. Context will make clear which one we mean.

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Interpreting the IGE
How long does a family’s disadvantage last?


Suppose a family starts 75% below the mean (roughly the poverty line), and the gap shrinks by a factor \(\beta\) each generation
Next generation: expected gap is \(\beta \times 75\%\); after \(k\) generations: \(\beta^{k} \times 75\%\)
Mazumder (2005): with \(\beta = 0.6\), it takes 5-6 generations (125-150 years) to get within 5% of the mean; with \(\beta=0.4\), about 3
Exercise: verify this. Find the smallest \(k\) such that \(0.75\,\beta^k < 0.05\) for \(\beta = 0.4\) and \(\beta = 0.6\).

title: Intergenerational Mobility
section: The IGE is not a correlation
text:
The IGE is not a correlation
Recall the OLS formula:
\[\beta = \frac{\text{cov}(y_{c}, y_{p})}{\text{var}(y_{p})} = \text{corr}(y_{c}, y_{p}) \times \frac{\sigma_{c}}{\sigma_{p}}\]


The IGE mixes two things:

how strongly parent and child positions are linked (the correlation)
how unequal the child generation is relative to the parent generation (\(\sigma_c/\sigma_p\))

If inequality is rising across generations, the IGE rises even if the correlation is unchanged
Keep this in mind when we compare countries

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Alternative Measure: Rank-Rank Slope
Chetty et al. (2014) popularized rank-based measures:
\[\text{rank}_{\text{child}, i} = \alpha + \beta_r \cdot \text{rank}_{\text{parent}, i} + \varepsilon_i\]


Ranks: 0-100 percentiles (children ranked within their birth cohort, parents against other parents)
\(\beta_r\): how much does parent rank predict child rank?
Ranks are uniformly distributed in both generations, so \(\beta_r\) is the rank correlation
Unaffected by changes in inequality between generations; handles zero incomes naturally

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Absolute vs Relative Mobility
Two distinct concepts:


Relative mobility: how much does your position depend on your parents’ position? (IGE, rank-rank slope)
Absolute mobility: how well do children from a given background do in absolute terms?

e.g. do you earn more than your parents did?
e.g. what rank do children of parents at the 25th percentile reach?




Key insight: Can have high absolute mobility (everyone richer) with low relative mobility (ranks unchanged). Lower relative mobility can also come from worse outcomes for the rich, not better outcomes for the poor.

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
The Solon-Zimmerman Estimates
Early 1990s: Solon (1992) and Zimmerman (1992) used PSID and NLS
Key finding: \(\beta \approx 0.4\)


Much higher than previous estimates (about 0.2)
Previous work suffered from:

Measurement error
Life-cycle bias (measuring parents/children at unrepresentative ages)

Think: what does our work on income processes tell us about income over the life-cycle?
Let’s formalize both problems using the tools from Lecture 3

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
The Setup
Let \(x_i\) be the parent’s permanent log income and \(Y_i\) the child’s. The object we want is:
\[Y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \varepsilon_i, \qquad \text{cov}(x_i, \varepsilon_i) = 0\]

But we observe parent income in year \(t\), which includes a transitory component:
\[y_{p,it} = x_i + \nu_{it}, \qquad \nu_{it} \sim \text{i.i.d.}(0, \sigma^2_{\nu})\]


\(\sigma^2_p = \text{var}(x_i)\): dispersion in permanent income
\(\sigma^2_\nu\): transitory shocks plus measurement error (recall the Meghir-Pistaferri decomposition)
Suppose we average parent income over \(T\) years: \(\bar{y}_{p,i} = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} y_{p,it}\)

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Exercise: Attenuation Bias
Regress \(Y_i\) on \(\bar{y}_{p,i}\). Show that:
\[\text{plim}\ \hat{\beta} = \beta \cdot \frac{\sigma^2_p}{\sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_\nu / T}\]


Step 1: write \(\bar{y}_{p,i} = x_i + \bar{\nu}_i\) where \(\bar{\nu}_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_t \nu_{it}\)
Step 2: what is \(\text{var}(\bar{\nu}_i)\)?
Step 3: compute \(\text{cov}(Y_i, \bar{y}_{p,i})\) and \(\text{var}(\bar{y}_{p,i})\)
Step 4: take the ratio

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Solution (Board)


\(\text{var}(\bar{\nu}_i) = \frac{1}{T^2}\sum_{t}\text{var}(\nu_{it}) = \frac{\sigma^2_\nu}{T}\) (independence across years)
\(\text{cov}(Y_i, \bar{y}_{p,i}) = \text{cov}(\alpha + \beta x_i + \varepsilon_i,\ x_i + \bar{\nu}_i) = \beta \sigma^2_p\)
\(\text{var}(\bar{y}_{p,i}) = \sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_\nu/T\)
So \(\text{plim}\ \hat{\beta} = \beta \lambda_T\) where \(\lambda_T = \frac{\sigma^2_p}{\sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_\nu/T}\) is the reliability ratio
\(\lambda_T < 1\): the IGE is biased toward zero
Averaging helps: \(\lambda_T \to 1\) as \(T\to\infty\)

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Discussion


If half the variance of annual log income is transitory (\(\sigma^2_\nu = \sigma^2_p\)):

\(T = 1\): \(\lambda_1 = 0.5\), so the IGE is cut in half!
\(T = 5\): \(\lambda_5 = 1/1.2 \approx 0.83\)

What about the child’s income? Transitory noise in \(Y_i\) is error in the dependent variable: it reduces precision but does not bias \(\hat\beta\)
What if transitory shocks are persistent? (e.g. AR(1) with coefficient \(\delta\), as in Lecture 3.) Averaging adjacent years removes less noise, so \(\lambda_T\) is smaller for each \(T\)

title: Intergenerational Mobility
section: Persistent Transitory Shocks Make Things Worse
text:
Persistent Transitory Shocks Make Things Worse


Code
using StatsPlots

# Reliability ratio when the transitory component is AR(1) with coefficient δ:
# var(ν̄) = σ²_ν / T² × [T + 2 Σ_{k=1}^{T-1} (T-k) δ^k]
function reliability(T; σ2_p = 0.5, σ2_ν = 0.5, δ = 0.0)
    var_νbar = σ2_ν / T^2 * (T + 2 * sum((T - k) * δ^k for k in 1:T-1; init = 0.0))
    return σ2_p / (σ2_p + var_νbar)
end

Tgrid = 1:30
plot(Tgrid, reliability.(Tgrid), label = "i.i.d. transitory (δ = 0)", linewidth = 2,
     xlabel = "Years of parent income averaged (T)", ylabel = "Reliability ratio λ_T",
     ylims = (0.4, 1.0), legend = :bottomright, size = (900, 380),
     tickfontsize = 10, guidefontsize = 12, legendfontsize = 10, left_margin = 5Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 3Plots.mm)
plot!(Tgrid, reliability.(Tgrid; δ = 0.5), label = "AR(1) transitory (δ = 0.5)", linewidth = 2)
vline!([5], linestyle = :dash, color = :gray, label = "T = 5")





  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  








































With half the variance transitory and \(\delta = 0.5\), a 5-year average gives \(\lambda_5 \approx 0.69\): an estimate of 0.4 would be consistent with a true IGE of about 0.6 (Mazumder 2005, Table 1).

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Recall: Heterogeneous Income Profiles
From Lecture 3, the HIP model (Guvenen 2009):
\[y_{ia} = \alpha_i + g_i \cdot a + u_{ia}\]


\(a\): age (or years of experience)
\(g_i\): individual-specific growth rate (we called it \(\beta_i\) in Lecture 3; renamed here to avoid confusion with the IGE)
Define lifetime log income as the average over the career: \(Y_i = \alpha_i + g_i \bar{a}\), where \(\bar{a}\) is the midpoint of the career
Then we can rewrite: \(y_{ia} = Y_i + g_i(a - \bar{a}) + u_{ia}\)
People with high lifetime income (e.g. doctors, lawyers) often have low income early and steep profiles

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Exercise: Life-Cycle Bias
Suppose \(Y_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \varepsilon_i\) and that children from richer families have steeper profiles:
\[g_i = \bar{g} + \kappa (Y_i - \mathbb{E}[Y_i]) + \xi_i, \qquad \kappa > 0\]
with \(\xi_i\) and \(u_{ia}\) independent of \(x_i\). We measure the child’s income at a single age \(a\) and regress \(y_{ia}\) on \(x_i\) (true parent permanent income).


(a) Show that \(\text{plim}\ \hat{\beta}_a = \beta\left[1 + \kappa(a - \bar{a})\right]\)
(b) At what age is the estimate unbiased? What happens if we measure children’s income at age 25?
(c) Why doesn’t the transitory term \(u_{ia}\) cause bias here?

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Solution (Board)


\(\text{cov}(y_{ia}, x_i) = \text{cov}(Y_i, x_i) + (a-\bar{a})\,\text{cov}(g_i, x_i)\)
\(\text{cov}(Y_i, x_i) = \beta\sigma^2_p\)
\(\text{cov}(g_i, x_i) = \kappa\,\text{cov}(Y_i, x_i) = \kappa\beta\sigma^2_p\)
So \(\text{plim}\ \hat\beta_a = \frac{\beta\sigma^2_p\left[1 + \kappa(a-\bar a)\right]}{\sigma^2_p} = \beta\left[1+\kappa(a-\bar{a})\right]\)
For \(a < \bar{a}\) (young children): biased down. Unbiased only near mid-career.
This is the logic of Haider and Solon (2006): current income at age \(a\) is \(\lambda_a \times\) lifetime income plus noise, and \(\lambda_a < 1\) at young ages

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Life-Cycle Bias: Evidence


Haider and Solon (2006) find current earnings are a poor proxy for lifetime earnings in the early career; a rule of thumb is to measure children’s income closer to age 40 (Mazumder 2018)
The same issue arises for parents: if parent income is measured very late (or early) in their career, it is a noisier proxy of lifetime income, which acts like additional measurement error
Chetty et al. (2014) check this for the rank-rank slope: it rises steeply in the early 20s but is stable after about age 30, and barely changes with more years of parent income
Does the same hold for the IGE? This is where the debate lies…

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Mazumder’s Higher Estimates
Mazumder (2005) used the SIPP matched to Social Security earnings records:


Administrative earnings histories: no survey attrition, long panels
Long averages: up to 16 years of fathers’ earnings
Children born 1963-1968, earnings measured 1995-1998 (at least age 27)
Result: the IGE rises steadily with the length of the parent average

2-year average of fathers’ earnings: 0.30 (sons)
16-year average: 0.61 (sons), 0.60 (sons and daughters pooled)

Exactly the pattern our attenuation formula predicts

title: Intergenerational Mobility
section: Chetty et al. (2014): The Tax Data
text:
Chetty et al. (2014): The Tax Data
Chetty et al. (2014) used de-identified federal tax records:


Core sample: about 10 million children born 1980-1982 (the extended 1980-1991 sample has about 44 million)
Linked to parents via dependent claiming on tax returns (parents identified for about 95% of children)
Child income: mean family income in 2011-2012 (around age 30)
Parent income: mean family income 1996-2000 (when children were 15-20)
Geographic detail: commuting zones (CZs), based on where the child lived at age 16



Unprecedented scale and precision

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
National Findings
Using these data:


IGE (log-log, excluding children with zero income): \(\beta = 0.344\)
Rank-rank slope: \(\beta_r = 0.341\)
The rank-rank relationship is remarkably linear across the entire distribution
The log-log relationship is not linear, and the IGE is fragile (next slide)

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
The Rank-Rank Relationship

Rank-Rank Relationship in U.S. Tax Records (Chetty et al. 2014)National average slope: \(\beta_r = 0.341\), remarkably linear across the distribution

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
How Fragile is the IGE?
From Chetty et al. (2014), Section IV:


Baseline (drop children with zero income): 0.344
Restrict to parents between the 10th and 90th percentiles: 0.452
Recode zero incomes to $1: 0.618; recode to $1,000: 0.413
Across subsamples and specifications: 0.26 to 0.70
Why? The share of children with zero income falls from 17% (poorest families) to 3% (richest). Dropping zeros throws away the worst outcomes for poor children, which overstates mobility.
And because log child income is nonlinear in log parent income, the IGE depends on which part of the distribution is weighted most

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Reconciling: The Critique
Mazumder (2018) summarizes the critique of the 0.34 estimate:


Parent income is a short average, often measured when fathers are in their 50s (high transitory variance): attenuation bias
Children measured around 30, still subject to life-cycle bias; zero incomes are common at these ages and in these years
Imposing Chetty-style restrictions in the PSID (child 2-year average at 29-32, father 5-year average centered at 46) gives IGEs of 0.28-0.33
Using IRS data with children measured at 35-38 and 9 years of parent income, Mitnik et al. find IGEs of 0.55-0.74 (as summarized in Mazumder 2018)

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Reconciling: Takeaways


Measurement: short parent averages and young children push the IGE down. Our two exercises tell us the direction and rough magnitude.
Specification: the IGE depends on the treatment of zeros and on nonlinearity; the rank-rank slope is much more robust.
Different questions: the IGE also depends on how inequality changes across generations (\(\sigma_c/\sigma_p\)); the rank slope does not.


The two measures are complements: ranks for robust comparisons across places; the IGE for questions about income levels and regression to the mean.
What do you think? If you had to give one number for the U.S. IGE, what would it be, and why?

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
How Does the U.S. Compare?
Direct comparison of rank-rank slopes in administrative data (Chetty et al. 2014):


United States: 0.341
Denmark: 0.180
Canada: 0.174
P(bottom quintile to top quintile): 7.5% (U.S.), 11.7% (Denmark), 13.4% (Canada)
Caveat: ranks are defined within each country, so a lower slope alone does not mean poor children do better in absolute terms

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
The Great Gatsby Curve
Corak (2013) plots the IGE against income inequality (Gini coefficient) across countries:


Countries with more inequality in the parents’ generation have less mobility (higher IGE)
Nordic countries and Canada: low inequality and low IGEs (roughly 0.2 or below)
U.S. and U.K.: high inequality and high IGEs (roughly 0.4-0.5)
Chetty et al. (2014) replicate Corak’s correlation for 13 developed countries: standardized coefficient of 0.72 on the 1985 Gini
Named the “Great Gatsby curve” by Alan Krueger (2012)

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Correlation vs Causation
Does inequality cause low mobility? What do you think?


Mechanical channel: \(\beta = \text{corr} \times \sigma_c/\sigma_p\). Rising inequality raises the IGE even with a fixed correlation.
Common cause: higher returns to skill raise both inequality and the payoff to parental investments (we’ll see this in the Becker-Tomes model)
Institutions: countries differ in schools, taxes, labor markets, family policy; these may drive both
Reverse causality: low mobility today produces more inequality tomorrow
Only about a dozen countries, measured with different data and methods: hard to separate these explanations

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Getting the Data

What do you think? Which measure should a policymaker target?

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Where is Mobility Highest?
High upward-mobility areas tend to have (Chetty et al. 2014):


Less residential segregation (by income and race; shorter commutes)
Less inequality in the bottom 99% (a larger middle class); the top 1% share barely matters
Better K-12 schools (test scores, dropout rates)
More social capital (an index of civic participation and community involvement)
More stable family structure (fewer single-parent households)



A within-U.S. Great Gatsby curve: CZs with more bottom-99% inequality have lower upward mobility.

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
A Simple Regression
Standardize everything, regress upward mobility on one proxy from each category (as in Chetty et al. (2014), Table VI):


Code
zscore_(x) = (x .- mean(x)) ./ std(x)
d = dropmissing(cz[:, [:am, :frac_commute_lt15, :gini_bottom99, :hs_dropout_resid,
                       :social_capital, :frac_single_mothers]])
X = hcat(ones(nrow(d)), zscore_(d.frac_commute_lt15), zscore_(d.gini_bottom99),
         zscore_(d.hs_dropout_resid), zscore_(d.social_capital), zscore_(d.frac_single_mothers))
b = X \ zscore_(d.am)
vars = ["Commute < 15 min", "Gini bottom 99%", "HS dropout (inc. adj.)",
        "Social capital", "Single mothers"]
using Markdown
Markdown.parse("| Variable | Coefficient |\n|:--|--:|\n" *
    join(["| $(v) | $(round(c, digits = 3)) |" for (v, c) in zip(vars, b[2:end])], "\n"))

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Social Capital: Economic Connectedness
More recent work measures social capital directly (Chetty et al. 2022):


Uses friendship networks on Facebook for tens of millions of U.S. adults
Economic connectedness: the share of friends with high socioeconomic status among people with low socioeconomic status
Economic connectedness is among the strongest predictors of upward mobility across areas, stronger than other measures of social capital (e.g. civic engagement, network cohesiveness)
Still a correlation: connected places differ in many other ways

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
These Are Correlations


Chetty et al. (2014) emphasize that these factors “should not be interpreted as causal determinants of mobility”
Two very different explanations for why poor children in Salt Lake City do better than in Charlotte:

Causal place effects: growing up in Salt Lake City changes children’s outcomes
Sorting: families who live in Salt Lake City are different (in ways not captured by parent income)

How could we tell these apart?

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
The Movers Design
Chetty and Hendren (2018a) study families who move across areas while their children are growing up:


Compare children who move to the same destination at different ages
If places have causal effects, children who move earlier get more years of exposure to the destination
Prediction: outcomes converge toward those of children who grew up in the destination, in proportion to years of exposure
Concern: families who move earlier may be different. Addressed with sibling comparisons (same family, different ages at the move) and placebo tests.

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Childhood Exposure Effects
Key findings (Chetty and Hendren 2018a, 2018b):


Children’s outcomes converge to those of permanent residents of the destination at roughly 4% per year of childhood exposure
Moving after the early 20s has little effect: what matters is where you grow up
Areas with larger causal effects have less segregation and concentrated poverty, less inequality, better schools, and more two-parent families: the same correlates as before

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Experimental Evidence: Moving to Opportunity


1990s experiment: families in high-poverty public housing were randomly offered vouchers to move to lower-poverty neighborhoods
Chetty, Hendren, and Katz (2016): children who moved before age 13 had substantially higher earnings as adults (about 30% higher in their mid-20s) and higher college attendance
Children who moved as teenagers did not benefit, consistent with exposure effects
Randomization rules out sorting: neighborhoods matter causally

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Key Takeaways


The U.S. has lower relative mobility than many developed countries: an IGE of 0.4-0.6, a rank-rank slope of about 0.34
Measuring the IGE is hard: transitory income and life-cycle profiles bias estimates toward zero
The rank-rank slope is a more robust summary; relative and absolute mobility can tell different stories
Mobility varies dramatically by geography, and movers and experimental evidence show that where children grow up has causal effects
Absolute mobility (earning more than your parents) has also fallen: from about 90% for children born in 1940 to about 50% for children born in the 1980s (Chetty et al. 2017)

title: Intergenerational Mobility
section: Looking Ahead: A Model of the IGE
text:
Looking Ahead: A Model of the IGE
So far we have measured persistence. What model of family behavior could generate an IGE?


Parents may pass on ability or preferences (nature, culture)
Parents invest money and time in children’s human capital
Some parents may be borrowing constrained: they would like to invest more but cannot

Mazumder (2005) finds a higher IGE for families with little or no wealth

Neighborhoods are another input chosen (and paid for) by parents
Next lecture: the Becker-Tomes model (Becker and Tomes 1979, 1986) makes these channels precise. Watch for how \(\beta\) (the IGE) depends on ability persistence, returns to human capital, and credit constraints

title: Intergenerational Mobility
text:

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Overview


We documented that inequality is increasing in the US
We don’t yet have a model to think about policy implications
A natural policy to consider is taxes and transfers
Look at planner’s problem
Distinguish between insurance vs redistribution effects
Look at a research application: Storesletten, Telmer, and Yaron (2004)

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Example 1: Static Economy


One period economy
Two types of agent: \(\tau\in\{L,H\}\) (equal proportions)
Uncertain income: \(\{y_{L},y_{H}\}\), \(y_{L}<y_{H}\)
Distributions: \(\{\pi,1-\pi\}\) for low type, \(\{1-\pi,\pi\}\) for high type, \(\pi>0.5\).
Concave utility \(u(\cdot)\)
No insurance market (and symmetrically for \(V_{H}\)): \[ V_{L} = \mathbb{E}[u(y)|L] = \pi u(y_{L}) + (1-\pi) u(y_{H})\]

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Example 1: Planner’s Problem


Let \(c(\tau,y)\) be consumption of type \(\tau\) when income \(y\) is realized.
Planner’s objective: \[ W = \mathbb{E}[u(c(\tau,y))] = 0.5\mathbb{E}[u(c(L,y))|L] + 0.5\mathbb{E}[u(c(H,y))|H] \]
In the laissez-faire economy: \[ W_{0} = 0.5u(y_{L}) + 0.5u(y_{H}) \]
Planner’s problem: \[\max_{c(\tau,y)}\mathbb{E}[u(c(\tau,y))]\ s.t. \mathbb{E}[c(\tau,y)] = 0.5y_{L} + 0.5y_{H} \]
Exercise: show that \(c^*(\tau,y) = 0.5y_{L} + 0.5y_{H} \equiv C^*\) (perfect smoothing), so \(W_{1} = u(C^*)\)

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Example 1: Separating insurance and redistribution


Notice: the planner cares only about average utility, not about changes in \(V_{H}\) and \(V_{L}\)
Exercise: study changes in \(V_{\tau}\) for different values of \(\pi\)
Redistribution and insurance effects are bundled together
How to separate?
Define the certainty equivalent \(\bar{c}_{\tau}\) of each type: \[ u(\bar{c}_{\tau}) = \mathbb{E}[u(y)|\tau],\ \tau\in\{L,H\}\]
Interpretation: guaranteed consumption that would deliver the same expected utility as the risky income stream

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Example 1: Gains from redistribution


Let \(\bar{C} = 0.5\bar{c}_{L} + 0.5\bar{c}_{H}\) be the average certainty equivalent
\(u(\bar{C})\) is utility if everyone could be given the average certainty equivalent from the benchmark economy.
The difference \[u(\bar{C}) - \mathbb{E}[u(y)] = u(0.5\bar{c}_{L}+0.5\bar{c}_{H}) - 0.5u(\bar{c}_{L}) - 0.5u(\bar{c}_{H})\] is a measure of the gains from redistribution when uncertainty is removed via certainty equivalence

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Example 1: A decomposition


\(u(C^*) - u(\bar{C})\) is likewise a measure of the gains from insurance derived from valuing gains in certainty equivalents.
This gives a decomposition: \[\begin{aligned}
W_{1} - W_{0} &= \Big[u(C^*) - u(\bar{C})\Big] + \Big[u(\bar{C}) - \mathbb{E}[u(y)]\Big]\\[0.3em]
&= \text{insurance} + \text{redistribution}
\end{aligned}\]
Exercises:

Calculate the decomposition with log utility
Look at how it changes with \(\pi\)
