title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
The decomposition in general


The same idea works for comparing any two regimes \(A\) and \(B\) (e.g. no taxes vs. a progressive tax), neither of which needs to provide perfect insurance
Let \(\mathcal{V}(c)\) be the value of receiving \(c\) for sure (\(\mathcal{V}(c)=u(c)\) in a static economy)
For each person \(i\): value \(V^{r}_{i}\) and certainty equivalent \(\mathcal{V}(\bar{c}^{r}_{i}) = V^{r}_{i}\)
Welfare \(W^{r} = \int V^{r}_{i}di\), average certainty equivalent \(\bar{C}^{r} = \int\bar{c}^{r}_{i}di\), average consumption \(C^*\) (same in both regimes)
Decomposition: \[\begin{aligned}
W^{B} - W^{A} = &\ \Big[\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B}) - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})\Big] && \text{(insurance)}\\
&+ \Big[\big(W^{B} - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})\big) - \big(W^{A} - \mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})\big)\Big] && \text{(redistribution)}
\end{aligned}\]
Exercise: check that with \(A\) = laissez-faire and \(B\) = perfect insurance (\(\bar{C}^{B} = C^*\), \(W^{B} = u(C^*)\)) this is the decomposition from Example 1

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Measuring gains in consumption units


Utils are hard to interpret. The consumption equivalent \(\omega\) is the percentage increase in consumption, in every period and state, that makes regime \(A\) as good as regime \(B\): \[ \int\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t}\beta^{t}u((1+\omega)c^{A}_{it})\right]di = W^{B}\]
We can split it multiplicatively: \(1+\omega = (1+\omega_{I})(1+\omega_{R})\), where \[ 1+\omega_{I} = \frac{\bar{C}^{B}}{\bar{C}^{A}}\qquad\text{(insurance)}\]

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Consumption units with CRRA utility


With CRRA utility \(u(c) = c^{1-\sigma}/(1-\sigma)\), scaling consumption by \((1+\omega)\) scales values by \((1+\omega)^{1-\sigma}\), so: \[ 1+\omega = \left[\frac{W^{B}}{W^{A}}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)},\qquad 1+\omega_{R} = \left[\frac{W^{B}/\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{B})}{W^{A}/\mathcal{V}(\bar{C}^{A})}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)}\]
With log utility: \(\log(1+\omega) = (1-\beta)(W^{B}-W^{A})\) in an infinite horizon economy
We will compute these in recitation using a life-cycle model

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Example 2: a dynamic economy


Assume same type structure, \(\tau(i)\in\{L,H\}\) for all agents \(i\)
But now infinite horizon, \(t=0,1,2,...,\infty\)
\(\log(y_{it}) = \mu_{\tau(i)} + \varepsilon_{it}\), \(\ \varepsilon_{it}\sim{N}(0,\sigma^2)\) i.i.d., \(\ \mu_{L}<\mu_{H}\)
Benchmark: no private insurance markets, \(c_{it} = y_{it}\).
\(V_{i} = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^\infty \beta^{t}u(c_{it})\right]\), \(\ 0<\beta<1\)
Assume \(u(\cdot) = \log(\cdot)\).

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Example 2: Welfare and \(C^*\)


Since \(\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t} = 1/(1-\beta)\), we know that: \[ V_{\tau} = \mu_{\tau} / (1-\beta) \]
If \(\log(X)\) is normal with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), we know that \[\mathbb{E}[X] = \exp(\mu + 0.5\sigma^2)\] hence \[\mathbb{E}[y_{i,t}] = 0.5\exp(\mu_{L}+0.5\sigma^2) + 0.5\exp(\mu_{H}+0.5\sigma^2)\]
This is also what the planner would allocate to everyone. Call this \(C^*\).

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Example 2: Certainty equivalents


For type \(\tau\), \(\bar{c}_{\tau}\) solves: \[ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\beta^{t} \log(\bar{c}_{\tau}) = \mu_{\tau}/(1-\beta) \] and so \(\bar{c}_{\tau} = \exp(\mu_{\tau})\)
Thus \(\bar{C} = 0.5\exp(\mu_{L}) + 0.5\exp(\mu_{H})\)

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Example 2: Exercise


Exercise (board): show that the insurance term simplifies to \[ \text{insurance} = \frac{\sigma^2/2}{1-\beta}\]
Hint: factor \(\exp(0.5\sigma^2)\) out of the first sum
Notice that this does not depend on \(\mu_{L}\) or \(\mu_{H}\): the value of insurance depends only on how much risk there is, not on inequality between types
In consumption units: \(\log(1+\omega_{I}) = (1-\beta)\times\text{insurance}\), so \(1+\omega_{I} = \exp(\sigma^2/2) = C^*/\bar{C}\)
Similarly, the redistribution term depends only on \(\mu_{L}\) and \(\mu_{H}\), not on \(\sigma^2\)

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Overview: Storesletten, Telmer, and Yaron (2004)
Main Question: Can individual earnings risk explain why consumption and income inequality increase with age?


Key Finding: Yes! An overlapping generations model with uninsurable earnings shocks can account for:

Both earnings and consumption inequality over the life cycle
The fact that consumption inequality increases less than earnings inequality

Data Sources:

Earnings: Panel Study of Income Dynamics (PSID), 1969-1992
Consumption: Consumer Expenditure Survey (CEX), 1980-1990

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
The Empirical Facts




Three striking patterns in U.S. data:

Both earnings and consumption inequality increase substantially with age (ages 23-60)
Consumption inequality rises less than earnings inequality
Both increase approximately linearly over working years

Interpretation: Imperfect risk sharing - something between complete markets and autarky

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Is It Just Predetermined Skills?






We see rising inequality within each education group
Even controlling for broad skill measures, idiosyncratic risk matters

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
The Earnings Process
Log earnings for household \(i\) at age \(h\): \[ \log(n_{ih}) = \kappa_h + \alpha_i + z_{ih} + \varepsilon_{ih} \]


\(\kappa_h\): deterministic age profile
\(\alpha_i \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\alpha)\): fixed effect (realized at birth, permanent)
\(z_{ih}\): persistent shock: \(z_{ih} = \rho z_{i,h-1} + \eta_{ih}\), where \(\eta_{ih} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\eta)\)
\(\varepsilon_{ih} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\varepsilon)\): transitory shock (i.i.d.)



Key Estimate: \(\rho \approx 0.999\) (near unit root!)

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Why Near Unit-Root Persistence?






The linear shape of the age-variance profile is crucial
Lower persistence (ρ < 0.95) would generate concave profiles
Near unit-root (ρ ≈ 1) generates the linear pattern we see in data
This is a robust finding across different specifications

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
The Model: Key Features
Overlapping Generations Economy:


Agents live ages 22-100, retire at 65
Face uninsurable idiosyncratic earnings shocks
Can save/borrow via a single asset (capital)
Pay-as-you-go social security system
General equilibrium: aggregate wealth is endogenous



Calibration Strategy:

Match aggregate wealth/income ratio = 3.1 (for bottom 99%)
Match earnings process to PSID data
Check if model matches consumption inequality from CEX

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
The Model: Household Problem
Recursive formulation: agent of age \(h\) with assets \(a\), fixed effect \(\alpha\), persistent shock \(z\) and transitory shock \(\varepsilon\) solves: \[ V_h(a,\alpha,z,\varepsilon) = \max_{c, a'} \left\{ u(c) + \beta \psi_h \mathbb{E}[V_{h+1}(a',\alpha,z',\varepsilon')|z] \right\} \]
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{subject to}\quad c + a' &= (1+r)a + w\,e_h(\alpha,z,\varepsilon) - T\big(w\,e_h(\alpha,z,\varepsilon)\big) \\
a' &\geq \underline{a} \quad \text{(borrowing limit)} \\
z' &= \rho z + \eta', \quad \eta' \sim N(0,\sigma^2_\eta),\quad \varepsilon'\sim N(0,\sigma^2_{\varepsilon})
\end{aligned}\]


\(\psi_h\): survival probability to age \(h+1\)
\(e_h(\alpha,z,\varepsilon) = \exp(\kappa_h + \alpha + z + \varepsilon)\): labor efficiency units (zero after retirement at 65)
Labor earnings are \(n_{h} = w\,e_h\), which is the process estimated from the PSID
\(T(\cdot)\): tax/transfer function (includes social security contributions and benefits)

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
The Model: Equilibrium
Stationary Competitive Equilibrium consists of:


Value and policy functions: \(\{V_h(x), c_h(x), a_{h+1}(x)\}_{h=22}^{100}\), where \(x = (a,\alpha,z,\varepsilon)\)
Distribution: Stationary distribution \(\Phi(h,x)\) over age, assets, fixed effect, persistent and transitory shocks
Prices: \(r = f_K(K, L) - \delta\) and \(w = f_L(K, L)\), where \(f(K,L) = K^\theta L^{1-\theta}\) is the aggregate production function
Market clearing: \[K = \int a \, d\Phi(h,x),\ \ L = \int e_h(\alpha,z,\varepsilon) \, d\Phi(h,x)\] (\(L\) is total efficiency units of labor, not total earnings)
Government budget balance: Social security system is self-financing

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Main Results






Model matches earnings inequality by construction (calibration target)
Benchmark (no social security): 20% too much consumption inequality
With social security: Nearly perfect match!
Social security’s concave replacement rate provides implicit insurance within generations

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
The Role of Wealth

Aggregate wealth is crucial for risk sharing:

More wealth → more buffer-stock savings → more consumption smoothing
Model calibrated to match U.S. wealth/income ratio = 3.1
Experiment: Reduce wealth/income ratio from 3.1 to 1.5

Result: Consumption inequality ↑ by 17%
Would need 36% (vs. 20%) reduction in shock variances to match data

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Insurance vs. Redistribution Decomposition
Key Welfare Question: Which matters more?

Fixed effects (\(\alpha_i\)): Inequality determined at birth
Life-cycle shocks (\(z_{ih}, \varepsilon_{ih}\)): Shocks received during working years


Results:



Type of Risk
Welfare Cost (% of consumption)




Life-cycle shocks
27.4%


Fixed effects
20.2%

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Connecting back to the decomposition


Map to Example 2: fixed effects \(\alpha_{i}\) play the role of types \(\mu_{\tau}\); life-cycle shocks \(z_{ih},\varepsilon_{ih}\) play the role of \(\varepsilon_{it}\)
Fixed effects are known at birth: there is no risk after birth to insure. Removing them is a gain from redistribution across people who are permanently different
Life-cycle shocks are risk faced by each person. Removing them is a gain from insurance
So the table says: in this economy, the potential gain from better insurance (27.4%) is at least as large as the potential gain from removing inequality determined at birth (20.2%)
Caveat: these numbers are welfare costs of each source of inequality behind the veil of ignorance, not the effect of a specific policy. Real policies (e.g. progressive taxes) typically deliver some of both
In recitation we will compute the insurance and redistribution components of a progressive tax in a model like this one

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Policy Implications


Life-cycle shocks are important for welfare

Not just predetermined heterogeneity!
Buffer-stock savings and precautionary behavior matter

Social security provides valuable insurance

Concave replacement rate redistributes within generations
Accounts for ~1.6% of lifetime consumption in welfare gains

Policy design matters

Insurance against life-cycle shocks is as important as addressing inequality at birth
Both pre-labor market interventions (education) AND insurance mechanisms (social security, unemployment insurance) are valuable

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
Conclusion: What We Learned


Empirical: Earnings shocks are highly persistent (ρ ≈ 1)

This is necessary to match linear increase in inequality

Theoretical: Incomplete markets model can quantitatively account for consumption inequality over life cycle

Key ingredients: persistent shocks + calibrated wealth + social security

Normative: Life-cycle uncertainty is at least as important as fixed heterogeneity

Challenges the view that all inequality is predetermined
Supports role for insurance mechanisms and financial markets

Methodological: Age profiles of inequality are informative about risk sharing

Rising consumption inequality → imperfect insurance
General equilibrium + quantitative calibration crucial

title: Policy Implications: Insurance vs Redistribution
text:
References


Storesletten, Kjetil, Christopher I. Telmer, and Amir Yaron. 2004. “Consumption and Risk Sharing over the Life Cycle.” Journal of Monetary Economics, no. 3: 609–33. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmoneco.2003.06.005.

text:
Education Premia

Define the “college premium” or “returns to college” as: \[\begin{aligned}
&\mathbb{E}[\log(\text{wage})\ |\ \text{bachelor's degree or more}] \\
&\quad - \mathbb{E}[\log(\text{wage})\ |\ \text{high school diploma, no college}]
\end{aligned}\]
Similarly, a “two-year premium” compares an associate’s degree (or 2-3 years of college) to a high school diploma
In IPUMS EDUC: high school diploma is 73 (72 in the 1990-91 surveys), 71 is grade 12 without a diploma, associate’s degrees are 91-92, a bachelor’s is 111
Caveat: before the 1992 survey the CPS recorded years of schooling rather than degrees, so there is a coding break at income year 1991
Note: there are other definitions Heathcote et al. (2023)

title: Documenting Inequality
text:
Life-cycle wage dynamics


So far we have seen changes in wage distributions and wage gaps over time
But perhaps these statistics vary with age, too.
We have 36 years of data (income years 1989-2024) to follow cohorts as they age
Beware the rank condition!

title: Documenting Inequality
section: The Rank Condition: Age, Period, Cohort
text:
The Rank Condition: Age, Period, Cohort


We might like to write the variance of log wages as the sum of three effects: \[ \text{var}(\log w)_{a,t} = f(\text{age}) + g(\text{year}) + h(\text{cohort}) \]
But age, year, and cohort (birth year) are tied together by an identity: \(\text{age} = \text{year} - \text{cohort}\)
So the three regressors are perfectly collinear: the design matrix does not have full rank
E.g. a linear age trend can always be relabeled as a linear year trend minus a linear cohort trend
To separate them we need a restriction from outside the data, e.g. “no time effects”, “no cohort effects”, or “cohort effects are zero within 10-year bins”
Keep this in mind for the next plot: how much of the rise with age might really be a time or cohort effect?

title: Documenting Inequality

title: Documenting Inequality
section: Key Finding 3: The Declining Role of the Household
text:
Key Finding 3: The Declining Role of the Household


Define index of household income pooling: \[ HP_{t} = \left(var(y_{it}) - var(\bar{y}_{it})\right) / var(y_{it}) \]
\(\bar{y}_{i}\): per-person income in household \(i\)
Interpretation: the share of variance in income reduced by pooling at household level
Household income pooling used to reduce inequality by 60% in 1967
By 2021, only reduces inequality by 35%
Why the decline? (decomposition exercise at board)

Narrowing gender earnings gap → women less reliant on spousal income
Rising correlation of earnings within couples → less insurance

Single households increasingly disadvantaged

title: Documenting Inequality
section: Main Takeaways from Heathcote et al. (2023)
text:
Main Takeaways from Heathcote et al. (2023)


Inequality at top: Driven by wage differentials, continues to grow (but more slowly)
Inequality at bottom: Driven by employment, dominated by cyclical fluctuations
The household: Declining importance as inequality-reducing mechanism
The government: Increasing role in redistribution and stabilization
Consumption: Remains remarkably stable despite income inequality trends

title: Documenting Inequality
section: Summary: What We Found in the CPS
text:
Summary: What We Found in the CPS


In the CPS-ASEC (income years 1989-2024), the p90-p10 gap in log wages widened, driven by fast growth at the 90th percentile; the p75-p25 gap changed much less
The gender gap in mean log wages roughly halved; the Black-white gap shows no clear trend
The four-year college premium rose, the two-year premium did not
Wage inequality within a cohort grows with age, but age, period, and cohort effects cannot all be separated
Data details matter: weights, the timing of income questions, survey redesigns, and coding breaks

title: Documenting Inequality
text:
What’s next?

We’ve got a good picture of:

Patterns of inequality over time and over the life-cycle
The role that government transfers can play in off-setting this

But we don’t yet know:

What are the welfare implications of these facts?
How much would people value programs that insure / redistribute?
What are the origins of this inequality and should we counteract with policy?

These are the topics we will work on for the rest of this course

title: ECON4538 - Syllabus
text: This is an advanced undergraduate course in Labor Economics. Please read below for the course outline and syllabus.

title: ECON4538 - Syllabus
text:
Admin Details
For details on assessment, lecture times, and office hours, please refer to the course Canvas page.

title: ECON4538 - Syllabus
text:
Course Overview and Objectives
In this class we will address questions at the forefront of modern economic policy. What factors drive economic inequality over the life-cycle? How are these evolving over time? What are the potential costs and benefits to collective provision of insurance and redistribution? What policies are effective in creating equal opportunity?
To answer these questions you will learn the basic tools of modern quantitative economics. We will be interested in understanding the models and tools that economists have developed to understand labor market inequality, as well as in using these models to analyze the welfare implications of various government interventions. Topics to be covered include: dynamic programming, solution methods of general equilibrium models, heterogeneous-agent macroeconomic models, models of human capital formation, and modern empirical evidence on the nature human capital.

title: ECON4538 - Syllabus
text:
Student Learning Outcomes
On successfully completing this course, students should be familiar with some of the core concepts in modern quantitative economics. Students should be able to formalize an appropriate dynamic, stochastic, general equilibrium model to analyze a question of interest. Students should be able to solve and simulate such a model on a computer, for the purpose of interpreting data and conducting policy experiments.

title: ECON4538 - Syllabus
text:
Course Prerequisites
I will assume that you are comfortable with micro concepts at the level of Econ 3101, 3102, such as the utility maximization problem and its related topics. I will also assume that you are comfortable with basic econometrics such as multivariate regression techniques as well as statistics at the level of Stat 3011. With regards to your math background, I will take as granted that you know how to work with calculus (derivatives). Students should be willing to invest time in learning a computer programming language such as julia.

title: ECON4538 - Syllabus
text:
Textbook
We will use some chapters and problem sets from Recursive Macroeconomic Theory (Ljungqvist and Sargent 2012, 3rd edition) available online via the University Library. We will also make use of Journal Articles. I have provided links to electronic versions of the textbook and journal articles are available on the “Library Course Page”.

Additional Readings
You may also find some of the following books useful.

John Stachurski, Economic Dynamics: Theory and Computation, 2nd edition, (2022).
Christopher Pissarides, Equilibrium Unemployment Theory, 2nd edition, (2000).
Jérôme Adda and Russell Cooper, Dynamic Economics: Quantitative Methods and Applications, (2003).
Mario Miranda and Paul Fackler, Applied Computational Economics and Finance, (2002).
Kenneth Judd, Numerical Methods in Economics, (1998).

title: ECON4538 - Syllabus
text:
Course Software and Resources
We will demonstrate and develop the computational tools you are learning using the julia programming language, which is well-suited for scientific computation and data analysis. LATIS provides a copy of julia on AppstoGo, but we recommend installing your own version, since it is completely free and open source. See the website for more details on the language and installation instructions.
Throughout the course, you may find the QuantEcon julia course (by Tom Sargent, John Stachurski, and Jesse Perla) a useful additional resource.

title: ECON4538 - Syllabus
text:
Course Outline

Dynamic Programming and Applications
An important set of mathematical tools for solving dynamic models. Topics include:

Bellman’s principal of optimality and contraction mappings
Mathematical and computational exposition (using julia) of dynamic programming tools, applied to:

Models of job search
Infinite horizon and life-cycle models of savings


Reading: Ljungqvist and Sargent (2012) Chapters 3-6.


Savings and incomplete markets
Review of the main theoretical models describing savings and self-insurance of agents under uncertainity and incomplete markets.

Main savings problems
Incomplete markets models as Huggett (1993), Aiyagari (1994), Krusell and Smith (1998)
Consumption inequality and income uncertainity.

Reading: Ljungqvist and Sargent (2012) Chapters 17-18. Deaton (1991), Blundell and Preston (1998), Huggett (1993), Aiyagari (1994), Krusell and Smith (1998)


Facts about Inequality
We review and replicate facts about labor market inequality in the United States. Topics include:

Documenting income inequality (Moffitt and Gottschalk 2011; Heathcote, Perri, and Violante 2010; Heathcote et al. 2023; Guvenen et al. 2021)
Estimation of income risk (Moffitt and Gottschalk 2011; Meghir and Pistaferri 2004; Low, Meghir, and Pistaferri 2010; Guvenen 2009)
Welfare implications of income inequality (Storesletten, Telmer, and Yaron 2004)

Redistribution vs Insurance

The Intergenerational Elasticity of Earnings (Corak 2013; Mazumder 2005, 2018)



Theories of Human Capital and Inequality
We introduce textbook theories of human capital formation and examine their empirical content. We develop computational tools to bring these theories to data. Topics include:

The Becker-Tomes model of intergenerational inequality via human capital investment (Becker and Tomes 1979, 1986)

Policy implications of the model (efficiency and redistribution)

Debates on the empirical and conceptual merits of the Becker-Tomes model (Goldberger 1989; Mulligan 1999; Cunha et al. 2006; Cunha and Heckman 2007)
Skills and Inequality (J. Heckman, Stixrud, and Urzua 2006; Cunha and Heckman 2008a; Cunha and Heckman 2009)
Quantitative and theoretical extensions of the baseline model (Lee and Seshadri 2019; Caucutt and Lochner 2020)



Connecting Human Capital Theory with Evidence
We survey some empirical work that connects the theory with data. Topics include:

A review of econometric methods for causal inference
Evidence of the effect of social programs on child skill formation and long-run outcomes (Dahl and Lochner 2012; Barr, Eggleston, and Smith 2022; Bastian and Michelmore 2018; Carneiro et al. 2021; Bailey et al. 2024)
Evidence of the effect of early childhood education on skill formation and long-run outcomes (J. J. Heckman et al. 2010; García et al. 2020; Kline and Walters 2016)
Evidence of the effect of parenting and home interventions on skill formation and long-run outcomes (Attanasio, Meghir, and Nix 2020; Walker et al. 2022; Carneiro et al. 2024)
Estimating the technology of skill formation. (Cunha and Heckman 2008b; Attanasio, Meghir, and Nix 2020)

title: Assignment 6
text:
This assignment works with the technology of skill formation from Lecture 6 (Cunha and Heckman 2007; Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach 2010). A child is born with initial skill \(\theta_1\). A parent invests \(I_1\) in early childhood and \(I_2\) in late childhood. Skills evolve according to
\[
\theta_{2} = \left[\gamma_1\theta_1^{\phi_1} + (1-\gamma_1)I_1^{\phi_1}\right]^{1/\phi_1}, \qquad
\theta_{3} = \left[\gamma_2\theta_2^{\phi_2} + (1-\gamma_2)I_2^{\phi_2}\right]^{1/\phi_2}
\]
where \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\in(0,1)\) and \(\phi_1,\phi_2 < 1\). When \(\phi_t \to 0\) the corresponding stage is Cobb-Douglas: \(\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t^{\gamma_t}I_t^{1-\gamma_t}\). The parent has a fixed budget \(B\) (in period-1 units) and can borrow and save at gross interest rate \(R\), so that
\[ I_1 + \frac{I_2}{R} = B. \]
The parent chooses \((I_1, I_2)\) to maximize the child’s adult skill \(\theta_3\). Unless stated otherwise, use \(\gamma_1 = 0.3\), \(\gamma_2 = 0.7\) and \(R = 1.1\).

Optimal timing (analytical). Suppose \(\phi_1 = \phi_2 = \phi\).

Substitute \(\theta_2\) into the second-stage technology to write \(\theta_3\) as a function of \(\theta_1\), \(I_1\) and \(I_2\).
Show that the optimal ratio of early to late investment is \[ \frac{I_1}{I_2} = \left(\frac{\gamma_2(1-\gamma_1)}{(1-\gamma_2)R}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\phi}}. \]
Explain in words what \(\gamma_2(1-\gamma_1)\) and \((1-\gamma_2)R\) represent. How does the ratio change as \(\phi \to -\infty\)? As \(\phi \to 1\)?
Does the optimal ratio depend on the child’s initial skill \(\theta_1\)? Does the child’s final skill \(\theta_3\)?

Optimal timing (numerical). Write a function that, given \(\theta_1\), \(B\) and the parameters, finds the share of the budget \(s = I_1/B\) that maximizes \(\theta_3\).

Check your code against the formula from question 1 for \(\phi \in \{-1, 0, 0.5\}\).
With \(B = 1\), plot the optimal early share \(s\) and the resulting \(\theta_3\) against \(\phi \in [-2, 0.8]\), for \(\theta_1 \in \{0.25, 0.5, 1, 2\}\). Describe what you find.
Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach (2010) find that, for cognitive skills, the elasticity of substitution is higher early in childhood than later. Set \(\phi_1 = 0.5\) and \(\phi_2 = -0.5\) and plot the optimal early share against \(\theta_1 \in [0.1, 2]\). Does the answer to 1(d) still hold? Give some intuition.

The cost of delaying remediation. Consider an advantaged child with \(\theta_1 = 1\) who receives \(I_1 = I_2 = 1\), and let \(\bar{\theta}\) be the adult skill this child reaches. A disadvantaged child starts with \(\theta_1 = 0.5\). Assume \(\phi_1 = \phi_2 = \phi\).

Early remediation: find the smallest budget \(B\) such that, investing optimally, the disadvantaged child reaches \(\bar{\theta}\).
Delayed remediation: suppose the disadvantaged child only receives \(I_1 = 0.5\) in early childhood, and help arrives only in late childhood. Find the \(I_2\) needed to reach \(\bar{\theta}\), and the total cost \(0.5 + I_2/R\).
Report both costs and their ratio for \(\phi \in \{-0.5, -0.25, 0, 0.25, 0.5\}\). What happens as \(\phi\) falls?
Show that when \(\phi < 0\), there is an upper bound on \(\theta_3\) that no amount of late investment can exceed. What is it? Connect your answer to the idea of a critical period.

Measurement error (optional, extra credit). In the data we never observe skills directly, only test scores (Lecture 6). Set \(\phi_1 = 0\), so that \(\log\theta_2 = \gamma_1\log\theta_1 + (1-\gamma_1)\log I_1\).

Simulate \(N = 5{,}000\) children with \(\log\theta_1 \sim N(0, 0.5^2)\) and \(\log I_1 = 0.3\log\theta_1 + \nu\), \(\nu\sim N(0,0.5^2)\) (better-endowed children receive more investment). Compute \(\theta_2\).
Generate two test scores \(Z_j = \log\theta_1 + \varepsilon_j\), \(j=1,2\), and an outcome measure \(Y = \log\theta_2 + u\), with independent normal errors (\(\text{sd}(\varepsilon_j) = 0.5\), \(\text{sd}(u) = 0.3\)).
Regress \(Y\) on a constant, \(Z_1\) and \(\log I_1\). Compare the estimates of \(\gamma_1\) and \(1-\gamma_1\) to the truth. Why is the coefficient on investment also biased?
Re-estimate by two-stage least squares, using \(Z_2\) as an instrument for \(Z_1\). Explain why this works.






References

Cunha, Flavio, and James Heckman. 2007. “The Technology of Skill Formation.” The American Economic Review, no. 2: 31–47. https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.97.2.31.


Cunha, Flavio, James J. Heckman, and Susanne M. Schennach. 2010. “Estimating the Technology of Cognitive and Noncognitive Skill Formation.” Econometrica 78 (3): 883–931. https://doi.org/10.3982/ECTA6551.

title: Assignment 4
text:
Question 2: Life-Cycle Bias
Now suppose that the child’s log income at age \(a\) follows a heterogeneous income profile (as in Lecture 3):
\[ y_{ia} = Y_i + g_i (a - \bar{a}) + u_{ia}, \qquad g_i = \bar{g} + \kappa (Y_i - \mathbb{E}[Y_i]) + \xi_i\]

section: Question 3: Relative and Absolute Mobility Across Commuting Zones
text:
Question 3: Relative and Absolute Mobility Across Commuting Zones
The data contain, for each CZ, absolute upward mobility (am, the expected income rank of children whose parents are at the 25th percentile of the national distribution), relative mobility (rm, the rank-rank slope), the probability of reaching the top quintile from the bottom quintile (p_q5_q1), the population in 2000 (pop2000), and a set of CZ characteristics.

Load the data and drop CZs with missing mobility estimates. Plot am against rm and report the correlation between them, both unweighted and weighted by population (use weights(:pop2000)). (this question requires code)
Because the rank-rank relationship is linear within each CZ, the expected rank of a child with parents at percentile \(p\) is \(\text{am} + (p - 25)\times\text{rm}\). For the 50 largest CZs, compute the expected rank at \(p = 10\) and \(p = 90\). List the 5 CZs with the highest expected rank at \(p=10\) and the 5 with the highest at \(p = 90\). text:
Following Recitation 1, load the CPS-ASEC data and perform the same steps to deflate nominal $ values to 2017 dollars. title: Assignment 3
text:
Consider the life-cycle model we have used in Assignment 2 and Recitation 4. Assume that the income process is as follows:
\[ y_{it} = \mu_{t} + \alpha_{i} + \zeta_{it} + \epsilon_{it} \]
where
\[ \zeta_{it} = \rho \zeta_{it-1} + \eta_{it} \]
and \(\alpha_{i}\), \(\epsilon_{it}\), and \(\eta_{it}\) are iid, with \(\epsilon_{it}\sim N(0,\sigma_{\epsilon}^2)\), \(\eta_{it}\sim N(0,\sigma^2_{\eta})\). Let \(\sigma^2_{\alpha} = \mathbb{V}[\alpha_{i}]\) and let \(\mathbb{E}[\alpha_{i}]=0\) such that \(\mathbb{E}[y_{it}] = \mu_{t}\). Here \(y_{it}\) is log income and \(\mu_{t}\) is the (deterministic) age profile of mean log income.
Stationarity assumption. Assume that the persistent component starts from its stationary distribution: \(\zeta_{i0}\) is drawn from \(N(0, \sigma^2_{\eta}/(1-\rho^2))\). This implies that \(\mathbb{V}[\zeta_{it}] = \sigma^2_{\eta}/(1-\rho^2)\) for every \(t\), so variances and covariances do not depend on age. (This is a simplification: Recitation 4 showed that the variance of log income actually rises with age. We make the assumption so that we can pool all ages when computing moments.)
You are going to estimate the parameters of this income process using the psid data from Recitation 4 and repeat the welfare analysis from that session. Use the same cleaning steps as Recitation 4: drop household-years with income below $1,000 and measure income in thousands of dollars. The function load_psid in income_tools.jl does both.

Repeating the analysis from class, show that the following relationships hold under the assumptions above: \[ \begin{align}
\mathbb{V}[y_{it}] = \sigma^2_{\alpha} + \mathbb{V}[\zeta_{it}] + \sigma^2_{\epsilon} \\
\mathbb{C}(y_{it},y_{it+s}) = \sigma^2_{\alpha} + \rho^{s}\mathbb{V}[\zeta_{it}]
\end{align}
\] (this question requires only math)
Use these relationships above to express the parameters \((\rho,\sigma^2_{\epsilon},\sigma^2_{\eta},\sigma^2_{\alpha})\) in terms of variances and lagged covariances. A hint: start by showing something like: \[
\rho = \frac{\mathbb{C}(y_{it},y_{it+3}) - \mathbb{C}(y_{it},y_{it+2})}{\mathbb{C}(y_{it},y_{it+2}) - \mathbb{C}(y_{it},y_{it+1})}.
\] Then you can assume you know \(\rho\), use this to get \(\mathbb{V}[\zeta_{it}]\), then \(\sigma^2_{\alpha}\), then finally \(\sigma^2_{\epsilon}\). (this question requires only math)
Following the steps in Recitation 4, use your answers to question 2 to construct estimates of the parameters of the income process: the age profile \(\{\mu_{t}\}\) (mean log income at each age from 25 to 64) and \((\rho,\sigma^2_{\epsilon},\sigma^2_{\eta},\sigma^2_{\alpha})\). Note: you will need to adjust the strategy above to account for the fact that the PSID only has data every two years. (this question requires code)
Check your answer: \(\rho\) should be between 0 and 1, and all three variance estimates should be positive. The model-implied covariances \(\sigma^2_{\alpha}+\rho^{s}\mathbb{V}[\zeta_{it}]\) should exactly match the data at the lags you used for estimation (plot them, as in Recitation 4). If \(\rho\) is negative or above one, check which lags you are differencing.
How does the estimate of \(\rho\) compare to the estimate from Recitation 4? Please provide some intuition for why.
(extra credit, 3%) Repeat the analysis of Recitation 4 (where we introduced a progressive tax) with this new income process and comment on differences you find in overall welfare impacts and differences in the insurance vs redistribution decomposition. You should use the function below, which uses the tauchen function from income_tools.jl to construct a transition matrix \(\Pi\) to approximate the income process above, assuming that \(\alpha_{i}\) can take one of three evenly spaced grid points with equal probability, and assuming that \(\epsilon_{it}\) is measurement error (i.e. does not reflect real changes in income). Note that \(\sigma\) here is the standard deviation of the innovation \(\eta\), not of \(\zeta\).
Because \(\alpha_{i}\) never changes, \(\Pi\) is block-diagonal: a household never moves between \(\alpha\) types. This means solve_steady_state(Π) does not give the right initial distribution (there is a separate stationary distribution for each type, and the eigenvalue one is repeated three times). Instead, the function also returns the correct initial distribution pi_star: each \(\alpha\) type has probability \(1/3\), and within each type \(\zeta\) is drawn from the stationary distribution of the AR(1) chain. Use pi_star wherever Recitation 4 used the stationary distribution.
Check your answer: pi_star should sum to one, and each block of \(N\) entries (one block per \(\alpha\) type) should sum to \(1/3\). Your \(\lambda\) should satisfy the resource constraint: average net income should equal average gross income at age 25 under pi_star. And your decomposition should satisfy \(1+\omega = (1+\omega_{I})(1+\omega_{R})\).


include("../recitations/income_tools.jl")   #<- loads tauchen, solve_steady_state, etc.

function approx_income_process(N, ρ, σ, σ_α)
    # use tauchen method to approximate the AR(1) component
    egrid, Π_AR = tauchen(N, ρ, σ)
    agrid = [-sqrt(3/2)*σ_α, 0., sqrt(3/2)*σ_α]
    # construct a larger grid of α .+ egrid for each α
    # (ordering: all ζ states for the first α, then the second α, etc.)
    grid = [α + e for α in agrid for e in egrid]
    # create a larger transition matrix where the
    # probability of moving from α to any other α' is zero
    Π = kron(I(3), Π_AR)
    # initial distribution: each α with probability 1/3, and ζ drawn
    # from the stationary distribution of the AR(1) chain
    pi_star = kron(fill(1/3, 3), solve_steady_state(Π_AR))
    return grid, Π, pi_star
end

title: Assignment 5
text: In this assignment you will solve the two-period Becker-Tomes model from Lecture 5 numerically, use it to study how borrowing constraints shape intergenerational mobility across the income distribution, and compare two policies.

title: Assignment 5
text:
The Model
A parent with wealth \(\Omega\) and a child with ability \(z\) (in levels) solves:
\[\max_{C_1, C_2, X, A'} \log(C_1) + \beta \log(C_2)\]
subject to:
\[
\begin{eqnarray}
C_1 + \psi X + \frac{A'}{1+r} &\leq& \Omega + T \\
C_2 &=& A' + b + (1-\tau)wzX^{\delta} \\
A' &\geq& 0
\end{eqnarray}
\]
where \(T\) is a transfer to the parent, \(\tau\) is a tax on the child’s earnings, and \(b\) is a lump-sum transfer to the child. In the baseline, \(T = \tau = b = 0\). We call \(wzX^{\delta}\) the child’s (pre-tax) earnings.
Population. Parents’ log ability is \(\zeta_{p}\sim N(0,\sigma^2_{\eta}/(1-\rho^2))\) and the child’s log ability is \(\zeta_{c} = \rho\zeta_{p} + \eta\) with \(\eta\sim N(0,\sigma^2_{\eta})\). Parental wealth and child ability are: \[ \log(\Omega) = m + \frac{\zeta_{p}}{1-\delta},\qquad z = \exp(\zeta_{c}). \] Recall from Lecture 5 that \(\frac{\zeta_{p}}{1-\delta}\) is (up to a constant) the parent’s log earnings in the unconstrained model.
Use the parameters and the code below, which draws a population of families.

using Random, Statistics

Base.@kwdef struct Params
    β::Float64 = 0.9      # altruism / discount factor
    r::Float64 = 1.0      # interest rate over one generation
    w::Float64 = 1.0      # price of human capital
    ψ::Float64 = 1.0      # price of investment
    δ::Float64 = 0.5      # returns to investment
    ρ::Float64 = 0.4      # persistence of log ability
    σ_η::Float64 = 0.5    # sd of ability innovations
    m::Float64 = -1.0     # mean of log wealth
end

function draw_population(p; N=200_000, seed=1)
    Random.seed!(seed)
    ζp = p.σ_η / sqrt(1 - p.ρ^2) * randn(N)
    ζc = p.ρ * ζp + p.σ_η * randn(N)
    return exp.(p.m .+ ζp ./ (1 - p.δ)), exp.(ζc)    # (Ω, z)
end

text:
Questions

(math)

Show that a family that is not constrained invests \(X^{*}(\tau) = \left(\frac{(1-\tau)\delta wz}{(1+r)\psi}\right)^{1/(1-\delta)}\).
Show that when \(A'=0\), the optimal \(X\) solves \[ \frac{\psi}{\Omega + T - \psi X} = \frac{\beta(1-\tau)\delta wzX^{\delta-1}}{b + (1-\tau)wzX^{\delta}}. \] Call the solution \(X_{c}\). Show that the left-hand side is increasing and the right-hand side decreasing in \(X\), so the solution is unique.
Argue that the family is constrained if and only if \(X_{c} < X^{*}(\tau)\), and that its investment is \(\min\{X_{c}, X^{*}(\tau)\}\).
Show that when \(b = 0\), \(X_{c} = \frac{\beta\delta}{\psi(1+\beta\delta)}(\Omega + T)\), which depends on neither \(\tau\) nor \(z\).

(math) In the baseline (\(T=\tau=b=0\)), let the IGE be the slope coefficient from a regression of log child earnings on \(\log(\Omega)\). Show that:

If no family is constrained, the IGE is \(\rho\).
If every family is constrained, the IGE is \(\delta + \rho(1-\delta)\).

Why is the second number larger than the first?
(code) Write a function solve_household(Ω, z, p; τ=0, b=0) that returns the optimal \(X\) and whether the family is constrained. Find \(X_{c}\) by bisection on the condition in 1(b) (do not use the closed form). Check that your function matches the closed form from 1(d) when \(b=0\).
(code) Draw the baseline population and solve every family’s problem.

Report the share of families that are constrained and the overall IGE.
Split families into quintiles of \(\Omega\). Within each quintile, compute the share constrained, \(s_{k}\), and the local IGE (the regression slope using only families in that quintile).
Compare the local IGE in each quintile to the approximation \(\rho + s_{k}\,\delta(1-\rho)\). Where does this approximation come from? Plot both against the quintile.

(code) Vary \(m\) from \(-3\) to \(1\) in steps of \(0.5\). For each value, compute the share constrained and the IGE. Plot the IGE against the share constrained. In Lecture 4 we saw that mobility varies a lot across places. What does this exercise suggest about one possible reason?
(code) Compare two policies, each evaluated on the same population:

Policy A (earnings tax): \(\tau = 0.2\), with the revenue rebated to every child as a lump sum, \(b = \tau\,\mathbb{E}[wzX^{\delta}]\). Since \(X\) depends on \(b\), you will need to iterate until \(b\) is consistent with the revenue it generates.
Policy B (targeted transfer): a transfer \(T\) to parents in the bottom quartile of \(\Omega\), financed by a proportional tax on all parents’ wealth, so that every parent has \((1-\tau_{\Omega})\Omega + T\cdot\mathbb{1}\{\Omega < \Omega_{25}\}\). Choose \(\tau_{\Omega}\) to raise the same present value of revenue per family as Policy A, \(b/(1+r)\), and \(T\) to balance the budget.

For the baseline and both policies, report: the share constrained, mean log child earnings, the IGE, and average net output per family \(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{wzX^{\delta}}{1+r} - \psi X\right]\). Explain the differences using your answers to Question 1.
(extra credit) Policy A lowers the share of constrained families. Is this good news for children? Explain.

title: Practice Exercises
text:
Consider the income process:
\[y_{it} = \alpha_i + \xi_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}\]
where \(\xi_{it} = \rho \xi_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\) and \(\eta_{it}, \varepsilon_{it}\) are iid with \(\mathbb{V}[\alpha_i] = \sigma_\alpha^2\), \(\mathbb{V}[\eta_{it}] = \sigma_\eta^2\), \(\mathbb{V}[\varepsilon_{it}] = \sigma_{\varepsilon,t}^2\).
Use population moments to argue that the parameters \(\sigma_\alpha^2, \rho, \sigma_\eta^2, \sigma_{\varepsilon,t}^2\) can be identified with panel data. Note that \(\sigma^2_{\varepsilon,t}\) is specific to the age \(t\).






Solution





Variance of income:
\[\mathbb{V}[y_{it}] = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) + \sigma_{\varepsilon,t}^2\]
\[\mathbb{V}[y_{it+1}] = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \underbrace{\rho^2 \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) + \sigma_\eta^2}_{\mathbb{V}(\xi_{it+1})} + \sigma_{\varepsilon,t+1}^2\]
Covariances:
\[\mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+1}) = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \rho \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})\]
\[\mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+2}) = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \rho^2 \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})\]
\[\mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+3}) = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \rho^3 \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})\]
Identification:
\[\rho = \frac{\mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+3}) - \mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+2})}{\mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+2}) - \mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+1})} = \frac{(\rho^3 - \rho^2) \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})}{(\rho^2 - \rho) \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})}\]
\[\mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) = \frac{\mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+2}) - \mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+1})}{\rho^2 - \rho}\]
\[\sigma_\alpha^2 = \mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+1}) - \rho \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})\]
\[\sigma_{\varepsilon,t}^2 = \mathbb{V}[y_{it}] - \sigma_\alpha^2 - \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) \quad \text{for each } t\]
Repeating the steps above starting from age \(t+1\) (using \(\mathcal{C}(y_{it+1},y_{it+2})\), \(\mathcal{C}(y_{it+1},y_{it+3})\)) identifies \(\mathbb{V}(\xi_{it+1})\), and hence \(\sigma^2_{\varepsilon,t+1}\). Since \(\mathbb{V}(\xi_{it+1}) = \rho^2\mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) + \sigma^2_{\eta}\):
\[\sigma_\eta^2 = \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it+1}) - \rho^2 \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) = \mathbb{V}[y_{it+1}] - \sigma_\alpha^2 - \rho^2 \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) - \sigma_{\varepsilon,t+1}^2\]
Done.

Consider the income process:

where \(\xi_{it} = \rho \xi_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\) and \(\eta_{it}, \varepsilon_{it}\) are iid with \(\mathbb{V}[\alpha_i] = \sigma_\alpha^2\), \(\mathbb{V}[\eta_{it}] = \sigma_\eta^2\), \(\mathbb{V}[\varepsilon_{it}] = \sigma_{\varepsilon,t}^2\).

\[\mathbb{V}[y_{it}] = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) + \sigma_{\varepsilon,t}^2\]

title: Practice Exercises
text:
Problem 3: Income Process Identification
Consider the income process:
\[y_{it} = \alpha_i + \xi_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} + \theta \varepsilon_{i,t-1}\]
where \(\xi_{it} = \rho \xi_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\), and \((\eta_{it}, \varepsilon_{it})\) are iid with \(\mathbb{V}[\alpha_i] = \sigma_\alpha^2\), \(\mathbb{V}[\varepsilon_{it}] = \sigma_{\varepsilon}^2\), \(\mathbb{V}[\eta_{it}] = \sigma_\eta^2\).
Use population moments to identify the parameters of the income process.






Solution





Variance of income:
\[\mathbb{V}[y_{it}] = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) + (1+\theta^2) \sigma_{\varepsilon}^2\]
\[\mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+1}) = C_1 = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \rho \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) + \theta \sigma_{\varepsilon}^2\]
\[\mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+2}) = C_2 = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \rho^2 \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})\]
\[\mathcal{C}(y_{it}, y_{it+s}) = C_s = \sigma_\alpha^2 + \rho^s \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) \quad \forall \, s > 1\]
Identification:
\[\rho = \frac{C_4 - C_3}{C_3 - C_2} = \frac{\rho^4 - \rho^3}{\rho^3 - \rho^2}\]
\[\mathbb{V}(\xi_{it}) = \frac{C_3 - C_2}{\rho^3 - \rho^2}, \quad \sigma_\alpha^2 = C_2 - \rho^2 \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})\]
\[\frac{(1+\theta^2)}{\theta} = \frac{\mathbb{V}(y_{it}) - \sigma_\alpha^2 - \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})}{C_1 - \sigma_\alpha^2 - \rho \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})}\]
\(\Rightarrow\) \(\theta\) is solution to quadratic.
\[\Rightarrow \sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 = \frac{\mathbb{V}(y_{it}) - \sigma_\alpha^2 - \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})}{(1+\theta^2)}\]
Finally, repeating the steps from age \(t+1\) identifies \(\mathbb{V}(\xi_{it+1})\), so \(\sigma_\eta^2 = \mathbb{V}(\xi_{it+1}) - \rho^2\mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})\) (or, if \(\xi\) is stationary, \(\sigma^2_\eta = (1-\rho^2)\mathbb{V}(\xi_{it})\)).
Done.

title: Practice Exercises
section: Problem 4: One-Period Model with Lognormal Income
text:
Problem 4: One-Period Model with Lognormal Income
Consider the following one period model:
\[C_i = Y_i = \exp(\alpha_i + \varepsilon_i)\]
where \(\varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{\varepsilon}^2)\), \(\alpha_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma_\alpha^2)\). Suppose that \(\alpha_i\) is known to each individual and \(\varepsilon_i\) is income risk. Assume log utility s.t. \(V(\alpha_i) = \mathbb{E}[\log(C_i) | \alpha_i]\).

Part (a)
Show that \(V(\alpha_i) = \alpha_i\).






Solution





\[V(\alpha_i) = \mathbb{E}[\log(C_i) | \alpha_i] = \mathbb{E}[\alpha_i + \varepsilon_i | \alpha_i] = \alpha_i\]





Part (b)
Suppose a planner solves:
\[\max_{\{C_i\}_{i\in[0,1]}} \int \log(C_i) di \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \int C_i di = \int \exp(\alpha_i + \varepsilon_i)di\]
Show that the solution is
\[C_i^* = C^* = \exp(\mu + \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 + \sigma_\alpha^2))\]
Hint: if \(Z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\), \(\mathbb{E}[\exp(Z)] = \exp(\mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\).






Solution





Since \(\alpha_i + \varepsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma_\alpha^2 + \sigma_{\varepsilon}^2)\), \(\int\exp(\alpha_{i}+\varepsilon_{i})di = \exp(\mu + \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 + \sigma_\alpha^2))\).
Planner’s FOC: \(\frac{1}{C_i} = \lambda \quad \forall \, i\)
where \(\lambda\) is multiplier on resource constraint. Hence \(C_i = C^* \quad \forall \, i\).
Plugging into resource constraint gives
\[C^* = \exp(\mu + \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 + \sigma_\alpha^2))\]





Part (c)
Show that the certainty equivalent \(\overline{C}(\alpha_i)\) that delivers \(V(\alpha_i)\) is \(\overline{C}(\alpha_i) = \exp(\alpha_i)\).






Solution





\(\overline{C}(\alpha_i)\) solves
\[\log(\overline{C}(\alpha_i)) = V(\alpha_i) = \alpha_i\]
\[\Rightarrow \overline{C}(\alpha_i) = \exp(\alpha_i)\]





Part (d)
Show that \(\overline{C} = \int \overline{C}(\alpha_{i})di = \exp(\mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2_{\alpha})\)






Solution





Since \(\alpha_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma_\alpha^2)\),
\[\overline{C} = \int \overline{C}(\alpha_i) di = \exp(\mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma_\alpha^2)\]





Part (e)
Show that the planner’s objective is \(\mu\) in the baseline and \(\mu + \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 + \sigma_\alpha^2)\) at the optimum.






Solution





Baseline: \(W = \int \log(C_i) = \int \log(\exp(\alpha_i + \varepsilon_i)) di = \mathbb{E}[\alpha_i + \varepsilon_i] = \mu\)
\[W^* = \log(C^*) = \mu + \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 + \sigma_\alpha^2)\]





Part (f)
Decompose \(W^* - W\) into two components:

\(W^* - \log(\overline{C})\)
\(\log(\overline{C}) - W\)

What is (1)? What is (2)? Which term represents the gains from insurance?






Solution






\(W^* - \log(\overline{C}) = \frac{1}{2}\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2 \leftarrow\) Insurance
\(\log(\overline{C}) - W = \frac{1}{2}\sigma_\alpha^2 \leftarrow\) Redistribution






Part (g)
Interpret this result.






Interpretation





\(\sigma_{\varepsilon}^2\) measures the variance in income coming from idiosyncratic risk that individuals face. Insurance eliminates this uncertainty.
\(\sigma_\alpha^2\) measures the variance in income coming from permanent differences across individuals (ex-ante inequality). Redistribution addresses this component.

title: Practice Exercises
text:
Problem 5: Two-Period Becker-Tomes Model
Consider the 2-period Becker-Tomes model:
\[\max_{C_1, C_2, X, A} U(C_1) + \beta U(C_2)\]
\[\text{s.t.} \quad C_1 + \psi X + A / (1+r) \leq \Omega + T / (1+r)\]
\[C_2 = A + wz X^\delta - T, \quad A \geq 0\]
where \(T\) is a lump-sum tax paid by generation 2 to generation 1.

Part (a)
Show that if a household is not constrained, the value of \(T\) does not affect any allocations of \(C_1, C_2, X\) at the optimum. (Hint: try combining budget constraints).






Solution





If \(A > 0\) at the optimum, can combine to get:
\[C_1 + C_2/(1+r) \leq \Omega + wz X^\delta/(1+r) - \psi X \quad (*)\]
since the \(T/(1+r)\) received in period 1 exactly offsets the present value of the \(T\) paid in period 2. So the household solves:
\[\max_{C_1, C_2, X} U(C_1) + \beta U(C_2) \quad \text{s.t.} \quad (*)\]
Hence \(T\) does not feature (as long as \(A\) remains positive at the new optimum).





Part (b)
Show that for constrained households:
\[U'(C_1) = \beta\frac{\delta wz X^{\delta-1}}{\psi} U'(C_2) \quad \text{and} \quad (1+r) \leq \frac{\delta wz X^{\delta-1}}{\psi}\]






Solution





When \(A = 0\), solve:
\[\max_{C_1, C_2} U(\Omega + T/(1+r) - \psi X) + \beta U(wz X^\delta - T)\]
get
\[\psi U'(\Omega + T/(1+r) - \psi X) = \beta \delta wz X^{\delta-1} U'(wz X^\delta - T)\]
\[\Leftrightarrow U'(C_1) = \beta \frac{\delta wz X^{\delta-1}}{\psi} U'(C_2)\]
Note that the marginal return (in assets) is
\[-\frac{1}{1+r} U'(C_1) + \beta U'(C_2) \leq 0 \quad \Leftrightarrow (1+r) \leq \frac{\delta wz X^{\delta-1}}{\psi}\]
where the equivalence substitutes the FOC for \(U'(C_1)\) (if the marginal value were \(> 0\), the household would optimally increase \(A\) above 0).





Part (c)
Consider a marginal increase in \(T\). What happens to the welfare of constrained vs unconstrained households?






Solution





If \(T \nearrow\) marginally, change in welfare is
\[u'(C_1) \frac{1}{(1+r)} - \beta u'(C_2) \geq 0\]
for constrained households (by the envelope theorem), where the inequality follows from (b) and is strict when the constraint binds strictly.
Since allocations of unconstrained households are unaffected by \(T\) (part (a)) \(\Rightarrow\) no welfare effect.
Note: not clear if welfare of children \(\nearrow\) in this intervention.

title: Practice Exercises
section: Problem 6: Two-Period Model with Progressive Taxation
text:
Problem 6: Two-Period Model with Progressive Taxation
For the same 2-period model, suppose budget constraints are now:
\[C_1 + A/(1+r) + \psi X \leq \lambda_{1} \Omega^{1-\tau}\]
\[C_2 = A + \lambda_2 (wz X^\delta)^{1-\tau}, \quad A \geq 0\]
where \(\lambda_1\) and \(\lambda_2\) are chosen to balance budget in each period.

Part (a)
Write the FOC for unconstrained households.






Solution





For unconstrained:
\[U'(C_1) = \beta(1+r)U'(C_2), \qquad (1+r) = \frac{\lambda_2 (1-\tau) \delta(w z)^{1-\tau} X^{\delta(1-\tau)-1}}{\psi}\]





Part (b)
Recall that the planner would set, if possible, \((1+r) = \frac{\delta wz X^{\delta-1}}{\psi}\) in each household \(i\). Can the equilibrium with taxation be efficient?






Solution





Comparing to the condition \((1+r) = \frac{\delta wz X^{\delta-1}}{\psi}\),
the private return to \(X\) is now \(\lambda_2(1-\tau)(wzX^{\delta})^{-\tau}\) times the social return. Except by coincidence this factor is not equal to one, so taxation distorts the choice between financial assets and human capital \(\Rightarrow\) not efficient.





Part (c)
Explain, in words, the efficiency cost of progressive taxation in this model. (Hint: compare the household’s FOC to the planner’s).






Solution





Redistribution reduces the incentives for parents to invest. \(\Rightarrow\) An equity-efficiency tradeoff.





Part (d)
Assuming log utility, solve for \(X\) when households are constrained. Comment on solution relative to Baseline.






Solution





\[\max_X \log(\lambda_1 \Omega^{1-\tau} - \psi X) + \beta \log\left(\lambda_2 (wz X^\delta)^{1-\tau}\right)\]
\[\Rightarrow \frac{\psi}{\lambda_1 \Omega^{1-\tau} - \psi X} = \frac{\beta (1-\tau) \delta}{X}\]
\[\Leftrightarrow X = \frac{1}{\psi} \times \frac{\beta (1-\tau) \delta}{1 + \beta(1-\tau) \delta} \lambda_1 \Omega^{1-\tau}\]
\[\Rightarrow \text{compared to } X = \frac{1}{\psi} \frac{\beta \delta}{1+\beta \delta} \Omega\]
So taxation also distorts investment of constrained households: it lowers the share of period-1 resources invested, \(\frac{\beta(1-\tau)\delta}{1+\beta(1-\tau)\delta} < \frac{\beta\delta}{1+\beta\delta}\), but for poor households it also raises those resources (\(\lambda_1\Omega^{1-\tau} > \Omega\) when \(\Omega\) is low). The second effect could offset the distortion from incomplete markets, but this depends on parameters \((\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \tau)\).

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Overview


Last time: experiments show early programs can change skills and adult outcomes
But experiments alone do not tell us the technology \(f\)

Is early investment more productive than late investment?
How substitutable are investment and existing skills?

Today: how economists estimate the technology of skill formation

Why it is hard
Measurement systems and factor models
Estimates: Cunha and Heckman (2008), Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach (2010), Attanasio, Meghir, and Nix (2020)
Identification concerns: normalizations and scale

A simulation in Julia to see measurement error at work

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
The Object of Interest
From lecture 6: \[ \theta_{t+1} = \left[\gamma_t I_{t}^{\phi_t} + (1-\gamma_t)\theta_{t}^{\phi_t}\right]^{1/\phi_t}e^{\eta_{t}} \]


\(\gamma_t\): productivity of investment at stage \(t\)
\(\phi_t\): governs substitutability between investment and current skills, \(\sigma_t = 1/(1-\phi_t)\)
As \(\phi_t \to 0\), Cobb-Douglas: \(\ln\theta_{t+1} = \gamma_t\ln I_t + (1-\gamma_t)\ln\theta_t + \eta_t\)
We want \(\gamma_t\) and \(\phi_t\) by age: that is what tells us when to invest and whom to target

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Problem 1: Skills Are Latent


We never observe \(\theta_t\), only test scores and survey answers
Each measure is a noisy signal: \(M_{t} = \theta_{t} + \varepsilon_{t}\)
Same for investment: books in the home, trips to the museum, family income…
How noisy? In Cunha and Heckman (2008), the share of variance in each investment proxy that is due to the latent investment factor is between about 4% and 28%, depending on the measure and age

Most of the variation in “number of books” is not investment

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Problem 2: Scales Are Arbitrary


A test score has no natural units
Any increasing transformation of a test score is an equally valid test score (Cunha and Heckman 2008)

Raw score, percentile, IRT score, \(\exp(\text{score})\)…

Changes in test scores (“value added”) are not invariant to these transformations
So is a gain from 40 to 50 “bigger” than a gain from 80 to 90? The data do not say



What do you think? Can you think of an outcome that does have natural units?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Problem 3: Investment Is Endogenous


Parents choose \(I_t\), and they observe things we do not

e.g., a child gets sick (\(\eta_t\) low) and parents invest more to compensate
or parents invest more in children who seem more able

Then \(I_t\) is correlated with \(\eta_t\) and OLS is biased
Plus there are many candidate input measures and few instruments



This is the same problem as in lecture 8: we cannot just regress outcomes on inputs.

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
A Measurement System
For each latent variable \(k\in\{C,N,I\}\) (cognitive, noncognitive, investment), several measures: \[ M^{k}_{j,t} = \mu^{k}_{j,t} + \alpha^{k}_{j,t}\ln\theta^{k}_{t} + \varepsilon^{k}_{j,t}, \quad j = 1,\ldots,m^k_t \]


\(\alpha^{k}_{j,t}\): factor loading (how strongly measure \(j\) reflects the skill)
\(\varepsilon^{k}_{j,t}\): measurement error, independent of \(\theta\) and of other errors
Normalization: set \(\alpha^k_{1,t} = 1\) and \(\mu^k_{1,t}=0\) (or \(E[\ln\theta^k_t]=0\))

The latent skill has no units, so we give it the units of measure 1

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Identifying the Loadings
With two measures per period and \(\alpha_{1,t}=1\) (Cunha and Heckman 2008):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Cov}(M_{1,t}, M_{1,t+1}) &= \text{Cov}(\theta_t,\theta_{t+1}) \\
\text{Cov}(M_{2,t}, M_{1,t+1}) &= \alpha_{2,t}\,\text{Cov}(\theta_t,\theta_{t+1}) \\
\text{Cov}(M_{1,t}, M_{2,t}) &= \alpha_{2,t}\,\text{Var}(\theta_t)
\end{aligned}
\]


Ratio of the second to the first gives \(\alpha_{2,t}\)
Then the third gives \(\text{Var}(\theta_t)\), and the measurement error variances follow
With classical errors, the full distribution of \(\theta\) is identified (Kotlarski’s theorem)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
section: Why One Measure Is Not Enough
text:
Why One Measure Is Not Enough
Suppose \(\ln\theta_{t+1} = a\ln\theta_t + \eta_t\) and we only have \(M_{1,t} = \ln\theta_t + \varepsilon_{1,t}\).


OLS of \(M_{1,t+1}\) on \(M_{1,t}\): \[ \text{plim}\ \hat a_{OLS} = a\cdot\frac{\text{Var}(\theta_t)}{\text{Var}(\theta_t)+\text{Var}(\varepsilon_{1,t})} < a \]
Attenuation bias: we understate self-productivity
Fix: use the second measure as an instrument \[ \hat a_{IV} = \frac{\text{Cov}(M_{1,t+1}, M_{2,t})}{\text{Cov}(M_{1,t}, M_{2,t})} \to \frac{a\,\alpha_{2,t}\text{Var}(\theta_t)}{\alpha_{2,t}\text{Var}(\theta_t)} = a \]
The loading \(\alpha_{2,t}\) cancels: the second test can be on any scale

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Exercise: Measurement Error
Show the results on the previous slide.


Derive \(\text{plim}\,\hat a_{OLS}\) and \(\text{plim}\,\hat a_{IV}\).
Suppose the errors in the two tests are correlated (e.g., the child had a bad day and did badly on both). What happens to \(\hat a_{IV}\)?
Suppose \(\text{Var}(\theta_t) = 1\) and \(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_{1,t}) = 0.5\). If the true \(a = 0.9\), what does OLS give you?
Why does measurement error in the outcome \(M_{1,t+1}\) not cause bias?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Simulation Setup


Latent log skill \(\ln\theta_1 \sim N(0,1)\)
Parents invest more in higher-skill children: \(\ln I = 0.5\ln\theta_1 + \nu\)
Cobb-Douglas technology: \(\ln\theta_2 = 0.8\ln\theta_1 + 0.3\ln I + \eta\)
Two noisy tests for \(\theta_1\), two noisy proxies for \(I\), one noisy test for \(\theta_2\)
Compare:

OLS using the latent variables (infeasible)
OLS using the first noisy measures (naive)
IV using the second measures as instruments

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Simulation Code

Code
using Random, Statistics, LinearAlgebra, StatsPlots

function simulate(N; a = 0.8, b = 0.3, σ_e = 1.0, λ = 0.8, seed = 1234)
    rng = MersenneTwister(seed)
    lθ1 = randn(rng, N)                                  # latent log skill
    lI  = 0.5 .* lθ1 .+ randn(rng, N)                     # endogenous-looking investment
    lθ2 = a .* lθ1 .+ b .* lI .+ 0.5 .* randn(rng, N)     # technology
    M1 = lθ1 .+ σ_e .* randn(rng, N)                      # test 1 (loading = 1)
    M2 = λ .* lθ1 .+ σ_e .* randn(rng, N)                 # test 2 (different scale)
    J1 = lI .+ σ_e .* randn(rng, N)                       # investment proxy 1
    J2 = 1.5 .* lI .+ σ_e .* randn(rng, N)                # investment proxy 2
    Y  = lθ2 .+ σ_e .* randn(rng, N)                      # noisy outcome test
    return (; lθ1, lI, lθ2, M1, M2, J1, J2, Y)
end

ols(y, X) = X \ y
iv(y, X, Z) = (Z' * X) \ (Z' * y)                        # just-identified IV

d = simulate(50_000)
c = ones(length(d.Y))
b_latent = ols(d.lθ2, [c d.lθ1 d.lI])
b_ols    = ols(d.Y, [c d.M1 d.J1])
b_iv     = iv(d.Y, [c d.M1 d.J1], [c d.M2 d.J2])
est = round.([b_latent[2:3] b_ols[2:3] b_iv[2:3]], digits = 3)
println("| | Latent | Naive OLS | IV |\n|---|---|---|---|")
for (k, name) in enumerate(["Persistence \$a\$", "Investment \$b\$"])
    println("| ", name, " | ", join(est[k, :], " | "), " |")
end

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Bias Grows with Noise


Code
σs = 0.0:0.25:1.5
res = map(σs) do s
    d = simulate(50_000; σ_e = s, seed = 99)
    c = ones(length(d.Y))
    (ols(d.Y, [c d.M1 d.J1])[2], iv(d.Y, [c d.M1 d.J1], [c d.M2 d.J2])[2])
end
sig_share = 1 ./ (1 .+ collect(σs) .^ 2)   # Var(θ)/Var(M1)
plot(sig_share, first.(res), marker = :circle, label = "OLS on noisy measures",
     xlabel = "Signal share of test 1: Var(θ)/Var(M₁)", ylabel = "Estimated persistence",
     legend = :bottomleft, xflip = true, size = (900, 450),
     tickfontsize = 11, guidefontsize = 12, legendfontsize = 11,
     left_margin = 6Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 6Plots.mm)
plot!(sig_share, last.(res), marker = :square, label = "IV using second measure")
hline!([0.8], linestyle = :dash, color = :black, label = "True value")

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
What About Substitutability?
Now generate data from a CES technology with \(\phi = -0.5\) (complements, \(\sigma \approx 0.67\)) and fit the CES by nonlinear least squares.

Code
function ces_sim(N; γ = 0.4, φ = -0.5, σ_e = 0.7, seed = 7)
    rng = MersenneTwister(seed)
    lθ1 = randn(rng, N); lI = 0.5 .* lθ1 .+ randn(rng, N)
    lθ2 = (1/φ) .* log.(γ .* exp.(φ .* lI) .+ (1-γ) .* exp.(φ .* lθ1)) .+ 0.3 .* randn(rng, N)
    M1 = lθ1 .+ σ_e .* randn(rng, N); J1 = lI .+ σ_e .* randn(rng, N)
    return (; lθ1, lI, lθ2, M1, J1)
end
ces_pred(lθ, lI, γ, φ) = (1/φ) .* log.(γ .* exp.(φ .* lI) .+ (1-γ) .* exp.(φ .* lθ))
function fit_ces(y, lθ, lI)    # grid search for nonlinear least squares
    best = (Inf, 0.0, 0.0)
    for γ in 0.05:0.01:0.95, φ in -2.0:0.02:0.98
        abs(φ) < 1e-6 && continue
        ssr = sum(abs2, y .- ces_pred(lθ, lI, γ, φ))
        ssr < best[1] && (best = (ssr, γ, φ))
    end
    return (γ = best[2], φ = best[3], σ = round(1 / (1 - best[3]), digits = 2))
end
dc = ces_sim(5_000)
fits = (latent = fit_ces(dc.lθ2, dc.lθ1, dc.lI), noisy = fit_ces(dc.lθ2, dc.M1, dc.J1))
println("| Inputs | \$\\gamma\$ | \$\\phi\$ | \$\\sigma\$ |\n|---|---|---|---|")
for (name, r) in pairs(fits)
    println("| ", name, " | ", r.γ, " | ", r.φ, " | ", r.σ, " |")
end

\(\phi\)
\(\sigma\)

With noisy inputs, the estimated \(\phi\) moves toward zero: we overstate how substitutable investment and skills are. Fixing this in a nonlinear model is much harder than IV, which is the contribution of Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach (2010).

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Cunha and Heckman (2008)
Cunha and Heckman (2008) estimate a linear (in logs) technology with two skills: \[ \ln\theta^{k}_{t+1} = \gamma^{k}_{1}\ln\theta^{N}_{t} + \gamma^{k}_{2}\ln\theta^{C}_{t} + \gamma^{k}_{3}\ln I_{t} + \eta^{k}_{t}, \quad k\in\{C,N\} \]


Data: Children of the NLSY79 (white males), ages 6–7 to 12–13
Measures: PIAT math and reading (cognitive), behavior problems subscores such as antisocial, anxious, hyperactive (noncognitive), HOME items such as books, museum trips, lessons, and family income (investment)
Instead of an ad hoc index of investment, they estimate the weights on each investment measure
To give skills meaningful units, they anchor them to adult outcomes: log earnings and high school graduation

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Correcting for Measurement Error Matters
Self-productivity estimates (Cunha and Heckman 2008, Tables 2 and 16):









Factor model

OLS even gives a “perverse” negative effect of the HOME score on math

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Cunha and Heckman (2008): Findings


Strong self-productivity of both skills
Cross-productivity: noncognitive skills help produce cognitive skills, but (in most specifications) not the other way around
Sensitive periods (stage-specific technology): the investment coefficient for

Cognitive skills: about 0.11 from ages 6–7 to 8–9, then about 0.04 in later transitions
Noncognitive skills: about 0.05, then 0.11, then 0.05

Sensitive periods for cognitive skills come earlier than for noncognitive skills
The relative effect of investment on the two skills depends on the metric (anchor) used

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach (2010)
Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach (2010) estimate the nonlinear CES technology:


Two skills (cognitive, noncognitive), two stages of childhood, CNLSY data
Allow for measurement error in a nonlinear model (nonparametric identification of the factor distributions)
Allow investment to be endogenous
Anchor skills to adult outcomes
Key finding: substitutability between investment and current skills decreases in the later stage for cognitive skills, and is roughly constant (or slightly increasing) for noncognitive skills

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Implications for Targeting


If \(\phi\) for cognitive skills falls with age, late remediation of cognitive gaps is expensive
So for children from disadvantaged families, the efficient policy invests relatively more early
Later remediation is more promising for noncognitive skills

e.g., mentoring and adolescent programs that work on motivation and behavior

This is the “no equity-efficiency trade-off” argument for early investment from lecture 6, now with estimates behind it



What do you think? How would your answer change if the estimated \(\phi\) were biased toward zero, as in our simulation?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Attanasio, Meghir, and Nix (2020)
Attanasio, Meghir, and Nix (2020): human capital development in India


Data: Young Lives survey, children aged 1–12
Estimate production functions for cognition and health
Measurement system for skills and investments, as above
Treat parental investment as endogenous: model investment choices as depending on skills, resources, and local prices, and use variables that shift investment but not skills directly
Findings:

Parental investment affects cognitive development at all ages, but more for younger children
Investment affects health only at early ages

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Handling Endogenous Investment
One common approach is a control function (a stylized version; \(w_t\) = household resources):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ln I_t &= \pi_1\ln\theta_t + \pi_2 \ln w_t + \pi_3 Z_t + \nu_t \quad &\text{(investment choice)} \\
\ln\theta_{t+1} &= f(\theta_t, I_t) + \rho\,\nu_t + \tilde\eta_t \quad &\text{(technology)}
\end{aligned}
\]


\(Z_t\): things that shift investment but do not enter the technology (e.g., prices)
Estimate \(\nu_t\) from the first equation, include it in the second
\(\rho \neq 0\) means investment responds to unobserved shocks
An RCT can play the role of \(Z_t\): in Colombia, Attanasio et al. (2020) use random assignment to the home-visiting program to shift investment

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Normalizations Are Not Always Innocent


Factor models need normalizations: a loading of 1 and a location for each latent skill
Researchers often normalize every period (e.g., each skill has mean 0 and the first loading is 1 at every age)
Agostinelli and Wiswall (2025): in a dynamic model, re-normalizing every period is not innocuous

It restricts how the scale of skills can change over time
It can bias estimates of the technology toward particular functional forms

Freyberger (2021): a restriction that is a harmless normalization for one production function can be a substantive (and false) restriction for another

Normalizing in the initial period, or through anchoring, can then lead to misspecification

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Scale and Anchoring


Because test scores have no units, statements like “investment at age 6 is twice as productive as at age 10” depend on the units of \(\theta\)
Anchoring (Cunha and Heckman 2008; Cunha, Heckman, and Schennach 2010): measure skills in units of an adult outcome (e.g., log earnings)

Then “productivity” means effect on adult earnings, which has meaning

But conclusions can still depend on which anchor is used
Lesson: read estimates of \(\gamma_t\) and \(\phi_t\) together with the normalization and anchor behind them

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
section: What Do We Learn from the Recent Work?
text:
What Do We Learn from the Recent Work?


With more careful normalizations, Agostinelli and Wiswall (2025) find that investment around ages 5–6 is most productive for cognitive skills, especially for children with lower initial skills
Common themes across the literature:

Measurement error is large; correcting it changes conclusions
Investment matters more at younger ages, especially for cognitive skills
Experiments are valuable inputs to estimating the technology, not just program evaluations

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Estimating the Technology of Skill Formation
text:
Key Takeaways


Estimating the technology of skill formation requires solving three problems: latent skills, arbitrary scales, and endogenous investment
Multiple measures solve measurement error: a second measure works as an instrument; factor models generalize this
Ignoring measurement error attenuates persistence and can distort the estimated substitutability
Estimates point to strong self-productivity and earlier sensitive periods for cognitive than for noncognitive skills
Substitutability for cognitive skills declines with age: invest early, especially for disadvantaged children
Results depend on normalizations and anchors: these choices deserve as much scrutiny as the data

title: Income Processes
text:
Overview


So far: documented inequality trends and their welfare implications
Today: the stochastic process generating earnings
Key questions:

How persistent are earnings shocks?
How can we separate earnings volatility from earnings risk?

The answers determine how much we value insurance

title: Income Processes
text:
What is a Stochastic Process?
A stochastic process describes how a variable evolves randomly over time.
For earnings, we might write: \[y_{it} = f(y_{it-1}, y_{it-2}, \ldots, \text{shock}_{it})\]


\(y_{it}\): person \(i\)’s log earnings at time \(t\)
\(\text{shock}_{it}\): random shock (the “new news” at time \(t\))
Different processes = different ways shocks affect future earnings

title: Income Processes
text:
Notation
We use the same notation for the whole lecture:


\(\eta_{it}\): innovation to a permanent or persistent component, variance \(\sigma^2_{\eta}\)
\(\varepsilon_{it}\): transitory shock, variance \(\sigma^2_{\varepsilon}\)

title: Income Processes
text:
White Noise (i.i.d. Process)
The simplest process: white noise
\[y_{it} = \varepsilon_{it}\]
where \(\varepsilon_{it} \sim\) i.i.d. \(N(0, \sigma^2_{\varepsilon})\)


Each period is independent of the past
Shocks have no persistence
Example: random measurement error
Not realistic for earnings (last year’s income predicts this year’s)

title: Income Processes
text:
Random Walk Process
A random walk accumulates all past shocks:
\[y_{it} = y_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\]
Expanding backward: \(y_{it} = y_{i0} + \sum_{s=1}^t \eta_{is}\)


Today’s value = yesterday’s value + new shock
Shocks are permanent (never fade)
Variance grows over time: \(\text{var}(y_{it}) = \text{var}(y_{i0}) + t\sigma^2_{\eta}\)
Example: stock prices, permanent disability

title: Income Processes
text:

Code
