title: Income Processes
text:
AR(1) Process
An autoregressive process with mean reversion:
\[y_{it} = \rho y_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\]
where \(|\rho| < 1\) (typically \(0 < \rho < 1\) for earnings)


Shocks fade over time at rate \(\rho\)
After \(k\) periods, effect is \(\rho^k\) of original shock
Long-run variance: \(\text{var}(y_{it}) = \frac{\sigma^2_{\eta}}{1-\rho^2}\)
Example: temporary illness, bonus, overtime

title: Income Processes
text:
AR(1): Simulation


Code
# Simulate AR(1) with ρ = 0.7
rho = 0.7
y_ar = zeros(T, N)

for i in 1:N
    for t in 2:T
        y_ar[t, i] = rho * y_ar[t-1, i] + randn()  # AR(1)
    end
end

plot(1:T, y_ar, linewidth=2, xlabel="Time", ylabel="Log Earnings",
     title="AR(1) with ρ=0.7: Paths Stabilize", legend=false, alpha=0.7,
     size=(900,400), tickfontsize=10, guidefontsize=11, titlefontsize=12,
     left_margin=5Plots.mm, bottom_margin=4Plots.mm)





  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  































Notice: paths fluctuate but don’t diverge.

title: Income Processes
text:
Comparing Random Walk vs AR(1)


Random Walk

Shocks permanent
Variance grows: \(t\sigma^2_{\eta}\)
No mean reversion
Paths diverge


AR(1)

Shocks fade
Variance converges
Mean reversion
Paths stabilize


Key question for earnings: Which better describes reality?

title: Income Processes
text:
MA(1) Process
A moving average process uses lagged shocks:
\[y_{it} = \varepsilon_{it} + \theta \varepsilon_{it-1}\]


Shock affects current period AND next period
After that, completely forgotten
Example: multi-period bonus, temporary layoff
\(\theta > 0\): a positive shock also raises next year’s earnings
\(\theta < 0\): a positive shock lowers next year’s earnings (smoothing)

title: Income Processes
text:
MA(1) vs AR(1): Key Difference
AR(1): persistence in the level

High earnings today → high earnings tomorrow
Effect fades gradually

MA(1): persistence in the shock

Shock today → affects next period
Then completely forgotten

title: Income Processes
text:
MA(1) and Earnings Growth
Suppose \(y_{it} = \varepsilon_{it} + \theta\varepsilon_{it-1}\). Earnings growth \(g_{it} = \Delta y_{it}\) is: \[ g_{it} = \varepsilon_{it} + (\theta - 1)\varepsilon_{it-1} - \theta\varepsilon_{it-2} \]


Differencing an MA(1) gives an MA(2) in growth rates
\(\text{cov}(g_{it},g_{it-1}) = -(1-\theta)^2\sigma^2_{\varepsilon} < 0\)
\(\text{cov}(g_{it},g_{it-2}) = -\theta\sigma^2_{\varepsilon}\): not zero unless \(\theta = 0\)
\(\text{cov}(g_{it},g_{it-j}) = 0\) for \(j\geq 3\)
Only if the transitory shock is i.i.d. (\(\theta=0\)) are \(g_{it}\) and \(g_{it-2}\) uncorrelated
Rule of thumb: an MA(\(q\)) transitory component shows up as nonzero growth autocovariances up to lag \(q+1\)
Adding a random walk (Exercise 4) changes the variance of \(g_{it}\), but not these autocovariances. Why?

title: Income Processes
text:
Why This Matters for Earnings
Different processes → different implications:


Random walk: job loss permanently lowers earnings
AR(1): earnings shocks fade over time
MA(1): shocks have short-term persistence
More persistent shocks are harder to self-insure against. Insurance more valuable.



Key question: Which process(es) best describe earnings data?

title: Income Processes
text:
Key Questions

How would each of these processes appear differently in panel data?
When we write down an income process, is it identified?

identified \(\Leftrightarrow\) parameters can be inferred from population moments

Replacing population moments with sample moments yields estimation strategy

title: Income Processes
text:
Exercise 1: Pure Random Walk
Suppose individual \(i\)’s log earnings follow:
\[y_{it} = y_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\]
where \(\eta_{it} \sim\) i.i.d. \(N(0, \sigma^2_{\eta})\). Questions:

What is the variance of \(y_{it}\) as a function of time?
If everyone starts at \(y_{i0} = 0\), how does inequality evolve?
What is the covariance at different lags? In growth rates?
How could we estimate this process?

title: Income Processes
text:
Exercise 2: AR(1) Process
Now suppose:
\[y_{it} = \rho y_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\]
where \(|\rho| < 1\) and \(\eta_{it} \sim\) i.i.d. \(N(0, \sigma_{\eta}^2)\). Questions:

What is the long-run variance of \(y_{it}\)?
How does inequality evolve compared to a random walk?
What is the covariance at different lags?
How could we estimate?

title: Income Processes
text:
Exercise 2: Solution Steps
Steps:


Show that \(\mathbb{C}(y_{it+1},y_{it}) = \mathbb{C}(\rho y_{it}+\eta_{it+1},y_{it}) = \rho \mathbb{V}[y_{it}]\).
Similarly show that \(\mathbb{C}(y_{it+2},y_{it}) = \rho^{2}\mathbb{V}[y_{it}]\)
Therefore \[ \rho = \frac{\mathbb{C}(y_{it+2},y_{it})}{\mathbb{C}(y_{it+1},y_{it})} \]
Estimate by plugging in sample covariances.
Similarly, since \(\mathbb{V}[y_{it+1}] = \rho^2\mathbb{V}[y_{it}] + \sigma^2_{\eta}\), we get: \[ \sigma^2_{\eta} = \mathbb{V}[y_{it+1}] - \rho^2\mathbb{V}[y_{it}]\]

title: Income Processes
text:
Exercise 3: AR(1) with Fixed Effects
Now add individual-specific fixed effects:
\[y_{it} = \alpha_i + \xi_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} \]
where \(\xi_{it} = \rho \xi_{i,t-1} + \eta_{it}\), \(\eta_{it}\sim\text{ i.i.d. }N(0,\sigma^2_{\eta})\), and \(\varepsilon_{it}\sim\text{ i.i.d. }N(0,\sigma^2_{\varepsilon})\). Questions:

What determines long-run inequality in this model?
What is the covariance at different lags?
How would you estimate \(\rho\) from panel data?
What could happen if you ignore the fixed effects?

title: Income Processes
text:
Exercise 4: Random walk + MA(1)
To think about:
\[y_{it} = p_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} + \theta \varepsilon_{i,t-1}\]
where \(p_{it} = p_{i,t-1} + \eta_{it}\), with \(\eta_{it}\) and \(\varepsilon_{it}\) i.i.d. and independent of each other.

What is the covariance in growth rates?
How can we estimate this model?

title: Income Processes
text:
Exercise 5 (harder): Permanent vs Transitory
Consider a model with both components:
\[y_{it} = p_{it} + e_{it}\]
where \(p_{it} = p_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\) and \(e_{it} = \rho e_{it-1} + \varepsilon_{it}\) with \(|\rho|<1\)
Questions:

What is the covariance in growth rates and / or levels?
How can we estimate this model?

title: Income Processes
text:
Key Insights from Exercises


Random walk: inequality grows without bound; shocks never fade
AR(1): inequality stabilizes; shocks fade over time
Fixed effects: permanent inequality, distinct from shocks
Permanent vs transitory: different implications for consumption smoothing, welfare costs of inequality, and policy design



Main lesson: The nature of shocks fundamentally affects policy!

title: Income Processes
text:
What Can Cross-Sections Tell Us?
Suppose log earnings at age \(a\) follow a random walk plus a transitory shock (RIP): \[ y_{ia} = \alpha_i + p_{ia} + \varepsilon_{ia},\qquad p_{ia} = p_{i,a-1} + \eta_{ia},\quad p_{i,a_0} = 0 \]


Then the cross-sectional variance at age \(a\) is: \[ \text{var}(y_{ia}) = \sigma^2_{\alpha} + (a - a_0)\sigma^2_{\eta} + \sigma^2_{\varepsilon} \]
The variance is linear in age, and the slope is \(\sigma^2_{\eta}\)
We don’t need a panel for this: repeated cross-sections (like the CPS) are enough
This is the idea behind Storesletten, Telmer, and Yaron (2004) from Lecture 2
What could go wrong? Let’s look first.

title: Income Processes
text:
Loading the CPS
Same data and cleaning as Lecture 1, but only the columns we need. We focus on men with positive earnings and use log real annual earnings.


Code
using DataFrames, DataFramesMeta, CSV, StatsBase, StatsPlots
pce = @select(CSV.read("../data/PCE_index.csv",DataFrame), :INCYEAR = :YEAR, :PCE)

cps = @chain CSV.read("../data/cps_00049.csv",DataFrame,
                      select=[:YEAR,:HFLAG,:ASECWT,:AGE,:SEX,:INCWAGE,:WKSWORK1]) begin
  @subset coalesce.(:HFLAG,1) .== 1 #<- one 2014 sample (see Lecture 1)
  @transform :INCYEAR = :YEAR .- 1 #<- income refers to the previous calendar year
  @subset (:SEX .== 1) .& (:INCWAGE .> 0) .& (:WKSWORK1 .> 10) #<- men with earnings
  innerjoin(pce,on=:INCYEAR)
  @transform begin
    :logy = log.(100 .* :INCWAGE ./ :PCE) #<- log real annual earnings (2017 dollars)
    :cohort = :YEAR .- :AGE #<- approximate birth year
  end
end

title: Income Processes
section: Variance of Log Earnings by Age

title: Income Processes
text:
A Rough Estimate of \(\sigma^2_{\eta}\)
Compute the variance in each (year, age) cell, then regress it on age between 25 and 55, controlling for either year effects or cohort effects:

Code
cells = @chain cps begin
  @subset 25 .<= :AGE .<= 55
  groupby([:INCYEAR,:AGE])
  @combine :var_logy = var(:logy,weights(:ASECWT))
  @transform :cohort = :INCYEAR .- :AGE
end

# OLS slope on age, with a full set of dummies for the variable `fe`
function age_slope(d, fe)
  lev = sort(unique(d[!,fe]))[2:end]   #<- drop one category
  D = Float64.(d[!,fe] .== permutedims(lev)) #<- matrix of dummies
  X = [ones(nrow(d)) d.AGE D]
  return (X \ d.var_logy)[2] #<- coefficient on age
end

println("| Controls | Slope on age |\n|:--|--:|")
for (lab,fe) in [("Year effects",:INCYEAR),("Cohort effects",:cohort)]
  println("| ", lab, " | ", round(age_slope(cells,fe),digits=4), " |")
end




Controls
Slope on age




Year effects
0.0043


Cohort effects
0.0062





Read off the slope as \(\hat{\sigma}^2_{\eta}\): roughly 0.004 to 0.006 per year, depending on the controls
Note the steep rise after age 55 in the plot: likely selection (partial retirement, part-year work), which is why we stop at 55
Compare: Meghir and Pistaferri (2004) estimate about 0.03 from PSID panel data on growth rates

title: Income Processes
text:
What Can (and Can’t) This Identify?


Time vs cohort effects: we cannot control for both, since age = year − cohort (the rank condition from Lecture 1)

With year effects, rising inequality over time is not attributed to age; with cohort effects, it is

HIP also fans out: under HIP, \(\text{var}(y_{ia}) = \sigma^2_{\alpha} + 2\sigma_{\alpha\kappa}(a-a_0) + \sigma^2_{\kappa}(a-a_0)^2 + \text{var}(u_{ia})\), which rises with age with no risk at all
Shape: an AR(1) with \(\rho<1\) makes the profile concave (it levels off); HIP makes it convex. Time effects and selection can blur both
Selection and hours: who works, and how much, changes with age (e.g. near retirement), so annual earnings mix wage shocks with hours and employment shocks
So the slope measures \(\sigma^2_{\eta}\) only if we rule out HIP and selection and pick the right time/cohort restriction. To do better we need panel data on growth rates (next sections)

title: Income Processes
text:
Exercise: What Do You Think?


Why might the cross-sectional estimate of \(\sigma^2_{\eta}\) be smaller than the panel estimate from Meghir and Pistaferri (2004)? (Think about the sample, measurement error, and the definition of earnings.)
Repeat the analysis with log hourly wages (as in Lecture 1). Is the slope larger or smaller? What does that suggest about the role of hours and employment?
If you only had this plot, could you tell the RIP and HIP models apart? What feature of the shape would help?

title: Income Processes
section: What if People Have Different Growth Rates?
text:
What if People Have Different Growth Rates?
Guvenen (2009) proposes an alternative to random walk:
\[y_{it} = \alpha_i + \kappa_i \cdot t + u_{it}\]


\(\alpha_i\): individual-specific level
\(\kappa_i\): individual-specific growth rate, variance \(\sigma^2_{\kappa}\)
\(u_{it} = \xi_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}\): stochastic part, with \(\xi_{it} = \rho\xi_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\) (an AR(1)) plus a transitory shock
Key idea: inequality grows because some people have steeper earnings profiles, not only because shocks pile up
RIP (“restricted income profiles”) is the special case \(\sigma^2_{\kappa} = 0\), usually with \(\rho\approx 1\)


Note: Guvenen (2009) writes the slope as \(\beta^i\). We use \(\kappa_i\) because \(\beta\) is the discount factor elsewhere in the course.

title: Income Processes
text:
HIP vs RIP: Conceptual Differences

HIP (Heterogeneous Profiles)RIP (Random Walk)



Inequality grows deterministically
Different people on different trajectories
Example: college grads vs high school grads
Inequality is somewhat predictable




Inequality grows via cumulative shocks
Everyone faces similar risk
Example: job loss, health shocks
Inequality is fundamentally uncertain

title: Income Processes
text:
Exercise: Testing HIP vs RIP
Take first differences: \(g_{it} = \Delta y_{it}\)
Under HIP: \[g_{it} = \kappa_i + \Delta u_{it}\]
Under RIP (random walk + MA(1) transitory, as in Exercise 4): \[g_{it} = \eta_{it} + \varepsilon_{it} + (\theta - 1)\varepsilon_{it-1} - \theta \varepsilon_{it-2}\]
Questions:

What is \(\text{cov}(g_{it}, g_{it-j})\) for large \(j\) under each model?
How would you distinguish the models empirically?
What do you think is more realistic?

title: Income Processes
section: Why Does HIP vs RIP Matter?
text:
Why Does HIP vs RIP Matter?
Recall from Lecture 2: redistribution smooths differences across types that are known in advance; insurance smooths risk that is realized later.


HIP: much of life-cycle inequality comes from \((\alpha_i,\kappa_i)\)

If these are known (or predetermined) at labor-market entry, they are not risk from then on
Smoothing them is a redistribution question across types, as with the fixed effects in Storesletten, Telmer, and Yaron (2004)
Policy levers: redistribution, and pre-labor-market investments (education, skills) that shape \(\alpha_i\) and \(\kappa_i\)

RIP: inequality comes from persistent shocks realized over the life cycle

This is risk, so the question is insurance
Persistent shocks are hard to self-insure, so the value of social insurance is large

Reality: probably a mix, which sets the insurance vs redistribution split

title: Income Processes
text:
Evidence on HIP vs RIP
Guvenen (2009) (PSID, 1968-1993) estimates both versions of \(y_{it} = \alpha_i + \kappa_i t + \xi_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}\):


RIP (\(\sigma^2_{\kappa}=0\) imposed): \(\rho \approx 0.99\), and a unit root cannot be rejected
HIP (\(\sigma^2_{\kappa}\) estimated): substantial profile heterogeneity; \(\rho\) falls to about 0.82

Ignoring heterogeneous profiles biases persistence upward: steady fanning out looks like persistent shocks

Profile heterogeneity explains 56-75% of income inequality at age 55, and is much larger for college graduates
Higher-order autocovariances of growth are small and mostly negative. This was read as evidence against HIP, but the estimated HIP process reproduces it
Caveat: income data alone may not settle the question



Implication: much of what looks like permanent risk could be predetermined heterogeneity, which changes the insurance vs redistribution answer

title: Income Processes
text:
A More Flexible Model
Meghir and Pistaferri (2004) nest several models and let the data decide:
\[y_{it} = m_t^e + Z_{it}'\psi^e + u_{it},\qquad u_{it} = p_{it} + e_{it} + r_{it}\]


\(p_{it} = p_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\): permanent component (random walk)
\(e_{it}\): transitory component (serially correlated)
\(r_{it}\): measurement error (i.i.d.)
Allow variance to change over time and across people


Note: notation differs from Meghir and Pistaferri (2004). We use \(\eta_{it}\) for the permanent shock and \(\varepsilon_{it}\) for the transitory shock throughout. They also write the MA with a minus sign, \(\varepsilon_{it} - \theta\varepsilon_{it-1}\); we use \(+\theta\).

title: Income Processes
text:
Why Three Components?


Permanent (\(p_{it}\)): job loss, promotions, health, career choices
Transitory (\(e_{it}\)): overtime, bonuses, temporary layoffs
Measurement error (\(r_{it}\)): survey reporting errors, imputation
Each has different implications for consumption and welfare
Need to separate them empirically

title: Income Processes
text:
Key Empirical Questions
Meghir and Pistaferri (2004) ask:


Are permanent shocks important? (test \(\text{var}(\eta) = 0\))
How persistent are transitory shocks?
Does variance change over time?
Do some people face more risk than others?



Let’s look at the evidence…

title: Income Processes
text:
Data: PSID 1967-1992
Sample:


Male heads of household, ages 25-55
At least 9 years of earnings data
2,069 individuals, 31,631 person-years
Separate analysis by education

title: Income Processes
text:
Finding 4: ARCH Effects
Big innovation: variance depends on recent shocks
\[E_{t-1}(\eta_{it}^2) = \bar{\sigma}^2_{\eta} + \varphi \eta_{it-1}^2, \qquad E_{t-1}(\varepsilon_{it}^2) = \bar{\sigma}^2_{\varepsilon} + \gamma \varepsilon_{it-1}^2\]
Estimates: \(\varphi \approx 0.56\) (permanent), \(\gamma \approx 0.40\) (transitory)
Interpretation:


If you experience large shock today → expect higher variance tomorrow
Risk is time-varying and persistent
Some people permanently face more risk

title: Income Processes
text:
What Generates Time-Varying Risk?
Possible mechanisms:


Job characteristics (risky occupations)
Business cycle (recessions)
Health problems (cascading effects)
Career instability
Skill depreciation



Policy question: Should social insurance respond to individual risk histories?

title: Income Processes
section: Where Do Earnings Shocks Come From?
text:
Where Do Earnings Shocks Come From?


So far: a “shock” is whatever is left in a statistical model of earnings
But earnings changes mix different sources of risk, and people’s responses to them (changing jobs, quitting, working less)
Low, Meghir, and Pistaferri (2010) build a life-cycle model of consumption, labor supply, and job mobility with search frictions. Two kinds of risk:

Productivity (wage) risk: permanent shocks to the worker’s own productivity, which follow them across jobs
Employment risk: job destruction, how often job offers arrive, and the quality of the worker-firm match

Wages: \(\ln w_{it} = d_t + x_{it}'\psi + u_{it} + a_{ij} + e_{it}\), with \(u_{it} = u_{it-1} + \eta_{it}\) (random walk), \(a_{ij}\) a match effect fixed for the length of a job, and \(e_{it}\) measurement error
Data: SIPP for wages and job mobility, PSID for employment and unemployment durations; separate estimates by education

title: Income Processes
text:
Separating the Two Risks


Moving to a better match raises wages. A model that ignores job mobility reads these gains as permanent shocks
Finding: if mobility is ignored, the estimated variance of the permanent wage shock doubles. Allowing for job mobility gives a much lower estimate of productivity risk
The two risks are insured differently:

Job loss is partly insured by unemployment insurance (UI)
Productivity shocks are rarely insured formally (moral hazard, limited commitment), which drives precautionary behavior

The model includes UI, Disability Insurance, a means-tested transfer modeled on Food Stamps, and Social Security, so self-insurance and public insurance interact

title: Income Processes
text:
Welfare: Which Risk Matters More?


More productivity risk: small output losses, large welfare losses

High-educated: a 50% rise in the permanent shock variance lowers output by 3.7%, but people would pay 19.2% of consumption to avoid it

More job destruction: large output losses (more time without work), smaller welfare losses

The income loss is mostly transitory, so savings smooth it, and time out of work has some value as leisure

Same 5% cut in the variance of income growth, achieved two ways: people value cutting productivity risk substantially more than cutting job destruction
Lesson: the variance of earnings changes is not a sufficient statistic for welfare. Persistence matters

title: Income Processes
text:
Policy: UI vs Food Stamps
Willingness to pay (% of consumption) for spending 1% more on each program, within an education group (insurance only, no redistribution across groups):



Program
High education
Low education




Unemployment insurance
0.19
0.24


Food Stamps (means-tested)
0.25
0.30


Proportional tax cut
0.08
0.15





The means-tested program is worth more than UI: it pays out after a large income loss whatever the cause, so it partly insures persistent productivity shocks
UI only pays after job loss, which is mostly transitory risk that people can partly self-insure
What do you think? Why might a program designed as “redistribution” (means-tested transfers) end up being valuable mainly as insurance? Connect to Lecture 2.

title: Income Processes
text:
Implication 1: Consumption and Savings
How should consumption respond to each type of shock?


Transitory shocks: smoothed by borrowing and saving, so consumption barely responds (if credit is available)
Permanent shocks: change lifetime resources, so they pass through to consumption (nearly one-for-one without other insurance)
Precautionary saving is driven mainly by persistent risk: future shocks will not wash out, so people build a buffer
ARCH effects → the precautionary motive varies over time and across people


Implication: how consumption responds to income changes is informative about which shocks people face and how well they are insured

title: Income Processes
text:
Implication 2: Welfare Costs
Recall certainty equivalent from Lecture 2:


Permanent shocks: very costly (hard to self-insure)
Transitory shocks: less costly (can smooth by saving)
ARCH effects: magnify costs (risk breeds risk)
Storesletten, Telmer, and Yaron (2004): an unborn agent would give up about 26% of lifetime consumption to insure life-cycle shocks (vs 19% for fixed effects)
Those numbers depend on the income process: more persistence, larger costs

title: Income Processes
text:
Implication 3: Income Mobility
With ARCH:


People at extremes (large shocks) have higher future variance
Increases probability of reverting to mean
Reduces poverty persistence by 2-6 percentage points
But also increases chance of falling into poverty



Implication: Mobility patterns more complex than simple mean reversion

title: Income Processes
text:
Implication 4: Policy Design
Different shocks → different policies:


Predetermined differences (\(\alpha_i\), HIP slopes \(\kappa_i\)): a redistribution question

Progressive taxes and transfers across types, pre-labor-market investment

Permanent / persistent shocks during working life: insurance is valuable because self-insurance is weak

Transfers that respond to realized income (progressive taxes, means-tested programs), disability insurance

Transitory shocks: mostly self-insurable, so the main role for policy is liquidity

Unemployment insurance, access to credit

ARCH effects: may need state-dependent transfers

Higher benefits after large shocks?

In practice, programs like progressive taxes do both insurance and redistribution

title: Income Processes
text:
Measurement Challenges


Top-coding: earnings censored at top
Imputation: some data imputed in surveys
Selection: who attrites from panel?
Small samples: survey panels are too small to study the tails of earnings changes
Administrative data: Guvenen et al. (2021) use Social Security earnings records for millions of workers (next slide)



Takeaway: Measurement matters for conclusions!

title: Income Processes
text:
Evidence from Administrative Data
Guvenen et al. (2021): 10% panel sample of US men from the SSA Master Earnings File (1978-2013)


Earnings changes are far from Gaussian (normal)

Very high kurtosis: most changes are tiny, a few are huge. 31% of annual changes are below 5%, vs 8% under a normal with the same standard deviation
Negative skewness: large falls are more likely than large rises

These features vary with age and earnings level: they are strongest around age 50 and between the 70th and 90th percentiles of earnings
Mean reversion is asymmetric: for high earners, gains are transitory and losses persistent; the reverse for low earners
Preferred process: persistent and transitory components with mixture-of-normals shocks, plus nonemployment shocks whose probability depends on age and earnings
Lesson: the variance alone (e.g. \(\sigma^2_{\eta}\)) misses much of the risk workers face

title: Income Processes
text:
Other Extensions
Recent work examines:


Non-Gaussian shocks: fat tails, skewness
Wages vs hours: separating margins of adjustment
Life-cycle patterns: how risk changes with age
Subjective expectations: what do people think their risk is?

title: Income Processes
text:
What We Still Don’t Know
Important open questions:


What fraction of income risk is truly uninsurable?
How much do people self-insure through savings/family?
Do ARCH effects reflect uncertainty or predictable volatility?
How do processes vary across countries/time periods?
What are optimal policy responses to time-varying risk?

title: Income Processes
text:
Key Takeaways


Income has permanent and transitory components
Permanent shocks important empirically (variance ≈ 0.03 per year in Meghir and Pistaferri (2004))
Transitory shocks show some persistence (MA(1))
Time-varying risk: variance depends on recent shocks (ARCH)
Some people face permanently higher risk
Simple i.i.d. assumption very misleading for policy

title: Income Processes
text:
Why This Matters


Consumption theory: explains savings behavior
Welfare analysis: determines value of insurance
Policy design: guides transfer program design
Structural models: key input for calibration
Inequality: helps explain trends and patterns

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Overview


We have learned that income inequality tends to persist across generations
Today: theory of intergenerational transmission
The Becker-Tomes model (Becker and Tomes 1979, 1986) is a workhorse framework
We’ll study some stylized versions
Key questions:

Why do earnings regress to the mean?
How do parents affect children’s outcomes?
What determines the speed of mobility?
Do the model’s predictions fit the data?

Building a unified framework for inequality and mobility

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Basic Setup
There are 5 basic ingredients in the model:


In each period \(t\), one generation of adults raises the next generation for \(t+1\) (an “OLG” framework)
Care only about consumption, with an altruistic weight \(\beta\) on future generations
Can transfer wealth through:

Financial assets \(A_{t}\), with rate of return \(r\); or
Human capital, \(H_{t}\), with price \(w\) (the wage)

A production function converts investments \(X_{t}\) into human capital \(H_{t+1}\)
An ability endowment, \(z_{t}\), evolves exogenously.

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
A Simple Version
Here is a simple version that captures important forces:


Ability is mean-reverting: \[ z_{t+1} = \rho z_{t} + \eta_{t+1},\ \rho \in(0,1) \]
Human capital production: \[ H_{t+1} = \exp(\mu + z_{t})X_{t}^{\delta} \] where \(X_{t}\) has price \(\psi\)
Budget constraint: \[ C_{t} + \frac{A_{t+1}}{1+r} + \psi X_{t} \leq A_{t} + wH_{t} \]

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
A Recursive Formulation
Let \(\Omega_{t} = A_{t} + wH_{t}\) be total wealth in period \(t\):
\[ V(\Omega_{t},z_{t}) = \max_{C_{t},X_{t},A_{t+1}}\left\{ u(C_{t}) + \beta \mathbb{E}[V(\Omega_{t+1},z_{t+1})] \right\} \]
subject to:
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_{t} + \psi X_{t} + \frac{A_{t+1}}{1+r} &\leq \Omega_{t} \\
\Omega_{t+1} &= A_{t+1} + wH_{t+1} \\
z_{t+1} &= \rho z_{t} + \eta_{t+1} \\
H_{t+1} &= \exp(\mu+z_{t})X_{t}^{\delta}
\end{aligned}
\]

Note: no constraints on borrowing (for now)

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Model Solution


This is quite a simple model, but we can learn some interesting and useful things from it
We’ll show that investment does not depend on wealth or income
We’ll derive the IGE in terms of model primitives
We’ll look at the effect of innovations in \(z_{t}\) in the long-run

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
section: Result 1: Investment does not depend on Income
text:
Result 1: Investment does not depend on Income
Exercise (board):
Steps:

Take FOC wrt \(X_{t}\) and \(A_{t+1}\)
Show that: \[ X_{t} = \left(\frac{\delta w \exp(\mu+z_{t})}{(1+r)\psi}\right)^{1/(1-\delta)} \]
Analyze. Notice no direct effect of income.

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Result 2: The IGE
Exercise (board):
Steps:

Show that \[\log(H_{t}) = c + \frac{1}{1-\delta}z_{t-1}\] where \(c\) is a constant.
Show that \[ \log(H_{t+1}) = \rho\log(H_{t}) + \frac{1}{1-\delta}\eta_{t} + b \] where \(b\) is a constant.
Show that the IGE is equal to \(\rho\).

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
section: Result 3: The Long-Run Effects of Good Fortune
text:
Result 3: The Long-Run Effects of Good Fortune
What is the long-run effect of an increase in \(z\)?


To do this, let’s assume that \(\beta(1+r) = 1\) for simplicity
We’ll take a derivative around the deterministic steady state
Assume \(u(\cdot) = \log(\cdot)\).

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
section: Result 3: The Long-Run Effects of Good Fortune
text:
Result 3: The Long-Run Effects of Good Fortune
Exercise (board):


Show that in general: \[ u'(C_{t}) = \beta(1+r)\mathbb{E}u'(C_{t+1}) \]
Under our assumptions at steady state: \[C_{t}=C_{t+1}=\bar{C}\]
Define \(Z_{t}=\exp(\mu+z_{t})\) and iterate the budget constraint forward (ruling out Ponzi schemes): \[ \sum_{t=0}^\infty \frac{1}{(1+r)^{t}} \bar{C} = \Omega_{0} + \sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(1+r)^t}\max_{X_{t}}\left[wZ_{t}X^{\delta}_{t}/(1+r) - \psi X_{t}\right] \]

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
section: Result 3: The Long-Run Effects of Good Fortune
text:
Result 3: The Long-Run Effects of Good Fortune


Show that \[ \begin{aligned} &\max_{X_{t}}\left[wZ_{t}X^{\delta}_{t}/(1+r) - \psi X_{t}\right] \\ &\qquad = \left(\frac{Z_{t}w}{(1+r)}\right)^{1/(1-\delta)}\psi^{-\delta/(1-\delta)}\left(\delta^{\delta/(1-\delta)} - \delta^{1/(1-\delta)}\right) \end{aligned}\]
Hence, since \(\sum_{t}(1+r)^{-t} = (1+r)/r\): \[ \frac{1+r}{r}\bar{C} = \Omega_{0} + B\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\frac{\exp(z_{t})^{1/(1-\delta)}}{(1+r)^{t}} \quad \left(= \Omega_{0}+B\frac{1+r}{r} \text{ when } z_{t}=0\ \forall t\right)\] where \(B\) collects constants in previous expression.

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
section: Result 3: The Long-Run Effects of Good Fortune
text:
Result 3: The Long-Run Effects of Good Fortune


Consider a one-time, small increase in \(z_{0}\), s.t. \(z_{t} = \rho^{t}z_{0}\): \[ \frac{d\bar{C}}{dz_{0}}\Big\vert_{z_{0}=0} = \frac{r}{1+r} \frac{1}{1-\delta} B\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\frac{\rho^{t}}{(1+r)^{t}} = \frac{1}{1-\delta}\times B\times \frac{r}{1+r-\rho}\]
Dividing by \(\bar{C} = \frac{r}{1+r}\left(\Omega_{0} + B\frac{1+r}{r}\right)\): \[ \frac{d\log(\bar{C})}{dz_{0}}\Big\vert_{z_{0}=0} = \underbrace{\frac{B(1+r)/r}{\Omega_{0}+B(1+r)/r}}_{\text{human capital share of wealth}} \times\frac{1}{1-\delta}\times \frac{r}{1+r-\rho}  \]
Interpret! (Hint: what happens to \(\frac{r}{1+r-\rho}\) when \(\rho\rightarrow 1\)? When \(\rho = 0\)?)

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Connecting to IGE Estimation
Recall from last lecture we estimated:
\[y_{\text{child}} = \alpha + \beta \cdot y_{\text{parent}} + \varepsilon\]


In this model: \(\beta = \rho\) (ability persistence)
Independent of technology parameter \(\delta\)
Independent of prices \(w\), \(\psi\), \(r\)
Policy invariant: transfers don’t change IGE



Think: Is this consistent with geographic variation in mobility we saw?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Takeaways So Far


Investment does not depend on income (when borrowing is unconstrained)
Human capital differences fade away, but consumption effects last forever
Rich households use wealth bequests to maintain dynasties as human capital fades away
IGE determined by ability persistence (\(\rho\)) alone; \(\delta\) scales the level of inequality in \(\log(H)\) (by \(\frac{1}{1-\delta}\)) but not its persistence
But is this realistic? What about credit constraints?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Why Start with Two Periods?


Simplify exposition of some key points
Two-period version captures key forces
Lessons generalize

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Two-Period Setup
Parent’s problem in period 1:
\[\max_{C_1, C_2, X} u(C_1) + \beta u(C_2)\]
subject to:
\[
\begin{eqnarray}
C_1 + \psi X + \frac{A'}{1+r} &\leq& \Omega \\
C_2 &=& A' + w z X^{\delta}
\end{eqnarray}
\]


\(\Omega = wH + A\): total lifetime wealth
\(A'\): bequests (can be negative = borrowing)
Notation change: from here on, \(z\) denotes the level of the child’s ability, i.e. \(z\) here plays the role of \(\exp(\mu+z_{t})\) in the infinite-horizon model

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Combining Budget Constraints
Combining the two constraints:
\[C_1 + \frac{1}{1+r} C_2 \leq \Omega + \frac{w z X^{\delta}}{1+r} - \psi X\]


Left side: present value of consumption
Right side: wealth plus net human capital investment
Net investment: returns \(\frac{w z X^{\delta}}{1+r}\) but costs \(\psi X\)

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
First-Order Conditions
Euler equation:
\[u'(C_1) = \beta(1+r) u'(C_2)\]

FOC with respect to \(X\):
\[\psi = \frac{\delta w z X^{\delta-1}}{1+r}\]


Same result as before on optimal \(X\).

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
section: Investment Does Not Depend on Income (again)
text:
Investment Does Not Depend on Income (again)
Just as before, we get: \[X^* = \left( \frac{\delta w z}{\psi(1+r)} \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\delta}}\]

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
With Log Utility
If \(u(C) = \log(C)\), we can solve explicitly:
From Euler equation: \[\frac{C_2}{C_1} = \beta(1+r)\]
Therefore: \[(1+\beta)C_1 = \Omega + \frac{w z X^{*\delta}}{1+r} - \psi X^{*}\]
Where \[X^* = \left( \frac{\delta w z}{\psi(1+r)} \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\delta}}\]

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Interpretation
What does this mean economically?


Parents optimize to equate marginal returns across uses
Rich and poor parents with same \(z\) invest the same in children
Differences in income absorbed by \(C_1\), \(C_2\), and \(A\)
Crucial assumption: can borrow against future returns to H.C. investment



Question: Is this realistic? What if parents can’t borrow?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Is the Market Outcome Efficient?
Consider a social planner who maximizes weighted welfare:
\[\max_{\{C_{i1}, C_{i2}, X_i\}_{i\in[0,1]}} \int \left(\mu_{i1} u(C_{i1}) + \mu_{i2} u(C_{i2})\right)di\]
subject to resource constraint:
\[\int C_{i1} di + \frac{1}{1+r} \int C_{i2} di \leq \int \Omega_i di + \frac{w}{1+r} \int z_i X_i^{\delta} di - \psi \int X_i di\]

Key question: Does the planner’s solution coincide with the market?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Planner’s First-Order Conditions
The planner’s FOCs are:
\[\frac{u'(C_{i1})}{u'(C_{i2})} = (1+r)\frac{\mu_{i2}}{\mu_{i1}}, \quad \frac{\delta w z_i X_i^{\delta-1}}{1+r} = \psi\]
Compare to market FOCs:
\[\frac{u'(C_{i1})}{u'(C_{i2})} = \beta(1+r), \quad \frac{\delta w z_{i} X_{i}^{\delta-1}}{1+r} = \psi\]


Investment is identical: \(X_i^* = X_i^{planner}\)
Only difference: consumption allocation via weights \(\mu_{i1}, \mu_{i2}\)
Consumption FOCs coincide when \(\mu_{i2}/\mu_{i1} = \beta\) (and \(\mu_{i1}\propto 1/u'(C_{i1})\))
Market outcome is efficient for some choice of weights

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Efficiency Interpretation
What does this mean?


The market outcome is Pareto efficient
“can’t make anyone better off without making someone worse off”
Relative to Laissez-Faire economy, Planner can redistribute but that’s it



But: This relies critically on perfect credit markets!

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Can Parents Borrow?


Is it really plausible that parents can borrow against returns on their investment in children?

And make the children pay for it?

No!!
All kinds of moral hazard problems + legal issues
Also implied no role for income in shaping human capital

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
A More Realistic Setup
\[\max_{C_1, C_2, X} u(C_1) + \beta u(C_2)\]
subject to:
\[
\begin{eqnarray}
C_1 + \psi X + \frac{A'}{1+r} &\leq& \Omega \\
C_2 &=& A' + w z X^{\delta} \\
A' &\geq& 0
\end{eqnarray}
\]

Positive bequests only!

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Inefficient Investment


This now implies: \[ \frac{\delta w z X^{\delta - 1}}{1+r} \geq \psi \] with equality if \(A'>0\), and weakly greater (strictly greater when the constraint binds) if \(A'=0\).
Equilibrium is inefficient whenever some families are constrained.
Introduces a role for policy to improve market outcomes
Make everyone better off (Pareto improvement)

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Investment When Constrained


Solve for \(X^*\) when \(A'=0\): \[ \max_{X} u(\Omega - \psi X) + \beta u(wzX^{\delta}) \]
With log utility: \[ X^* = \frac{1}{\psi}\frac{\beta\delta}{1+\beta\delta} \Omega \]
Note that \(X^{*}\) now depends on \(\Omega\)

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
When Do Constraints Bind?
The borrowing constraint binds if:
\[\frac{1}{\psi}\frac{\beta \delta }{1 + \beta \delta} \Omega \leq \left( \frac{\delta w z}{\psi(1+r)} \right)^{\frac{1}{1-\delta}}\]


More likely to bind when \(\Omega\) is low (poor families)
More likely to bind when \(z\) is high (high returns to investment)
Creates a region where investment increases with income

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Investment and Income: Two Regimes





  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  

































Note: the constrained slope \(\frac{\beta\delta}{\psi(1+\beta\delta)}\) does not depend on \(z\). But high-\(z\) children have a higher unconstrained target \(X^{*}\), so they are constrained over a wider range of wealth: losses from borrowing constraints are concentrated on high-ability children in poor families.

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Exercise: Simulating a Dynasty (Part 1)
Part 1 (infinite horizon, no constraint). Simulate \(N\) dynasties for \(T\) generations using Result 1: \[ \log(H_{t+1}) = \mu + z_{t} + \delta\log(X_{t}),\qquad X_{t} = \left(\frac{\delta w \exp(\mu+z_{t})}{(1+r)\psi}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\delta}} \]


Regress \(\log(wH_{t+1})\) on \(\log(wH_{t})\) for \(\delta\in\{0.2,0.5,0.8\}\). Verify that the IGE is \(\rho\) every time.
What does change with \(\delta\)?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Exercise: Simulating a Dynasty (Part 2)
Part 2 (two-period model with \(A'\geq 0\), log utility). Now let each parent have wealth \(\Omega_{t} = wH_{t}\) (ignoring inherited assets, for simplicity), child ability \(Z_{t}=\exp(\mu+z_{t})\), and invest \[ X_{t} = \min\left\{\frac{\beta\delta}{\psi(1+\beta\delta)}\Omega_{t},\ X^{*}(Z_{t})\right\} \]


Plot average \(\log\) child earnings against \(\log\) parent earnings. Is the relationship still linear?
Compare the IGE for parents below and above the median.
What do you think will happen to the IGE if \(\beta\) falls (less patient / less altruistic parents)?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
section: Part 1: The IGE does not depend on \(\delta\)
text:
Part 1: The IGE does not depend on \(\delta\)


Code
using Random, Statistics

# Infinite-horizon model without borrowing constraints
function simulate_dynasty(δ; ρ=0.4, σ_η=0.5, μ=0.0, w=1.0, ψ=1.0, r=1.0, N=10_000, T=20)
    Random.seed!(1234)
    z = σ_η / sqrt(1 - ρ^2) * randn(N)          # stationary distribution of ability
    logH = zeros(N, T)
    for t in 1:T-1
        X = @. (δ * w * exp(μ + z) / ((1 + r) * ψ))^(1 / (1 - δ))
        logH[:, t+1] = @. μ + z + δ * log(X)
        z = ρ * z + σ_η * randn(N)               # next generation's ability
    end
    return log(w) .+ logH                         # log earnings
end

ige(lp, lc) = cov(lp, lc) / var(lp)               # OLS slope

for δ in (0.2, 0.5, 0.8)
    logy = simulate_dynasty(δ)
    println("δ = $δ:  IGE = ", round(ige(logy[:, end-1], logy[:, end]), digits=3),
            ",  var(log earnings) = ", round(var(logy[:, end]), digits=2))
end


δ = 0.2:  IGE = 0.39,  var(log earnings) = 0.46
δ = 0.5:  IGE = 0.39,  var(log earnings) = 1.19
δ = 0.8:  IGE = 0.39,  var(log earnings) = 7.41



The IGE is \(\approx\rho = 0.4\) for every \(\delta\) (up to sampling error). \(\delta\) only scales inequality, since \(\mathbb{V}[\log(H)] = \mathbb{V}[z]/(1-\delta)^2\).

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
section: Part 2: Constraints Make the Relationship Concave
text:
Part 2: Constraints Make the Relationship Concave


Code
using Plots

# Two-period model with A' ≥ 0 and log utility (z now in levels: Z = exp(μ+z))
function investment_bt(Ω, Z; δ, β, r, w=1.0, ψ=1.0, constrained=true)
    Xstar = (δ * w * Z / ((1 + r) * ψ))^(1 / (1 - δ))   # unconstrained optimum
    Xc = β * δ / (ψ * (1 + β * δ)) * Ω                   # optimum if A' = 0
    return constrained ? min(Xc, Xstar) : Xstar
end

function simulate_bt(; δ=0.5, β=0.9, r=1.0, ρ=0.4, σ_η=0.5, μ=0.0, w=1.0,
                       constrained=true, N=20_000, T=30)
    Random.seed!(1234)
    z = σ_η / sqrt(1 - ρ^2) * randn(N)
    logy = zeros(N, T)
    for t in 1:T-1
        z = ρ * z + σ_η * randn(N)                       # child's ability
        Ω = w .* exp.(logy[:, t])                         # parent's wealth = earnings
        X = investment_bt.(Ω, exp.(μ .+ z); δ, β, r, w, constrained)
        logy[:, t+1] = @. log(w) + μ + z + δ * log(X)
    end
    return logy[:, end-1], logy[:, end]                   # (parent, child)
end

# average child outcome within 20 bins of parental earnings
function binned(lp, lc; nbins=20)
    edges = quantile(lp, range(0, 1, length=nbins + 1))
    bin = [clamp(searchsortedlast(edges, x), 1, nbins) for x in lp]
    return [mean(lp[bin .== b]) for b in 1:nbins], [mean(lc[bin .== b]) for b in 1:nbins]
end

pl = plot(xlabel="Log parent earnings", ylabel="Mean log child earnings",
          legend=:topleft, size=(900, 330), tickfontsize=11, guidefontsize=12,
          legendfontsize=11, left_margin=4Plots.mm, bottom_margin=4Plots.mm)
for (c, lab) in ((false, "No constraint"), (true, "A' ≥ 0"))
    lp, lc = simulate_bt(constrained=c)
    lo = lp .< median(lp)
    println(lab, ": IGE = ", round(ige(lp, lc), digits=2),
            ", below median = ", round(ige(lp[lo], lc[lo]), digits=2),
            ", above median = ", round(ige(lp[.!lo], lc[.!lo]), digits=2))
    bx, by = binned(lp, lc)
    scatter!(pl, bx, by .- mean(lc), label=lab, markersize=5)
end
pl


No constraint: IGE = 0.4, below median = 0.4, above median = 0.41
A' ≥ 0: IGE = 0.59, below median = 0.64, above median = 0.54





  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  





































































Constrained families pass on wealth shocks through investment, so the IGE is higher at the bottom. (Means are de-meaned to compare shapes.)

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
section: Why Is the IGE Higher for Constrained Families?
text:
Why Is the IGE Higher for Constrained Families?


For a constrained family, \(\log(wH') = \log(w) + \log(z) + \delta\log\left(\frac{\beta\delta}{\psi(1+\beta\delta)}\right) + \delta\log(\Omega)\)
So \(\log\) child earnings depend on \(\log\) parental wealth directly (coefficient \(\delta\)), on top of the inherited ability channel (coefficient \(\approx\rho\))
For unconstrained families, only the ability channel operates
Prediction (Becker and Tomes 1986): the relationship between parent and child earnings is concave; earnings regress to the mean more slowly among poor families
Can we test this?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Prediction 1: Concavity

“The direct relation between the earnings of parents and children … is likely to be concave rather than linear because obstacles to the self-financing investments in children decline as parents’ earnings increase.” (Becker and Tomes 1986)



Recall Chetty et al. (2014) from Lecture 4:

The rank-rank relationship is almost perfectly linear across the distribution
The log-log relationship is nonlinear, but it is flatter in the tails: restricting to parents between the 10th and 90th percentiles raises the IGE from 0.344 to 0.452
In levels, \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{c}|Y_{p}]\) is concave, but that happens mechanically even with a log-linear model, since \(\mathbb{E}[Y_{c}|Y_{p}] \propto Y_{p}^{\rho}\) for \(\rho<1\)

Little sign of a steeper relationship at the bottom of the distribution
What do you think? Does this rule out borrowing constraints?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Prediction 2: Persistence by Constraint Status
Mulligan (1999) derives nine predictions that distinguish Becker-Tomes from a purely “mechanical” (Galton) regression to the mean. A key test:


Split adult children (PSID, SCF) by whether they received, or expect, an inheritance of $25,000 or more

Group 1 (inheritance): parents very likely unconstrained; Group 2 (none): includes the constrained

Model predicts: earnings persistence higher in group 2; consumption should not regress to the mean in group 1 (coefficient of one)
Findings (of nine implications: four refuted, two verified, three mixed):

Earnings/wage persistence is not systematically higher in group 2 (OLS similar; IV estimates go both ways)
Consumption regresses to the mean even in group 1: a coefficient of one is rejected in most specifications

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Mulligan’s Conclusion


“the observed intergenerational dynamics of measures of economic status are not the result of borrowing constraints” (Mulligan 1999)
But: constraints can exist without changing mobility much, e.g. if parents are unwilling to substitute consumption across generations, or if returns to investment are not very diminishing in the relevant range
A prediction that does hold: consumption is more persistent than earnings

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
The Goldberger Critique


Goldberger (1989): Does the economic model tell us anything a mechanical model of transmission does not?

Galton: \(y_{c} = \alpha + \beta y_{p} + \varepsilon\), regression to the mean with no optimization at all
Goldberger argued that the Becker-Tomes apparatus (altruism, investment, bequests) adds little testable content beyond such a reduced form

We have already seen a version of this: in the unconstrained model, the IGE is just \(\rho\), the persistence of ability. The earnings dynamics are observationally equivalent to Galton’s.
The economics only has bite through auxiliary assumptions (e.g. borrowing constraints), which is exactly what Mulligan (1999) sets out to test
What do you think? Why might a policymaker still prefer the economic model?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Taking Stock


The simple Becker-Tomes model with constraints makes sharp predictions about the shape of mobility
Those predictions find limited support in income data
Possible reasons:

Constraints may bind at specific ages (early childhood) that a two-period model cannot capture
Public schooling may relax constraints for some investments but not others
Investments are multidimensional (time, money, skills of different kinds)

This motivates the richer models in Lecture 7 (Caucutt and Lochner 2020; Lee and Seshadri 2019)

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Policy Implications


Note that we would like to target transfers based on \(z\)
But \(z\) is unobservable
An alternative is income-targeted transfers

e.g. progressive taxation

Can also try direct public investment (e.g. education, early childhood programs)
The gains to society depend on the joint distribution of \((\Omega,z)\)
What does the evidence say?

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
What Does the Evidence Say?
In coming lectures we’ll see:


Evidence suggests borrowing constraints do bind for many families
Returns to college are high, but many don’t attend
Educational interventions (especially early childhood) show high returns
Suggests scope for welfare-improving policy

title: The Becker-Tomes Model
text:
Reading




Becker, Gary S., and Nigel Tomes. 1979. “An Equilibrium Theory of the Distribution of Income and Intergenerational Mobility.” The Journal of Political Economy, no. 6: 1153–89. https://doi.org/10.1086/260831.


———. 1986. “Human Capital and the Rise and Fall of Families.” Journal of Labor Economics, no. 3: S1–39. https://doi.org/10.1086/298118.


Caucutt, Elizabeth M., and Lance Lochner. 2020. “Early and Late Human Capital Investments, Borrowing Constraints, and the Family.” The Journal of Political Economy, no. 3: 1065–1147. https://doi.org/10.1086/704759.

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Overview


The two-period Becker-Tomes model (Becker and Tomes 1979, 1986) gave us sharp intuition:

Without borrowing constraints, investment does not depend on income and the IGE is \(\rho\)
With constraints, poor families under-invest and the IGE rises

From Lecture 6 we know skills are produced over many stages of childhood (Cunha and Heckman 2007)
Today: put these two ideas together in a model we can solve and simulate
Then describe two influential quantitative papers: Caucutt and Lochner (2020) and Lee and Seshadri (2019)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
section: What the Simple Model Can’t Do
text:
What the Simple Model Can’t Do


One investment period: can’t separate early vs late childhood investment
Parents’ income is fixed: but young parents earn less than they will later

Constraints are likely to bind when children are young

No sense of magnitudes: how much would a $1,000 transfer change a child’s earnings? Does it matter when it is paid?
What do you think? If you had a fixed budget to transfer to low-income families, would you give it when the child is 3 or when the child is 13?

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Timing
A parent lives for two periods while the child grows up, then the child becomes an adult:


Period 1 (child is young): parent earns \(y_{1}\), invests \(I_{1}\), saves \(A_{2}\)
Period 2 (child is older): parent earns \(y_{2} = (1+g)y_{1}\), invests \(I_{2}\), leaves a bequest \(A'\geq 0\)
Period 3 (child is an adult): child has resources \(A' + wH'\)
Life-cycle income growth \(g>0\) means young parents would like to borrow against their own future income
Two borrowing constraints:

\(A_{2} \geq -\kappa y_{2}\): young parents can borrow at most a fraction \(\kappa\) of future income
\(A' \geq 0\): parents cannot borrow against the child’s future earnings (as in Lecture 5)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Technology
Child’s adult human capital: \[ H' = Z\theta^{\delta},\qquad \theta = \left[\gamma I_{1}^{\phi} + (1-\gamma)I_{2}^{\phi}\right]^{1/\phi} \]


\(Z = \exp(\mu + z)\): child’s ability, with \(z' = \rho z + \eta'\) as in Lecture 5
\(\theta\): skills at the end of childhood, produced by a CES technology
Mapping to Lecture 6: there, \(\theta_{t+1} = [\gamma_{1}I_{t}^{\phi} + \gamma_{2}\theta_{t}^{\phi}]^{1/\phi}\). Set \(\theta_{1} = I_{1}\) (early skills come from early investment), then \[\theta_{2} = \left[\gamma_{1}I_{2}^{\phi} + \gamma_{2}I_{1}^{\phi}\right]^{1/\phi}\] which is our \(\theta\) with \(\gamma = \gamma_{2}\) and \(1-\gamma = \gamma_{1}\) (normalizing \(\gamma_{1}+\gamma_{2}=1\))
Mapping to Lecture 5: \(I_{1} = I_{2} = X\) gives \(\theta = X\) and \(H' = ZX^{\delta}\) (Becker-Tomes)
\(\phi\) governs substitutability: elasticity of substitution \(1/(1-\phi)\)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Dynamic Complementarity
Exercise (board): Show that \[ \frac{\partial^2 H'}{\partial I_{1}\partial I_{2}} > 0 \iff \phi < \delta \]


Hint: \(\theta\) is homogeneous of degree one, so \(\frac{\theta\,\theta_{12}}{\theta_{1}\theta_{2}} = 1-\phi\) (one over the elasticity of substitution)
Interpretation: early investment raises the return to late investment as long as early and late investments are complementary enough relative to the diminishing returns \(\delta\)
We’ll use \(\phi = -0.5\) (elasticity of substitution \(= 2/3\)) and \(\delta = 0.6\)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
The Parent’s Problem
\[\max\ \log(C_{1}) + \beta\log(C_{2}) + \beta^{2}\log(A' + wH')\]
subject to:
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_{1} + \psi I_{1} + \frac{A_{2}}{1+r} &= y_{1} \\
C_{2} + \psi I_{2} + \frac{A'}{1+r} &= y_{2} + A_{2} \\
A_{2} \geq -\kappa y_{2}, &\quad A' \geq 0
\end{aligned}
\]

As in Lecture 5, the parent values the child’s adult resources with log utility. A fully dynastic version would replace \(\log(A'+wH')\) with the child’s own value function.

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Recursive Formulation
Work backwards. In period 2, the state is \((A_{2}, I_{1})\) (plus \(y_{2}\) and \(Z\)):
\[ \begin{aligned} V_{2}(A_{2}, I_{1}) &= \max_{C_{2}, I_{2}, A'\geq 0}\Big\{\log(C_{2}) + \beta\log(A' + wZ\theta(I_{1},I_{2})^{\delta})\Big\} \\ &\text{s.t.}\quad C_{2} + \psi I_{2} + \frac{A'}{1+r} = y_{2} + A_{2} \end{aligned}\]

In period 1, the state is \((y_{1}, Z)\):
\[ \begin{aligned} V_{1}(y_{1}, Z) &= \max_{C_{1}, I_{1}, A_{2}\geq -\kappa y_{2}}\Big\{\log(C_{1}) + \beta V_{2}(A_{2}, I_{1})\Big\} \\ &\text{s.t.}\quad C_{1} + \psi I_{1} + \frac{A_{2}}{1+r} = y_{1} \end{aligned}\]



Early investment \(I_{1}\) is a state variable in period 2: it changes the return to \(I_{2}\)
Dynasty: the child’s earnings \(wH'\) become next generation’s \(y_{1}\), and \(z' = \rho z + \eta'\)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
The Unconstrained Benchmark


If both constraints are slack, the parent maximizes the present value of net returns: \[ \max_{I_{1},I_{2}} \frac{wZ\theta^{\delta}}{(1+r)^{2}} - \psi I_{1} - \frac{\psi I_{2}}{1+r} \]
Ratio of FOCs gives \[ \frac{I_{1}}{I_{2}} = \left(\frac{\gamma}{(1-\gamma)(1+r)}\right)^{\frac{1}{1-\phi}} \]
Both investments are proportional to \(Z^{1/(1-\delta)}\), so \(\log(H') = c + \frac{1}{1-\delta}\log(Z)\) and the IGE is still \(\rho\)
Neither parental income nor the timing of income matters
With constraints, both matter. Now we need the computer.

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Solving the Model


Each family’s problem is a small optimization problem over \((I_{1}, I_{2}, A_{2}, A')\)
Trick: given \((I_{1}, I_{2})\), what’s left is a consumption-savings problem with log utility, which we can solve by hand

Four cases: neither constraint binds, only \(A'\geq 0\) binds, only \(A_{2}\geq -\kappa y_{2}\) binds, both bind
Since the problem is concave, the case that satisfies the Kuhn-Tucker conditions is the solution

Then search over \(I_{1}\) (outer) and \(I_{2}\) (inner) with golden-section search

The inner search over \(I_{2}\) given \(I_{1}\) is exactly the period-2 problem \(V_{2}\)

Simulate dynasties for several generations to get a stationary distribution of \((y_{1}, Z)\)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Code: Model Primitives


Code
using Random, Statistics, StatsPlots

Base.@kwdef struct Params
    β::Float64 = 0.9      # discount factor (one period ≈ 8-9 years)
    r::Float64 = 0.3      # interest rate per period
    w::Float64 = 1.0      # price of human capital
    ψ::Float64 = 1.0      # price of investment goods
    g::Float64 = 0.35     # parental income growth, period 1 to period 2
    δ::Float64 = 0.6      # returns to skills in H'
    γ::Float64 = 0.6      # weight on early investment
    φ::Float64 = -0.5     # CES parameter: elasticity of substitution = 1/(1-φ)
    κ::Float64 = 0.0      # young parents can borrow up to κ*y2
    μ::Float64 = 1.2      # mean log ability (a scale normalization)
    ρ::Float64 = 0.4      # persistence of log ability
    σ_η::Float64 = 0.4    # sd of ability innovations
end
# copy a Params with some fields changed, e.g. Params(p; κ=0.5)
Params(p::Params; kw...) = Params(; (f => getfield(p, f) for f in fieldnames(Params))..., kw...)

skills(I1, I2, p) = (p.γ * I1^p.φ + (1 - p.γ) * I2^p.φ)^(1 / p.φ)
humancap(I1, I2, Z, p) = Z * skills(I1, I2, p)^p.δ

# Given investments, solve the savings problem in closed form.
# R1, R2: resources net of investment; E: child's earnings; b: borrowing limit for young parent
function savings(R1, R2, E, b, p)
    (; β, r) = p
    val(C1, C2, C3) = (C1 > 0 && C2 > 0 && C3 > 0) ? log(C1) + β * log(C2) + β^2 * log(C3) : -Inf
    # Case 1: neither constraint binds
    C1 = (R1 + R2 / (1 + r) + E / (1 + r)^2) / (1 + β + β^2)
    C2, C3 = β * (1 + r) * C1, (β * (1 + r))^2 * C1
    A2 = (1 + r) * (R1 - C1); Ap = (1 + r) * (R2 + A2 - C2)
    (A2 >= -b && Ap >= 0) && return val(C1, C2, C3), A2, Ap
    # Case 2: only A' ≥ 0 binds
    C1 = (R1 + R2 / (1 + r)) / (1 + β); C2 = β * (1 + r) * C1
    A2 = (1 + r) * (R1 - C1)
    (A2 >= -b && E >= β * (1 + r) * C2) && return val(C1, C2, E), A2, 0.0
    # Case 3: only A2 ≥ -b binds
    C1 = R1 + b / (1 + r)
    C2 = (R2 - b + E / (1 + r)) / (1 + β); C3 = β * (1 + r) * C2
    Ap = (1 + r) * (R2 - b - C2)
    (Ap >= 0 && C2 >= β * (1 + r) * C1) && return val(C1, C2, C3), -b, Ap
    # Case 4: both bind
    return val(R1 + b / (1 + r), R2 - b, E), -b, 0.0
end

# golden-section search for the maximum of a concave function on [lo, hi]
function golden_max(f, lo, hi; tol=1e-7)
    c = (sqrt(5) - 1) / 2
    x1, x2 = hi - c * (hi - lo), lo + c * (hi - lo)
    f1, f2 = f(x1), f(x2)
    while hi - lo > tol * (1 + abs(lo) + abs(hi))
        if f1 < f2
            lo, x1, f1 = x1, x2, f2
            x2 = lo + c * (hi - lo); f2 = f(x2)
        else
            hi, x2, f2 = x2, x1, f1
            x1 = hi - c * (hi - lo); f1 = f(x1)
        end
    end
    x = (lo + hi) / 2
    return x, f(x)
end

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Code: Solving and Simulating


Code
# Solve one family's problem. T1, T2: government transfers in periods 1 and 2.
function solve_family(y1, Z, p; T1=0.0, T2=0.0)
    (; r, ψ, w, g, κ) = p
    R1, R2 = y1 + T1, (1 + g) * y1 + T2
    b = κ * (1 + g) * y1
    ϵ = 1e-10
    # period-2 problem: given I1, choose I2 (savings solved in closed form)
    function period2(I1)
        I2max = (R2 + (1 + r) * (R1 - ψ * I1)) / ψ
        return golden_max(I2 -> savings(R1 - ψ * I1, R2 - ψ * I2, w * humancap(I1, I2, Z, p), b, p)[1],
                          ϵ, I2max - ϵ)
    end
    I1, _ = golden_max(I1 -> period2(I1)[2], ϵ, (R1 + b / (1 + r)) / ψ - ϵ)
    I2, _ = period2(I1)
    H = humancap(I1, I2, Z, p)
    _, A2, Ap = savings(R1 - ψ * I1, R2 - ψ * I2, w * H, b, p)
    return (; I1, I2, H, A2, Ap,
              young_constrained = A2 <= -b + 1e-6, child_constrained = Ap <= 1e-6)
end

# Unconstrained benchmark (closed form)
function unconstrained(Z, p)
    (; r, ψ, w, δ, γ, φ) = p
    k = (γ / ((1 - γ) * (1 + r)))^(1 / (1 - φ))      # I1/I2
    θk = skills(k, 1.0, p)                           # θ when I2 = 1
    I2 = (w * Z * δ * θk^(δ - 1) * (1 - γ) * θk^(1 - φ) / ((1 + r) * ψ))^(1 / (1 - δ))
    return (; I1 = k * I2, I2)
end

# Simulate N dynasties for T generations; return the last parent-child cross-section
function simulate(p; N=3000, T=6, seed=1234)
    Random.seed!(seed)
    z = p.σ_η / sqrt(1 - p.ρ^2) * randn(N)
    y1 = [p.w * humancap(unconstrained(exp(p.μ + zi), p)..., exp(p.μ + zi), p) for zi in z]
    local out
    for t in 1:T
        zc = p.ρ * z + p.σ_η * randn(N)                       # child's ability
        sols = [solve_family(y1[i], exp(p.μ + zc[i]), p) for i in 1:N]
        out = (; y1 = copy(y1), Z = exp.(p.μ .+ zc), sols)
        y1 = [p.w * s.H for s in sols]                        # child becomes next parent
        z = zc
    end
    return out
end

ige(x, y) = cov(x, y) / var(x)
quartile_of(x) = [min(4, 1 + floor(Int, 4 * (sum(x .< xi) / length(x)))) for xi in x]

text:
Investment Policies by Parental Income


Code
Zmed = exp(p0.μ)                                   # median ability
ygrid = exp.(range(log(0.05), log(5.0), length=60))
sol = [solve_family(y, Zmed, p0) for y in ygrid]

text:
Who Is Constrained?


Code
q = quartile_of(base.y1)
young = [mean(s.young_constrained for s in base.sols[q .== k]) for k in 1:4]

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
The Implied IGE


Code
lp = log.(base.y1)
lc = log.([p0.w * s.H for s in base.sols])
lo = lp .< median(lp)
println("IGE (all families):        ", round(ige(lp, lc), digits=2))
println("IGE (below median income): ", round(ige(lp[lo], lc[lo]), digits=2))
println("IGE (above median income): ", round(ige(lp[.!lo], lc[.!lo]), digits=2))

IGE (all families):        0.64
IGE (below median income): 0.68
IGE (above median income): 0.56
Unconstrained benchmark:   ρ = 0.4




Constraints raise the IGE above \(\rho\), and more so at the bottom (the concavity from Lecture 5)
What do you think? Which constraint matters more for the IGE here: the one on young parents, or the one on borrowing against the child?

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Early vs. Late Transfers


Give a transfer worth 10% of median income to one quartile of parents
Early: \(T_{1}\) paid in period 1, or Late: \(T_{2} = (1+r)T_{1}\) paid in period 2
Same present value, so an unconstrained family is indifferent and does not change investment at all
Compare the change in mean \(\log(H')\) for the children of recipients

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Early vs. Late Transfers


Code
T = 0.1 * median(base.y1)
lH(v) = mean(log(s.H) for s in v)
gain = zeros(4, 2)
for k in 1:4
    idx = findall(q .== k)
    b0 = base.sols[idx]
    early = [solve_family(base.y1[i], base.Z[i], p0; T1=T) for i in idx]
    late = [solve_family(base.y1[i], base.Z[i], p0; T2=(1 + p0.r) * T) for i in idx]
    gain[k, :] = [lH(early) - lH(b0), lH(late) - lH(b0)]
end
groupedbar(gain, bar_position=:dodge, xticks=(1:4, ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"]),
           xlabel="Quartile of parental income (recipients)", ylabel="Change in mean log H'",
           label=["Early transfer" "Late transfer"], size=(900, 420), tickfontsize=11,
           guidefontsize=12, legendfontsize=11, left_margin=4Plots.mm, bottom_margin=4Plots.mm)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Why Do Early Transfers Win?


Constraints bind when parents are young: income is low exactly when early investment is needed
An early transfer relaxes the binding constraint directly, so \(I_{1}\) rises
A late transfer arrives after \(I_{1}\) is sunk. With dynamic complementarity, a low \(I_{1}\) lowers the payoff to \(I_{2}\), so late money cannot fully make up for it
A late transfer can even lower \(I_{1}\): knowing more money is coming, the young parent wants to consume more today but cannot borrow
What do you think? What real-world programs look like “early transfers”? (Recall the EITC and cash transfer evidence coming in Lecture 8)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Loosening Credit Constraints


Code
p1 = Params(p0; κ=0.5)                     # young parents can borrow up to half of y2
loose = simulate(p1)




Code
function summary_stats(out, p)
    lp = log.(out.y1); lc = log.([p.w * s.H for s in out.sols])
    return (IGE = round(ige(lp, lc), digits=2),
            share_young_constrained = round(mean(s.young_constrained for s in out.sols), digits=2),
            share_bequest_constrained = round(mean(s.child_constrained for s in out.sols), digits=2),
            early_late_ratio = round(mean(s.I1 / s.I2 for s in out.sols), digits=2))
end
s0, s1 = summary_stats(base, p0), summary_stats(loose, p1)
println(rpad("", 28), rpad("κ = 0", 10), "κ = 0.5")
for k in keys(s0)
    println(rpad(string(k), 28), rpad(s0[k], 10), s1[k])
end
println("\nUnconstrained I₁/I₂ = ", round((p0.γ / ((1 - p0.γ) * (1 + p0.r)))^(1 / (1 - p0.φ)), digits=2))


                            κ = 0     κ = 0.5
IGE                         0.64      0.64
share_young_constrained     0.69      0.0
share_bequest_constrained   0.46      0.55
early_late_ratio            1.02      1.1

Unconstrained I₁/I₂ = 1.1




Young parents are no longer constrained, and investment shifts towards early childhood
But many families are still constrained by \(A'\geq 0\): they still can’t borrow against the child’s earnings
What do you think? Why might loosening credit for young parents do little to the IGE in this model?

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Exercise
Using the code above:

Set \(\phi = 0.5\) (early and late investment are substitutes). Repeat the early vs. late transfer experiment. Does the advantage of early transfers shrink? Why?
Set \(g = 0\) (flat life-cycle income). What happens to the share of young parents who are constrained, and to the early vs. late comparison?
Instead of a transfer, give a subsidy to \(\psi\) in period 1 only, targeted at the bottom quartile. Is it more or less effective per dollar spent than the early cash transfer? (Hint: you will need to give solve_family a period-specific price.)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Caucutt and Lochner (2020): Model



Our model is a stripped-down version of Caucutt and Lochner (2020)
Their model:

Dynastic altruism: parents value children’s utility, not just their resources
Parents invest in early and late childhood, with a CES technology allowing dynamic complementarity
Parents’ income rises over the life-cycle, and parents face borrowing constraints against both their own future income and their children’s
The technology is estimated from data on children’s skills and investment, and the model is matched to data on family income and investment

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Caucutt and Lochner (2020): Lessons


Qualitative lessons:

Many young parents are constrained, and constrained families under-invest in both early and late periods
Because of complementarity, policies that relax constraints early tend to be more effective than late ones, and late subsidies are less effective for children who received little early investment
Effects persist across generations through the dynasty

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Lee and Seshadri (2019): Model



Lee and Seshadri (2019) build a multigenerational life-cycle model with human capital accumulation:

Parents invest in children at several stages (early childhood, later childhood, college)
Adults continue to accumulate human capital over their working lives
Families can make financial transfers, and face borrowing constraints
Ability is partly inherited

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
section: Lee and Seshadri (2019): Sources of Persistence
text:
Lee and Seshadri (2019): Sources of Persistence


Calibrated to U.S. data on intergenerational persistence in earnings, education, and wealth
Use the model to ask: what are the sources of persistence?

Inherited ability vs. parental investment in human capital vs. financial transfers
Persistence across more than two generations: grandparents can matter through the human capital and wealth they pass on, not just through \(\rho\)

What do you think? In the AR(1) model from Lecture 5, the grandparent-grandchild IGE would be \(\rho^{2}\). Why might a model with investment predict more persistence than that?

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Why Build Quantitative Models?


Policy questions are about magnitudes and timing, not just signs
Reduced-form evidence (Lecture 8) tells us what a specific program did, in a specific place
A model lets us:

Compare policies that have never been tried
Account for general equilibrium and dynastic effects
Interpret why a program worked

The cost: results depend on functional forms and parameters, which must be disciplined by data (e.g. the technology estimates from Lecture 6)

title: Quantitative Models of Intergenerational Mobility
text:
Summary


Extending Becker-Tomes to early and late investment with life-cycle income changes the policy conclusions
Without constraints: investment, timing, and the IGE do not depend on parental income (IGE \(=\rho\))
With constraints that bind when parents are young:

Poor families under-invest early, and complementarity makes this hard to undo later
The IGE rises above \(\rho\), especially at the bottom
Early transfers raise children’s human capital more than late transfers of the same present value

Caucutt and Lochner (2020) and Lee and Seshadri (2019) take these models to the data to measure magnitudes
Next: what does the evidence from actual programs say?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Overview


Last time: the safety net (EITC, food stamps, cash transfers) affects child outcomes
Today: programs that target investment in children directly

Early childhood education: Perry, ABC/CARE, Head Start, public pre-K
Parenting and home-visiting programs: Jamaica, Colombia, Chile

Key questions:

Do early programs have lasting effects? On what outcomes?
Why do some programs look great and others look weak or even harmful?
What happens when a successful small program is scaled up?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
section: A Brief Recap: The Technology of Skill Formation
text:
A Brief Recap: The Technology of Skill Formation
From lecture 6: \[ \theta_{t+1} = \left[\gamma I_{t}^{\phi} + (1-\gamma)\theta_{t}^{\phi}\right]^{1/\phi} \]


Self-productivity: skills today raise skills tomorrow
Dynamic complementarity: higher \(\theta_t\) raises the return to \(I_t\)
Low \(\phi\) early in life: hard to make up for low early investment later
Skills are multidimensional: cognitive and noncognitive

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
What Does the Model Predict?
What do you think the model says about an early intervention that raises \(\theta_1\)?


Effects should persist (self-productivity) and could grow (dynamic complementarity)
But only if later investments \(I_2, I_3, \ldots\) are not cut back

If parents or schools substitute away, measured gains can fade

Effects may show up in skills we do not measure well

A program can raise noncognitive skill without raising test scores

The effect depends on the counterfactual investment the child would have received



Keep these four points in mind: they will help us reconcile the evidence.

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
The HighScope Perry Preschool Program
From James J. Heckman et al. (2010b):


Ypsilanti, Michigan, early 1960s; five cohorts of disadvantaged African-American children
Eligibility: IQ between 70 and 85 plus a low socioeconomic status index
Treatment: starting at age 3, two years of a 2.5-hour preschool program each weekday, plus weekly home visits by teachers
Curriculum: “plan-do-review”, with active learning and open-ended questions
123 children randomized into treatment and control
Followed at ages 15, 19, 27, and 40, with over 90% of the original sample interviewed at age 40
Cost: about $17,759 per child (2006 dollars, undiscounted)

Selected treatment-control comparisons (James J. Heckman et al. 2010b, Table 2):
