title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Perry: IQ Gains Fade Out

Source: Cunha et al. (2006), Figure 14A. By age 10 the IQ gap is gone, yet the adult outcomes differ.

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Perry: Statistical Challenges
Critics raised serious concerns (James J. Heckman et al. 2010b):


Small sample: 123 children. Are large-sample tests valid?
Compromised randomization: after assignment, some children were swapped

e.g., children of working mothers moved from treatment to control (31% of controls vs. 9% of treated had working mothers at entry)

Many outcomes: with dozens of outcomes, some will be “significant” by chance
Missing data and extrapolation: no data after age 40; crime must be valued in dollars

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
How Heckman et al. Respond


Small sample: a companion reanalysis (James J. Heckman et al. 2010a) uses permutation tests (reshuffle treatment labels many times) and finds the same conclusions as large-sample tests
Multiple testing: the companion paper also adjusts p-values for testing many outcomes at once; Anderson (2008) had raised this concern for Perry and other early programs
Compromised randomization: condition on the variables used to reassign children (e.g., mother’s employment)
Extrapolation: impute missing earnings and project past age 40 using NLSY and PSID; report results to age 40 without extrapolation as a check
Standard errors on the rate of return itself (earlier studies reported none)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Perry: Rate of Return
Main findings from James J. Heckman et al. (2010b):


Annual social rate of return: generally 7–10%

Lower than earlier estimates of 16–17%
But statistically different from zero, for both males and females
Above the post-WWII return on equities (5.8%)

Benefit-cost ratio at a 3% discount rate (with deadweight cost of taxes): roughly 7 to 12
A major share of the benefits comes from reduced crime



What do you think? Is a 7–10% return “large”? Compare with returns to a year of schooling.

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
ABC/CARE: The Program
From García et al. (2020):


Two closely related programs in Chapel Hill, North Carolina

ABC: cohorts born 1972–1976; CARE: cohorts born 1978–1980

Disadvantaged, mostly African-American children, eligibility based on a “risk index”
Started at about 8 weeks of age and ran until age 5
Full-time, educationally focused childcare, plus health check-ups
Randomized: ABC analysis sample of 58 treated and 56 control; CARE adds 17 treated and 23 controls
Followed through the mid-30s, including a medical exam
Cost: about $18,514 per participant per year (2014 dollars)

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
ABC/CARE: Life-Cycle Benefit-Cost
The problem: participants are only observed to their mid-30s. How do we value lifetime benefits?


Estimate production functions for adult outcomes in nonexperimental data (e.g., labor income as a function of education, earlier income, background)
Key assumption, structural invariance: treatment changes the inputs, not the mapping from inputs to outputs
Test this in the overlapping ages: forecasts match the experimental outcomes
Use the estimated functions to forecast labor income, health, crime, and parents’ income over the life cycle



Notice the connection to our course: the forecast uses a model, not just the experiment.

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
ABC/CARE: Results

García et al. (2020), Figure 3: net present values per participant (3% discount rate, 2014 dollars).

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
ABC/CARE: Results


Internal rate of return: 13.7% (SE 3%)
Benefit-cost ratio: 7.3 (SE 1.84)
Sensitivity analysis: IRR from 8.0% to 18.3%; benefit-cost ratio from 1.52 to 17.40
Each of four benefit categories (participants’ labor income, parents’ labor income, crime, health) is at least as large as the costs

So the conclusion survives dropping any one of them

Free childcare let mothers work and study: a benefit that test scores never capture
They show that the shortcut of monetizing early test score gains (the approach used by Kline and Walters (2016)) gives a much smaller benefit-cost ratio for ABC/CARE: counting more outcomes over a longer horizon raises it

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
section: Early vs. Late Programs and IQ
text:
Early vs. Late Programs and IQ
From Cunha et al. (2006):


Perry (starting at age 3): IQ gains faded by about age 10 (as we saw)
Abecedarian (starting in infancy): IQ gains persisted
Consistent with IQ being malleable mainly in the earliest years
Caveat: Abecedarian was also far more intensive, so we cannot separate timing from intensity

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Head Start


Largest U.S. early childhood program: about 900,000 three- and four-year-olds at a cost of $7.6 billion in 2013 (Kline and Walters 2016)
Observational studies find substantial long-run effects
But the Head Start Impact Study (HSIS), a randomized lottery, found small effects on test scores that faded out quickly
Intent-to-treat effects on a test score index (Kline and Walters 2016):

First year: 0.19 SD (age-3 cohort), 0.14 SD (age-4 cohort)
By year 3: 0.02 SD and insignificant

Widely interpreted as “Head Start doesn’t work”



What do you think? What did the control group children do instead?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
The Counterfactual Matters
From Kline and Walters (2016), first year of the experiment:




Control (no offer)
Offered Head Start




Other preschool centers
31.5%
8.3%


Home care
55%
9.5%





Roughly one third of the children induced to attend Head Start (“compliers”) would otherwise have attended another preschool
Many of those competing preschools are themselves publicly funded
So the experiment compares Head Start to a mix of home care and other preschools

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Interpreting the IV Estimate
Let \(h\) = Head Start, \(c\) = competing preschool, \(n\) = home care. Let \(S_c\) be the share of compliers drawn from competing preschools.
\[ \begin{aligned} \text{LATE}_h = {} & S_c \cdot E[Y(h)-Y(c)\mid c\text{-complier}] \\ & + (1-S_c)\cdot E[Y(h)-Y(n)\mid n\text{-complier}] \end{aligned} \]


The IV estimate (0.247 SD in year one) averages two very different comparisons
Their selection model: large gains relative to home care, roughly zero relative to other preschools
“Reverse Roy” selection: children less likely to enroll gain the most

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Implications for Cost-Benefit


When a child moves from a subsidized preschool into Head Start, the government saves the cost of the other program
This lowers Head Start’s net fiscal cost
Marginal value of public funds (MVPF) in Kline and Walters (2016):

Ignoring substitution: 1.10 (roughly breaks even)
Counting savings, with competing programs costing 50% / 75% of Head Start: 1.50 / 1.84

Lesson: the policy-relevant effect is relative to the next best alternative, and costs must be net of what that alternative costs

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Large-Scale Public Pre-K: Boston
Gray-Lobe, Pathak, and Walters (2023) study Boston’s public preschool using admission lotteries:


Compare children who did and did not win a seat in oversubscribed schools
No detectable effect on state achievement test scores in later grades
But preschool attendance raised:

High school graduation and SAT-taking
College enrollment

And reduced disciplinary incidents, including juvenile incarceration



Same pattern as Perry: test-score effects fade, but long-run outcomes improve.

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Large-Scale Public Pre-K: Tennessee
Durkin et al. (2022) study Tennessee’s Voluntary Pre-K program:


Randomized: about 3,000 children from low-income families who applied to oversubscribed sites (2009–10 and 2010–11)
Follow-up through sixth grade using state records
Children offered pre-K had lower state achievement test scores in grades 3–6, with the largest gap in sixth grade
Also more disciplinary infractions and special education placements, and worse attendance
The authors note that many control children attended other programs, such as Head Start



What do you think could make a pre-K program harmful?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Reconciling the Evidence


Program quality and intensity: Perry and ABC/CARE were small, intensive, carefully run demonstration programs; statewide programs vary in quality
Counterfactual care: the effect is always relative to what control children got

74–75% of ABC/CARE controls used other childcare (García et al. 2020); one third of Head Start compliers came from other preschools (Kline and Walters 2016)

Population: Perry targeted very disadvantaged children (IQ 70–85)
Fadeout vs. long-run effects: test scores may miss noncognitive skills that drive adult outcomes (Perry, Boston)
Later investment: with dynamic complementarity, gains depend on the schools and homes children go to next
Statistical power: small samples give imprecise estimates; large programs may have small effects that are hard to detect

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Exercise: Head Start with Substitutes
Suppose the effect of Head Start relative to home care is \(0.36\) SD, and relative to another preschool is \(0\) SD.


If \(S_c = 1/3\) of compliers come from other preschools, what is the LATE?
A policymaker says: “Head Start raises scores by your LATE, so for a child at home it would raise scores by the same amount.” What is wrong with this?
Head Start costs $8,000 per child. A competing program costs $6,000 and is publicly funded. What is the net cost to the government of enrolling a \(c\)-complier? An \(n\)-complier?
Now suppose competing programs are rationed (waitlisted). How does your answer change?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Why Target Parents?


In the model, \(I_t\) is chosen by parents
Parents may lack information about the technology, or have low skills themselves
A program that changes parental behavior may change investment for years, not just while the program lasts
And these programs are often cheap compared to center-based care

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
The Jamaica Study
The Jamaica early childhood stimulation trial (Walker et al. 2022):


Children with stunted growth aged 9–24 months
Two-year randomized trial of nutritional supplementation and/or psychosocial stimulation

Stimulation: community health workers visit homes and show mothers how to play with and talk to their children

A comparison group of non-stunted children was also followed
Small sample: roughly 130 stunted children in the trial

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Jamaica: Long-Run Effects


At age 22: stimulation raised earnings by about 25%, enough to catch up with the non-stunted comparison group (Gertler et al. 2014)
At age 31 (Walker et al. 2022), the stimulation group had:

Higher IQ and better executive function (e.g., cognitive flexibility)
Better psychosocial outcomes: e.g., less social inhibition, less risk-taking

But IQ was still below the non-stunted comparison group



A very cheap intervention with very large, long-lasting effects. Can it be done at scale?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
section: Colombia: Scaling Up the Jamaica Model
text:
Colombia: Scaling Up the Jamaica Model
Attanasio et al. (2020):


Cluster RCT in 96 towns; about 1,400 disadvantaged children aged 12–24 months
18 months of weekly home visits using a curriculum adapted from Jamaica, delivered by local women already working in a government program (not professionals)
Arms: stimulation, micronutrient supplements, both, control
Stimulation improved cognitive (and some socio-emotional) skills at the end of the program; micronutrients had no effect

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Colombia: The Mechanism
The paper estimates a production function: \[ \theta_{t+1} = f(\theta_t, \theta^{mother}, X_t, Y_t) \]
where \(X_t\) = material investment (toys, books), \(Y_t\) = time investment.


Investments are endogenous: the experiment provides variation in investment that is independent of the child’s unobservables
The program effect is explained by higher parental investment, not a change in the technology itself
Investments are complementary with maternal skills and with the child’s earlier skills
Exactly the language of dynamic complementarity

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Colombia: Two Years Later


A follow-up two years after the program ended found no detectable effect on child development (Andrew et al. 2018)
Possible explanations offered by the authors:

Initial effects were too small to be sustained
The home environment did not stay changed after visits stopped
Compromises in implementation when going to scale




What do you think? Does fadeout here mean the same thing as fadeout in Perry?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Chile: A National Parenting Program
Carneiro et al. (2024) evaluate Nadie es Perfecto (“Nobody’s Perfect”):


A national, low-cost, group-based parenting program, adapted from a Canadian model
Sessions over 6–8 weeks, in groups of about 8–12 parents
Delivered by staff of the national health system in existing facilities
Evaluated with a large-scale randomized experiment
About 0.1 SD improvements in children’s vocabulary and socio-emotional development, measured three years after the program ended, with improvements in parenting behaviors and beliefs



Small effects, but at very low cost and for a program already running at national scale.

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Effects Shrink at Scale: Why?


Who delivers: researchers and trained professionals vs. existing government workers with many other duties
Fidelity and dosage: fewer visits, less supervision, lower attendance
Who is served: Jamaica targeted stunted children; national programs serve broader populations with better counterfactuals
Counterfactual environment: improving home and childcare options reduce the gap a program can close
Follow-up investment: dynamic complementarity says early gains need later investment to persist
Publication and selection: the first famous trials may be those that happened to find large effects

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Exercise: Fadeout in the Model
Let \(\ln\theta_{t+1} = a\ln\theta_t + b\ln I_t\) with \(a = 0.8\).


A program raises \(\ln\theta_1\) by \(0.3\) at age 1 and nothing else changes. What is the effect on \(\ln\theta_4\)?
Now suppose parents respond to the higher \(\theta\) by reducing investment: \(\ln I_t\) falls by \(0.1\times\) the gain in \(\ln\theta_t\), with \(b = 0.3\). Recompute the effect on \(\ln\theta_4\).
Suppose instead parents learn from the program and permanently raise \(\ln I_t\) by \(0.1\). Recompute.
Which case looks like Colombia? Which looks like Jamaica?

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
What Have We Learned?


Small, intensive programs (Perry, ABC/CARE, Jamaica) have large long-run returns, even when test scores fade
Rates of return are high: about 7–10% for Perry, about 14% for ABC/CARE
The counterfactual matters: estimated effects and costs depend on what control children would have received
Test scores are not the whole story: Boston pre-K and Perry show long-run gains without lasting test score gains
Scale is hard: effects shrink when programs are delivered by existing systems to broad populations, and in Tennessee they were negative
Parental investment is a key mechanism, consistent with the skill formation model

title: Connecting Theory with Evidence: Early Childhood Education and Parenting
text:
Remaining Questions


Which features of high-quality programs matter most? Timing, intensity, curriculum, staff?
How do we design programs that keep working at scale?
How should we forecast long-run benefits when we only observe short-run outcomes?
How do we measure the skills that matter? (Next time)

title: Recitation 2
text: using LinearAlgebra, Plots

title: Recitation 2
text:
Model
Let’s assume that individuals live for \(T\) periods. They face an income process that follows:
\[ \log(y_{it}) = \mu_{t} + \varepsilon_{it} \]
where
\[ \varepsilon_{it} = \rho \varepsilon_{it-1} + \zeta_{it},\ \zeta_{it} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^2_{\zeta}).\]
We assume a single risk-free asset with a rate of return \(r\), so that the model can be phrased recursively:
\[ V_{t}(a,y) = \max_{a^\prime}\left\{u(y + a - (1+r)^{-1}a^\prime) + \beta \mathbb{E}_{y'}V_{t+1}(a',y') \right\} \]
with \(V_{T}=0\).
We assume that utility \(u\) is of the CRRA type, so we can write the function as:

utility(c,σ) = c^(1 - σ) / (1 - σ)

utility (generic function with 1 method)


Note that \(\mu_{t}\) is the mean of log income and can evolve with the age \(t\) of the agent, but this life-cycle profile in wages is known. \(\varepsilon\) is the unknown component of income and the source of risk in the model.

title: Recitation 2
text:
Approximating the income process
There are a number of methods for approximating the AR(1) process for income outlined above using a discrete state Markov process. A popular version is Tauchen’s method. The code below is a function to produce a transition matrix \(\Pi\) and a grid of values that approximates the variance and autocovariance of an AR(1) process.

using Distributions

function tauchen(N, ρ, σ)
    # Unconditional standard deviation of the process
    σ_y = σ / sqrt(1 - ρ^2)

    # Create the grid
    y_max = 3. * σ_y
    y_min = - 3. * σ_y
    grid = range(y_min, y_max, length=N)

    # Step size
    step = (y_max - y_min) / (N - 1)

    # Initialize transition matrix
    Π = zeros(N, N)

    # Standard normal distribution
    d = Normal(0, 1)

    # Fill in the transition matrix
    for i in 1:N
        for j in 1:N
            if j == 1
                # Probability of transitioning to the lowest state
                Π[j, i] = cdf(d, (grid[j] - ρ * grid[i] + step/2) / σ)
            elseif j == N
                # Probability of transitioning to the highest state
                Π[j, i] = 1 - cdf(d, (grid[j] - ρ * grid[i] - step/2) / σ)
            else
                # Probability of transitioning to intermediate states
                Π[j, i] = cdf(d, (grid[j] - ρ * grid[i] + step/2) / σ) -
                         cdf(d, (grid[j] - ρ * grid[i] - step/2) / σ)
            end
        end
    end
    return collect(grid), Π
end

tauchen (generic function with 1 method)


This is going to produce a matrix where \(\Pi[j,i]\) contains the probability of moving to state \(j\) when currently in state \(i\).

title: Recitation 2
text:
Solving the Model
This model can be solved almost identically to the infinite horizon version. We can start by writing a function to solve the maximization problem given a point in the asset and income grid.

function solve_value(ai,yi,V,p,t)
    (;σ,β,Π,r,asset_grid,income_grid) = p
    a = asset_grid[ai]
    y = exp(income_grid[yi,t])
    vmax = -Inf
    amax = 0
    for ai_next in eachindex(asset_grid)
        a_next = asset_grid[ai_next]
        c = y + a - a_next/(1+r)
        if c>0
            @views v = utility(c,σ) + β*dot(Π[:,yi],V[:,ai_next,t+1])
            if v>vmax
                vmax = v
                amax = a_next
            end
        end
    end
    return vmax,amax
end

solve_value (generic function with 1 method)


With this function in hand we can then write a function to iterate over each grid point and calculate \(V_{t}\) given \(V_{t+1}\):

function iterate_value_function!(p,V,A,t)
    for ai in axes(V,2), yi in axes(V,1)
        v,a_next = solve_value(ai,yi,V,p,t)
        V[yi,ai,t] = v
        A[yi,ai,t] = a_next
    end
end

iterate_value_function! (generic function with 1 method)


And finally we can solve the model by doing backward induction from \(T\) down to the first period.

function solve_model(p)
    (;T,Π,asset_grid) = p
    K_a = length(asset_grid)
    K_y = size(Π,1)
    V = zeros(K_y,K_a,T+1)
    A = zeros(K_y,K_a,T)
    for t in reverse(1:T)
        iterate_value_function!(p,V,A,t)
    end
    return (;V,A)
end

solve_model (generic function with 1 method)

title: Recitation 2
text:
An example solution
Let’s solve this model and take a look at the optimal savings policy.

model = solve_model(p)
(;V,A) = model

plot(p.asset_grid,A[1,:,1],label = "Low shock, period 1")
plot!(p.asset_grid,A[5,:,1],label = "High shock, period 1")
plot!(p.asset_grid,A[5,:,30],label = "High shock, period 30")
plot!(p.asset_grid,A[1,:,30],label = "Low shock, period 30")
plot!(p.asset_grid,A[1,:,55],label = "Low shock, period 55")
plot!(p.asset_grid,A[5,:,55],label = "High shock, period 55")




  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  








































Can you interpret what is going on here?

title: Recitation 2
text:
The stationary distribution
To compare welfare across economies we need to know where people start. We will assume that the initial draw of \(\varepsilon\) comes from the stationary distribution of \(\Pi\): the distribution \(\pi^*\) that satisfies \(\Pi\pi^* = \pi^*\). In words, if the population is distributed according to \(\pi^*\) today, it will still be distributed according to \(\pi^*\) tomorrow. Linear algebra tells us that \(\pi^*\) is the eigenvector of \(\Pi\) associated with the eigenvalue equal to one (rescaled so that it sums to one):

function solve_steady_state(Π)
    vals, e = eigen(Π)
    k = argmin(abs.(vals .- 1))   # eigenvalue closest to one
    v = real.(e[:, k])
    return v ./ sum(v)
end

pi_star = solve_steady_state(Π)

title: Recitation 2
text:
Calculating welfare effects
Let’s assume that everyone starts off with no assets, and then consider the welfare effects of differences in \(\rho\). In particular let’s let the persistence of \(\rho\) decline and see what happens.
We need to be careful here. If we lower \(\rho\) but keep \(\sigma_{\zeta}\) the same, the unconditional variance of \(\varepsilon\), \(\sigma^2_{\zeta}/(1-\rho^2)\), also falls. We would then be changing two things at once: how persistent shocks are and how much total risk there is. To isolate the role of persistence, we hold the unconditional variance fixed at its value when \(\rho=0.9\) and adjust \(\sigma_{\zeta}\):
\[ \sigma_{\zeta}(\rho) = \sigma_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{1-\rho^2},\qquad \sigma_{\varepsilon} = \frac{0.1}{\sqrt{1-0.9^2}}.\]

σ_ε = 0.1 / sqrt(1 - 0.9^2)    #<- unconditional SD of ε, held fixed
ρ2 = 0.45                        #<- move ρ from 0.9 to 0.45
egrid2,Π2 = tauchen(5,ρ2,σ_ε*sqrt(1-ρ2^2))
income_grid2 = [μ+egrid2[i] for i in 1:5, t in 1:T]
p2 = (;p...,income_grid = income_grid2,Π = Π2)
model2 = solve_model(p2)
pi_star2 = solve_steady_state(Π2)

title: Recitation 2
text:
Consumption equivalents
Values are in arbitrary units (“utils”). How can we convert them to something interpretable? One option is to think about a consumption equivalent: the percentage increase in consumption, in every period and every state, that would make someone in one economy as well off as in another.
Let \(W = \sum_{y}\pi^*(y)V_{0}(0,y)\) be expected lifetime utility for someone who starts with zero assets and draws initial income from the stationary distribution. Since each economy has its own \(\pi^*\) (and, in general, its own income grid), this average is the right object to compare. The consumption equivalent \(\omega\) solves:
\[ \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\beta^{t}u((1+\omega)c_{t}) \Big| \rho = 0.9\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\beta^{t}u(c_{t}) \Big| \rho = 0.45\right] \]
where expectations are taken over the initial draw from \(\pi^*\) as well as over future shocks. Since \(u((1+\omega)c) = (1+\omega)^{1-\sigma}u(c)\) with CRRA utility, this solves out to:
\[ 1+\omega = \left[\frac{W(\rho = 0.45)}{W(\rho = 0.9)}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)}.\]

(;σ,β) = p
W1 = dot(pi_star, model.V[:,1,1])
W2 = dot(pi_star2, model2.V[:,1,1])
ω = (W2 / W1)^(1/(1-σ)) - 1
println("Consumption equivalent of moving from ρ = 0.9 to ρ = 0.45: ", round(100ω, digits=2), "%")

Consumption equivalent of moving from ρ = 0.9 to ρ = 0.45: 4.0%


Spend some time interpreting this! Why does decreasing \(\rho\) (holding total variance fixed) have this effect on welfare?

Who gains the most?
Because we held the unconditional variance fixed, both economies use exactly the same income grid (check egrid and egrid2). This means we can also compare people who start at the same initial income \(y\). The consumption equivalent conditional on initial income solves the same equation without averaging over \(y\):
\[ \omega(y) = \left[\frac{V_{0}(0,y ; \rho = 0.45)}{V_{0}(0,y ; \rho = 0.9)}\right]^{1/(1-\sigma)} - 1 \]

cev = (model2.V[:,1,1] ./ model.V[:,1,1]) .^ (1/(1 - σ)) .- 1
plot(exp.(μ .+ egrid), 100cev, marker = :circle, legend = false,
    xlabel = "Initial income", ylabel = "Consumption equivalent (%)")




  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  

































println("Lowest initial income:  ", round(100cev[1], digits=1), "%")
println("Highest initial income: ", round(100cev[end], digits=1), "%")

Lowest initial income:  30.2%
Highest initial income: -18.3%


Individuals who begin at the lowest level of \(\varepsilon\) gain a lot from lower persistence: their bad luck is less likely to last. Those who begin at the top lose, since their good luck is also less likely to last. Note that this state-by-state comparison is only meaningful because the two grids coincide; if we had changed \(\rho\) without adjusting \(\sigma_{\zeta}\), state \(i\) would correspond to a different income level in each economy.

title: Recitation 4
text:
Loading and Exploring the Data
The data come from the PSID and contain information on household income \(y\) (in dollars) over the life cycle. Let’s start by loading the data and examining some basic patterns.
Two cleaning steps matter a lot here:

Trimming. A small number of household-years report income of $1 (or close to it). In logs these observations are extreme outliers: \(\log(1) = 0\) while median log income is about 11. Even a few dozen of them substantially inflate the variance of log income. We use a simple rule: drop household-years with income below $1,000. This removes only a few dozen of the roughly 19,000 observations.
Units. We measure income in thousands of dollars. This has no effect on variances or covariances of log income, but it matters for the model: the asset grid below is also in thousands of dollars, and the two must be in the same units.


d = @chain CSV.read("../data/abb_aea_data.csv", DataFrame) begin
    @subset :y .>= 1000          #<- trimming rule: drop incomes below $1,000
    @transform :y = :y ./ 1000   #<- income in thousands of dollars
    @transform :logy = log.(:y)
end;

The function load_psid in income_tools.jl performs exactly these steps. Exercise: re-run the analysis below without the trimming step and see how much the variance of log income and the estimated persistence change.
First, let’s look at how the variance of log income evolves with age:

var_by_age = @chain d begin
    groupby(:age)
    @combine begin
        :var_logy = var(:logy)
        :mean_logy = mean(:logy)
        :n = length(:y)
    end
    @subset :n .> 100
end

@df var_by_age plot(:age, :var_logy,
    xlabel="Age",
    ylabel="Variance of log income",
    title="Life-Cycle Profile of Income Variance",
    legend=false,
    linewidth=2)




  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  

























The variance of log income increases substantially over the life cycle. This is consistent with income shocks being persistent: the variance accumulates as people age.

title: Recitation 4
text:
Calculating Autocovariances
To understand the persistence of income shocks, we need to calculate the covariance of income at different lags. The code below constructs forward lags and calculates covariances (forward_lag is also saved in income_tools.jl).

# construct forward-lags
function forward_lag(d, l, var)
    d_lag = @chain d begin
        @select :person :year $var
        @transform :year = :year .- l
        @rename $(Symbol(var,"_",l)) = $var
    end
    d = leftjoin(d, d_lag, on=[:person,:year])
    return d
end

d = forward_lag(d, 2, :logy);
d = forward_lag(d, 4, :logy);
d = forward_lag(d, 6, :logy);

Now let’s calculate the covariances at different lags:

# Covariance of log income with itself at different lags
cov_data = pairwise(cov, eachcol(d[!,[:logy,:logy_2,:logy_4,:logy_6]]),
                    skipmissing = :pairwise)

# Extract covariances with current log income
lag = [0, 2, 4, 6]
cov_lag = cov_data[:,1]

display(DataFrame(lag = lag, covariance = cov_lag))

# Plot the covariance function

    xlabel="Lag (years)",

    title="Autocovariance Function of Log Income",

title: Recitation 4
text:
Calibrating an AR(1) Process
Now suppose that income in the model follows an AR(1) process:
\[ y_{it} = \mu_{t} + \varepsilon_{it} \]
where:
\[ \varepsilon_{t+1} = \rho \varepsilon_t + \zeta_{t+1}, \quad \zeta_{t+1} \sim N(0, \sigma^2_\zeta) \]
We can construct the residuals \(\varepsilon\) by first de-meaning by age. We take lags as well:

d = @chain d begin
    groupby(:age)
    @transform :eps = :logy .- mean(:logy)
end

d = forward_lag(d, 2, :eps);
d = forward_lag(d, 4, :eps);
d = forward_lag(d, 6, :eps);

Recall that:
\[ \text{Cov}(\varepsilon_t, \varepsilon_{t+s}) = \rho^{s}\text{Var}(\varepsilon_{t}).\]
This means that there are a multiple ways to estimate the persistence parameter \(\rho\), using different orders of lags.
There are also multiple ways to estimate \(\sigma^2_{\zeta}\). The simplest way is to assume that \(\varepsilon\) is in its stationary distribution which gives:
\[ \text{Var}(\varepsilon_{it}) = \sigma^2_{\zeta} / (1 - \rho^2) .\]
Below is code to calculate the covariance at different lags and estimate \(\rho\) as the mean of three alternative estimators.

cov_lag = pairwise(cov, eachcol(d[!,[:eps,:eps_2,:eps_4,:eps_6]]),
                    skipmissing = :pairwise)[:,1]


# Estimate ρ from the ratio of covariances at different lags
ρ_est_1 = sqrt(cov_lag[2] / cov_lag[1])  # (Cov(t,t+2) / Var(t))^(1/2)
ρ_est_2 = (cov_lag[3] / cov_lag[1])^(1/4)  # (Cov(t,t+4) / Var(t))^(1/4)
ρ_est_3 = (cov_lag[4] / cov_lag[1])^(1/6)  # (Cov(t,t+6) / Var(t))^(1/6)

ρ = mean([ρ_est_1, ρ_est_2, ρ_est_3])

println("Estimated persistence: ρ = ", round(ρ, digits=3))

# Given ρ, we can back out the innovation variance
σ_ε = sqrt(cov_lag[1])  # Unconditional SD
σ_ζ = σ_ε * sqrt(1 - ρ^2)  # Innovation SD

println("Unconditional SD: σ_ε = ", round(σ_ε, digits=3))
println("Innovation SD: σ_ζ = ", round(σ_ζ, digits=3))

Estimated persistence: ρ = 0.897
Unconditional SD: σ_ε = 0.698
Innovation SD: σ_ζ = 0.308


Let’s check how well our calibrated AR(1) matches the empirical covariances:

# Predicted covariances from AR(1)
σ2_ε = σ_ε^2
cov_predicted = [ρ^s * σ2_ε for s in lag]

# Plot comparison
plot(lag, cov_lag,
    label="Data",
    marker=:circle,
    markersize=6,
    linewidth=2,
    xlabel="Lag (years)",
    ylabel="Covariance",
    title="AR(1) Fit to Autocovariance Function")
plot!(lag, cov_predicted,
    label="AR(1) model",
    marker=:square,
    markersize=6,
    linewidth=2,
    linestyle=:dash)




  
    
  



  
    
  



  
    
  














































Notice: the autovariance does not decay as quickly in the data as in the model. Could individual fixed effects explain this pattern?

Model Setup

title: Recitation 4
text:
Setting Up the Calibrated Model
Now we use the calibrated parameters from the data:

# Use calibrated parameters
N_states = 7
egrid, Π = tauchen(N_states, ρ, σ_ζ)

# Model periods: assume working life from age 25 to 65
T = 40
age_start = 25

# Create income grid with age-varying mean
income_grid = zeros(N_states, T)
for t in 1:T
    age = age_start + t - 1
    for i in 1:N_states
        income_grid[i, t] = μ_t[t] + egrid[i]
    end
end

# Plot the income grid to visualize
plot(age_start:(age_start+T-1), exp.(income_grid[1, :]),
    label="Lowest state",
    xlabel="Age",
    ylabel="Income (thousands of dollars)",
    title="Income Paths by Shock State",
    linewidth=2)
plot!(age_start:(age_start+T-1), exp.(income_grid[4, :]),
    label="Middle state",
    linewidth=2)
plot!(age_start:(age_start+T-1), exp.(income_grid[N_states, :]),
    label="Highest state",
    linewidth=2)

title: Recitation 4
text:
Calibrating Progressive Taxation
We need to choose \(\lambda\) to ensure budget balance: average net income must equal average gross income. Since initial shocks are drawn from the stationary distribution \(\pi^*\), the distribution of \(\varepsilon\) is \(\pi^*\) at every age. But mean income \(\mu_{t}\) changes with age, and with a progressive tax the same \(\lambda\) cannot balance the budget at every age: a \(\lambda\) chosen for 25-year-olds would take resources away from higher-earning 45-year-olds. So we choose a separate \(\lambda_{t}\) for each age, and let net income depend on age:
\[ \tilde{y}_{t} = \lambda_{t}y^{1-\tau},\qquad \lambda_{t} = \frac{\sum_{y}\pi^*(y)\,y}{\sum_{y}\pi^*(y)\,y^{1-\tau}}\ \text{evaluated at age-}t\text{ incomes}.\]

# Solve for stationary distribution
pi_star = solve_steady_state(p.Π)

# Choose progressivity
τ = 0.2

# Solve for λ_t at each age
λ_t = [solve_lambda(τ, exp.(income_grid[:, t]), pi_star) for t in 1:T]

# Check budget balance at every age: average net income / average gross income
budget = [dot(pi_star, progressive_tax.(exp.(income_grid[:, t]), λ_t[t], τ)) /
          dot(pi_star, exp.(income_grid[:, t])) for t in 1:T]

println("Tax progressivity parameter: τ = ", τ)
println("Range of λ_t over the life cycle: ", round.(extrema(λ_t), digits=3))
println("Net / gross income, min and max over ages: ", round.(extrema(budget), digits=6))

title: Recitation 4
text:
Welfare Decomposition
Following recitation 3 (and the notation from Lecture 2), we decompose the welfare gain \(1+\omega\) into an insurance component \(1+\omega_{I}\) and a redistribution component \(1+\omega_{R}\), with \(1+\omega = (1+\omega_{I})(1+\omega_{R})\):

(;σ, β) = p

# Certainty equivalents by initial income state
cbar0 = cert_equiv(model0.V[:, 1, 1], p)
cbar1 = cert_equiv(model1.V[:, 1, 1], p)

# Average certainty equivalents
Cbar0 = dot(pi_star, cbar0)
Cbar1 = dot(pi_star, cbar1)

# Utilitarian welfare
W0 = dot(pi_star, model0.V[:, 1, 1])
W1 = dot(pi_star, model1.V[:, 1, 1])

# Decomposition
ω = (W1/W0)^(1/(1-σ)) - 1
ω_I = Cbar1 / Cbar0 - 1
ω_R = ((W1 / V_cert(Cbar1, p)) / (W0 / V_cert(Cbar0, p)))^(1/(1-σ)) - 1

println("\nWelfare Decomposition:")
println("=" ^ 50)
println("Total welfare gain (ω):         ", round(ω*100, digits=2), "%")
println("Insurance component (ω_I):      ", round(ω_I*100, digits=2), "%")
println("Redistribution component (ω_R): ", round(ω_R*100, digits=2), "%")
println("\nVerification: (1+ω_I)(1+ω_R) = ", round((1+ω_I)*(1+ω_R), digits=4), " ≈ ", round(1+ω, digits=4))

end
